### 3.3.1 The Problem with Mixed Concerns

Let's examine an early version of BuzzDB to see this problem in practice. In this version, the main `BuzzDB` class is responsible for everything. It manages an in-memory index, holds the collection of pages, and directly manipulates the database file on disk.

Consider the definition and constructor of the `BuzzDB` class before the storage manager was introduced:

```cpp
// Before: BuzzDB manages I/O directly
class BuzzDB {
private:
    std::map<int, std::vector<int>> index;
    std::fstream file; // Direct file handle

public:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>> pages;
    size_t num_pages = 0;

    BuzzDB() {
        // Create file if needed
        std::ifstream infile(database_filename);
        if (infile.good() == false) {
            std::ofstream outfile(database_filename);
        }

        file.open(database_filename, std::ios::in | std::ios::out);
        file.seekg(0, std::ios::end);
        num_pages = file.tellg() / PAGE_SIZE;

        if (num_pages == 0) {
            extendDatabaseFile();
        } else {
            std::cout << "Loading " << num_pages << " pages \n";
            for (size_t page_itr = 0; page_itr < num_pages; page_itr++) {
                auto loadedPage = SlottedPage::deserialize(file, page_itr);
                pages.push_back(std::move(loadedPage));
            }
        }
    }

    void extendDatabaseFile() {
        // ... logic to write an empty page to the file ...
    }
    // ... other methods for queries, insertions, etc. ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.048" chapter="3" section="3.3.1 The Problem with Mixed Concerns" kind="list" -->

The `BuzzDB` class has a `std::fstream file` member, giving it direct control over the database file. The constructor is a complex block of logic that checks if the file exists, creates it if not, opens it, calculates the number of pages based on the file size, and then proceeds to load every single page from disk into the `pages` vector. It even calls a helper method, `extendDatabaseFile`, to grow the file if it's empty.

This design tangles several distinct responsibilities:

1.  **Application Logic:** Managing the `index`.
2.  **Buffer Management:** Holding the collection of in-memory `pages`.
3.  **File Management:** Owning and manipulating the `file` handle.
4.  **I/O Operations:** Reading pages from disk (`SlottedPage::deserialize`) and writing new pages (`extendDatabaseFile`).

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.049" chapter="3" section="3.3.1 The Problem with Mixed Concerns" kind="code" -->

Now, let's look at the same `BuzzDB` class after a crucial refactoring that introduced a `StorageManager`:

```cpp
// After: BuzzDB delegates I/O to a StorageManager
class BuzzDB {
public:
    std::map<int, std::vector<int>> index;
    StorageManager sm; // The storage manager instance

public:
    size_t max_number_of_tuples = 5000;
    size_t tuple_insertion_attempt_counter = 0;

    BuzzDB() {
        // Storage Manager automatically created
    }
    // ... other methods for queries, insertions, etc. ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.050" chapter="3" section="3.3.1 The Problem with Mixed Concerns" kind="prose" -->

The transformation is dramatic. The `BuzzDB` class no longer has a file handle, a `pages` vector, or a `num_pages` counter. All of that has been moved. The constructor is now trivial. The class simply declares a `StorageManager sm;` member. All the complex logic for file creation, opening, sizing, and loading is now encapsulated within the `StorageManager`'s own constructor.

This new design is far superior. The `BuzzDB` class can now focus on its primary responsibilities: managing the index and executing queries. When it needs a page, it doesn't perform the I/O itself. Instead, it makes a simple request to its `sm` member, like `sm.load(page_id)`. The `StorageManager` handles the messy details of seeking to the right byte offset and reading the data. This clean separation of concerns makes the code easier to read, test, and evolve.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.051" chapter="3" section="3.3.2 Anatomy of the Storage Manager" kind="code" -->

### 3.3.2 Anatomy of the Storage Manager

The `StorageManager` acts as a gatekeeper for the database file. It is the only component in the system that is allowed to directly read from or write to the file. This centralization of I/O logic is the key to its power. By creating this abstraction, we establish a contract: the rest of the database system interacts with *pages*, while the storage manager is responsible for translating those page-level requests into byte-level operations on a file.

Let's look at the structure of the `StorageManager` in BuzzDB. It contains the state that was previously scattered inside the `BuzzDB` class.

```cpp
class StorageManager {
private:
    const std::string database_filename = "buzz.db";
    std::fstream fileStream;

public:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>> pages;
    size_t num_pages = 0;

    StorageManager() {
        // ... constructor logic to open file and load pages ...
    }

    // ... methods like load, flush, extend ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.052" chapter="3" section="3.3.2 Anatomy of the Storage Manager" kind="list" -->

The key members are:

*   `fileStream`: An `std::fstream` object that holds the open connection to the database file on disk. This is kept private to ensure that no outside component can bypass the storage manager's API.
*   `num_pages`: A counter that tracks the total number of pages in the database file. This is the authoritative source for the database's size.
*   `pages`: A `std::vector` of `SlottedPage` pointers. In this version of BuzzDB, this vector acts as a simple in-memory cache, or **buffer pool**. At startup, it loads every page from the database file into this vector, and all subsequent operations work on these in-memory copies.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.053" chapter="3" section="3.3.2 Anatomy of the Storage Manager" kind="code" -->

The relationship between the main `BuzzDB` engine and the `StorageManager` can be visualized as a clear hierarchy of responsibility.

```
+-----------------+
|     BuzzDB      |
|-----------------|
| - index         |
| - sm            | --owns--> +--------------------+
+-----------------+           |   StorageManager   |
      |                       |--------------------|
      | requests page         | - fileStream       | (private)
      '---------------------> | - num_pages        |
        (e.g., sm.load(5))    | - pages (vector)   |
                              +--------------------+
                                        |
                                        | interacts with
                                        v
                               +------------------+
                               | buzz.db (file)   |
                               +------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.054" chapter="3" section="3.3.2 Anatomy of the Storage Manager" kind="prose" -->

When a `BuzzDB` instance is created, its `sm` member is automatically constructed. The `StorageManager`'s constructor then performs the startup sequence: it opens `buzz.db`, determines how many pages it contains, and populates its `pages` vector by reading the entire file. From that point on, the `BuzzDB` object can operate on the data by asking the `StorageManager` for the pages it needs.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.055" chapter="3" section="3.3.3 Core I/O Primitives: `load` and `flush`" kind="prose" -->

### 3.3.3 Core I/O Primitives: `load` and `flush`

At the heart of the storage manager are two fundamental operations that move data between the disk and main memory: `load` and `flush`. These methods represent the smallest unit of I/O in the database. Every time the system needs to read a page that isn't already in memory or write a modified page back to disk to make it durable, one of these methods will be called.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.056" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="code" -->

#### 3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk

The `load` method is responsible for reading a single page from the database file into a newly allocated block of memory.

```cpp
std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage> load(uint16_t page_id) {
    fileStream.seekg(page_id * PAGE_SIZE, std::ios::beg);
    auto page = std::make_unique<SlottedPage>();
    // Read the content of the file into the page
    if (fileStream.read(page->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE)) {
        // ... success ...
    } else {
        // ... error handling ...
    }
    return page;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.057" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="list" -->

Let's break down this critical operation step-by-step:

1.  **Calculate the Offset:** The first line, `fileStream.seekg(page_id * PAGE_SIZE, std::ios::beg)`, is the most important. It tells the file stream where to start reading. The database file is treated as a contiguous array of pages. To find the starting position of any given page, we use the simple formula:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.058" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="list" -->

`offset = page_id * PAGE_SIZE`

The `seekg` function ("seek get") moves the file's read pointer to this calculated byte offset, measured from the beginning of the file (`std::ios::beg`).

2.  **Allocate Memory:** `auto page = std::make_unique<SlottedPage>();` creates a new `SlottedPage` object on the heap. This object contains a buffer of `PAGE_SIZE` bytes, ready to receive the data from the disk.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.059" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="list" -->

3.  **Perform the Read:** `fileStream.read(page->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE)` executes the actual I/O. It reads exactly `PAGE_SIZE` bytes from the current position in the file (which we set with `seekg`) and copies them directly into the memory buffer of the `SlottedPage` object. This is a single, blocking I/O call.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.060" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="list" -->

4.  **Return the Page:** The method returns the `std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>`, transferring ownership of the newly loaded page to the caller.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.061" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="table" -->

Let's trace a concrete example. Suppose `PAGE_SIZE` is 4096 bytes and the query processor needs to access data on page 3. It would call `sm.load(3)`.

| Step | Action | Calculation/Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Calculate offset | `3 * 4096 = 12288` |
| 2 | Seek file pointer | `fileStream.seekg(12288, ...)` |
| 3 | Allocate buffer | A new 4096-byte buffer is created in memory. |
| 4 | Read from disk | 4096 bytes are read starting from byte 12288 of `buzz.db`. |
| 5 | Return result | A pointer to the in-memory page is returned. |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.062" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.1 Loading a Page from Disk" kind="prose" -->

This `load` primitive is the foundation for all data retrieval. Any time the database needs to access a tuple, it must first identify the `page_id` where that tuple resides and then use `load` to bring that page into memory.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.063" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="code" -->

#### 3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk

The `flush` method is the inverse of `load`. It takes an in-memory page that has been modified and writes its contents back to the corresponding location in the database file, making the changes permanent.

```cpp
void flush(uint16_t page_id) {
    size_t page_offset = page_id * PAGE_SIZE;        

    // Move the write pointer
    fileStream.seekp(page_offset, std::ios::beg);
    fileStream.write(pages[page_id]->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE);        
    fileStream.flush();
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.064" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="list" -->

The process is symmetric to loading:

1.  **Calculate the Offset:** `size_t page_offset = page_id * PAGE_SIZE;` uses the same formula to determine where the page lives in the file.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.065" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="list" -->

2.  **Seek the Write Pointer:** `fileStream.seekp(page_offset, std::ios::beg)` moves the file's *write* pointer (`seekp` for "seek put") to the correct location. It's important that operating systems maintain separate read and write pointers for a file, and here we are explicitly setting the location for the next write.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.066" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="list" -->

3.  **Perform the Write:** `fileStream.write(pages[page_id]->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE)` executes the I/O. It finds the in-memory copy of the page in the `pages` vector, gets a pointer to its raw byte buffer, and writes `PAGE_SIZE` bytes from that buffer to the file. This overwrites the old version of the page on disk.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.067" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="list" -->

4.  **Force to Disk:** `fileStream.flush()` is a crucial final step. Modern operating systems heavily buffer file writes in memory for performance. A call to `write` may only copy the data to an OS buffer, not to the physical disk itself. If the system were to crash before the OS buffer is written, the change would be lost. `fileStream.flush()` requests that the operating system write its buffers for this file to the underlying storage device immediately, providing a guarantee of durability.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.068" chapter="3" section="3.3.3.2 Flushing a Page to Disk" kind="prose" -->

Together, `load` and `flush` form a clean and simple API for moving data. The rest of the database system no longer needs to know about file offsets or I/O buffering; it can simply think in terms of page IDs.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.069" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="code" -->

### 3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method

A database is not a static file; it must be able to grow as new data is inserted. When all existing pages are full, the system needs to allocate a new, empty page. The `StorageManager` is responsible for this process through its `extend` method.

```cpp
void extend() {
    // Create a slotted page
    auto empty_slotted_page = std::make_unique<SlottedPage>();

    // Move the write pointer
    fileStream.seekp(0, std::ios::end);

    // Write the page to the file, extending it
    fileStream.write(empty_slotted_page->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE);
    fileStream.flush();

    // Update number of pages
    num_pages += 1;

    // Load page into memory
    auto page_itr = num_pages - 1;
    auto page(load(page_itr));
    pages.push_back(std::move(page));
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.070" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="list" -->

This method orchestrates the allocation of a new page on disk and integrates it into the storage manager's in-memory state.

1.  **Create an Empty Page:** First, an `empty_slotted_page` is created in memory. This is a `SlottedPage` that has been initialized to a valid but empty state, with its header set up correctly.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.071" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="list" -->

2.  **Seek to the End:** The call `fileStream.seekp(0, std::ios::end)` is the key to growing the file. It moves the write pointer not to a calculated offset, but to the very end of the file.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.072" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="list" -->

3.  **Append the Page:** The `fileStream.write(...)` call now appends the `PAGE_SIZE` bytes of the empty page to the end of the file, increasing its total size. The `flush()` call ensures this extension is durable.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.073" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="list" -->

4.  **Update Metadata:** The storage manager increments its internal `num_pages` counter. This is critical; the manager's view of the database size must remain consistent with the physical file's size.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.074" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="list" -->

5.  **Load into Buffer Pool:** Finally, the newly created page is loaded into the `pages` vector. This ensures that BuzzDB's simple buffer pool, which expects to hold all pages, is kept up-to-date. The new page is now available for use, and the system can begin inserting tuples into it.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.075" chapter="3" section="3.3.4 Growing the Database: The `extend` Method" kind="prose" -->

By centralizing file growth logic in the `extend` method, the `StorageManager` maintains its role as the sole authority on the physical layout of the database. This prevents a scenario where one part of the system tries to write to a page that another part doesn't even know exists. This abstraction is the first step toward building a robust and scalable database storage layer.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.076" chapter="3" section="3.3.4.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

#### 3.3.4.1 Check Your Understanding

1.  **Refactoring for Flexibility:** Suppose you need to change the `PAGE_SIZE` from 4096 to 8192 bytes. In the "after" design with the `StorageManager`, which files and functions would you need to examine and potentially change? How does this compare to the "before" design?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.077" chapter="3" section="3.3.4.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

Explain the risk of this change in the context of a database transaction that a user expects to be permanent once it completes.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.080" chapter="3" section="3.4 The Cost of I/O: A Simple Performance Model" kind="prose" -->

## 3.4 The Cost of I/O: A Simple Performance Model

Imagine you've built the first version of a database system. It can store data, and it can retrieve it. You run a simple query to find a single customer record in a file containing a million customers. You hit "enter," and you wait. And wait. The CPU meter on your machine is barely moving, but the hard drive activity light is blinking furiously. Seconds, maybe even minutes, tick by before the result appears. Why is it so slow? The computer's processor can execute billions of instructions per second, yet this seemingly simple task brings the system to a crawl.

The bottleneck isn't the speed of the processor or the amount of memory. The bottleneck is the enormous time gap between the electronic speed of the CPU and the mechanical slowness of the storage device. To process data, it must first be moved from persistent storage (like a hard disk drive or solid-state drive) into main memory. This journey, called an I/O (Input/Output) operation, is often the most expensive part of any database query. The processor spends most of its time waiting for the data to arrive.

To build efficient database systems, we cannot treat all operations as equal. We must understand the physical realities of data storage and develop a way to measure and compare the performance of our algorithms in terms_of their I/O cost. This section introduces a simple but powerful performance model based on one central idea: in a database, the most important resource to manage is not CPU cycles, but disk access. By learning to count and minimize I/O, we can design systems that are orders of magnitude faster.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.081" chapter="3" section="3.4 The Cost of I/O: A Simple Performance Model" kind="code" -->

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.083" chapter="3" section="3.4.1 The Physics of Disk Access" kind="list" -->

### 3.4.1 The Physics of Disk Access

To understand why I/O is so expensive, we need to look inside a traditional Hard Disk Drive (HDD), which for decades was the primary storage medium for databases. While Solid-State Drives (SSDs) are now common, the design principles developed for HDDs remain profoundly influential, and HDDs are still widely used for cost-effective bulk storage.

An HDD is a mechanical device. It stores data on a set of spinning platters coated with a magnetic material. A read/write head, attached to an actuator arm, moves across the surface of the platters to access the data. Think of it like a sophisticated record player, but with multiple platters and heads, and spinning at thousands of revolutions per minute (RPM).

When the database requests a page of data from a specific location on the disk, the HDD must perform three distinct steps to fulfill the request:

1.  **Seek Time:** The actuator arm must physically move the read/write head from its current position to the correct circular track on the platter. This is a mechanical movement, like a robotic arm swinging into place. It is the slowest part of the process, typically taking several milliseconds (ms).
2.  **Rotational Latency (or Rotational Delay):** Once the head is over the correct track, it must wait for the platter to spin around until the desired data block (or sector) is directly underneath it. On average, this takes half a revolution. For a disk spinning at 7,200 RPM, a full rotation takes about 8.3ms, so the average rotational latency is around 4.15ms. This is another mechanical delay.
3.  **Transfer Time:** Once the head is positioned and the data is spinning underneath it, the data can be read from the magnetic surface and transferred to the system's memory. This part is electronic and is very fast compared to the mechanical delays. The transfer rate depends on the density of the data on the platter and the speed of the connection, but it's typically measured in megabytes per second (MB/s).

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.084" chapter="3" section="3.4.1 The Physics of Disk Access" kind="prose" -->

The total time to read a single, randomly located page from disk is the sum of these three components:

*Time<sub>I/O</sub> = Seek Time + Rotational Latency + Transfer Time*

The crucial insight is that for a single small read, the first two components—the mechanical delays—completely dominate the total time. Reading a 4KB page from a disk with a 100 MB/s transfer rate takes only 0.04ms. If the seek time is 8ms and the rotational latency is 4ms, the total time is `8ms + 4ms + 0.04ms = 12.04ms`. The actual data transfer accounts for less than 0.4% of the total time! The other 99.6% is spent just getting the head to the right place.

We can visualize the breakdown of a single random I/O operation on a timeline:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.085" chapter="3" section="3.4.1 The Physics of Disk Access" kind="code" -->

```
A Single Random I/O Request (e.g., 12.04 ms total)
|--------------------------------| Seek Time (e.g., 8 ms)
                                 |----------------| Rotational Latency (e.g., 4 ms)
                                                  |·| Transfer Time (e.g., 0.04 ms)
|-------------------------------------------------|>
0 ms                                              ~12 ms
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.086" chapter="3" section="3.4.1 The Physics of Disk Access" kind="prose" -->

This diagram makes the disparity clear. The vast majority of the time is spent on mechanical positioning. This physical reality has a profound implication for how we design database software: the number of times we ask the disk to move its head to a new, random location is the primary driver of performance.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.087" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="list" -->

### 3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O

The analysis above explains the cost of reading one page from a random location. But what if we need to read many pages? This is where the distinction between *random I/O* and *sequential I/O* becomes the single most important concept for understanding storage performance.

*   **Random I/O** occurs when we access pages that are scattered across different locations on the disk. To read 100 different pages stored at 100 random locations, the disk must perform 100 separate seek and rotational delay operations. The total time is roughly 100 times the cost of a single random I/O.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.088" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="list" -->

*   **Sequential I/O** occurs when we access pages that are stored contiguously on the disk, one after the other on the same track (or adjacent tracks). To read 100 sequential pages, the disk pays the price of one seek and one rotational delay to get to the *first* page. After that, the remaining 99 pages can be read as they spin under the head, with no additional mechanical delay. The head just stays put and reads a long, continuous stream of data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.089" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="list" -->

Let's quantify this difference with a worked example. Suppose we have a system with the following typical HDD performance characteristics:

*   Average Seek Time: 8 ms
*   Average Rotational Latency: 4 ms
*   Transfer Rate: 100 MB/s
*   Page Size: 4 KB (0.004 MB)

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.090" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="prose" -->

First, let's calculate the transfer time for a single 4 KB page:

*Transfer Time<sub>1 page</sub> = Page Size / Transfer Rate = 0.004 MB / 100 MB/s = 0.00004 s = 0.04 ms*

Now, let's calculate the total time to read 100 pages under two different scenarios.

**Case A: Random I/O**

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.091" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="prose" -->

The 100 pages are located at random positions on the disk. We must perform a full seek and wait for rotational latency for each and every page.

The general formula is:

*Time<sub>Random</sub>(N) = N × (Seek Time + Rotational Latency + Transfer Time<sub>1 page</sub>)*

Plugging in our values for N=100:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.092" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="prose" -->

*Time<sub>Random</sub>(100) = 100 × (8 ms + 4 ms + 0.04 ms)* *Time<sub>Random</sub>(100) = 100 × (12.04 ms)* *Time<sub>Random</sub>(100) = 1204 ms ≈ **1.2 seconds**

**Case B: Sequential I/O**

The 100 pages are stored contiguously. We perform only one seek and one rotational delay for the entire block of pages.

The general formula is:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.093" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="prose" -->

*Time<sub>Sequential</sub>(N) = (Seek Time + Rotational Latency) + N × (Transfer Time<sub>1 page</sub>)*

Plugging in our values for N=100:

*Time<sub>Sequential</sub>(100) = (8 ms + 4 ms) + 100 × (0.04 ms)* *Time<sub>Sequential</sub>(100) = 12 ms + 4 ms* *Time<sub>Sequential</sub>(100) = **16 ms**

The performance difference is staggering.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.094" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="table" -->

| I/O Pattern | Calculation                               | Total Time |
| :---------- | :---------------------------------------- | :--------- |
| Random      | 100 × (8ms + 4ms + 0.04ms)                | 1,204 ms   |
| Sequential  | (8ms + 4ms) + (100 × 0.04ms)              | 16 ms      |
| **Ratio**   | **Random is ~75 times slower**            |            |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.095" chapter="3" section="3.4.2 The Crucial Difference: Random vs. Sequential I/O" kind="prose" -->

Reading the same amount of data sequentially is about 75 times faster than reading it randomly. This isn't a small optimization; it's a fundamental architectural principle. Database systems are designed from the ground up to convert random access patterns into sequential ones whenever possible. This is why we have techniques like indexing, clustering, and careful data placement.

What about SSDs? Solid-State Drives have no moving parts. There are no spinning platters or actuator arms, so seek time and rotational latency are effectively zero. Does this mean the distinction between random and sequential I/O is irrelevant? Not entirely. While the penalty for random access is dramatically lower on an SSD, sequential access is still faster. This is due to the internal architecture of SSDs, which read data in larger blocks, and efficiencies in the operating system's I/O scheduling and device drivers. The performance gap is much smaller than on an HDD, but a well-designed algorithm that favors sequential I/O will still outperform one that doesn't, even on modern hardware.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.096" chapter="3" section="3.4.3 The I/O Cost Model: Counting Pages" kind="prose" -->

### 3.4.3 The I/O Cost Model: Counting Pages

The worked example above shows that we can, in principle, calculate the time for any database operation by modeling the underlying hardware. However, this is cumbersome. The exact values for seek time, latency, and transfer rate vary between devices and change over time. A model that depends on specific hardware parameters is brittle and not very useful for comparing the fundamental efficiency of different algorithms.

We need a simpler, more abstract model. Given that the mechanical delays of seek and latency are the dominant factors in I/O cost on HDDs, and that even on SSDs the number of I/O requests matters, we can make a powerful simplification: **we will estimate the performance of an algorithm by counting the number of pages it transfers to or from the disk.**

This is the **I/O Cost Model**. Instead of measuring time in milliseconds, we measure cost in units of "pages read" and "pages written."

The model's core assumptions are:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.097" chapter="3" section="3.4.3 The I/O Cost Model: Counting Pages" kind="list" -->

1.  The primary bottleneck is I/O. CPU processing time is considered negligible in comparison.
2.  All page transfers (I/Os) have roughly the same cost.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.098" chapter="3" section="3.4.3 The I/O Cost Model: Counting Pages" kind="quote" -->

This model is an abstraction, and it has limitations. It doesn't inherently distinguish between the cost of a random I/O and a sequential I/O. A scan of 100 sequential pages and 100 random page reads are both counted as "100 I/Os." However, when we use the model, we are typically aware of the access pattern. We might analyze the cost of a table scan as *B* sequential I/Os, and the cost of a B-Tree index lookup as *H* random I/Os (where *B* is the number of pages in the table and *H* is the height of the tree). We know the sequential I/Os are cheaper in reality, but the model still allows us to compare the raw number of pages touched, which is an excellent proxy for performance.

The great strength of the I/O cost model is its simplicity and predictive power. If Algorithm A requires 10,000 I/Os to answer a query and Algorithm B requires only 100 I/Os, we can be very confident that Algorithm B will be substantially faster on any storage device, without needing to know anything about the hardware. It allows us to reason about the performance of our designs at a high level and make architectural decisions that will stand the test of time.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> A university database contains a `Students` table with 10 million records. The data is stored in 8 KB pages, and 50 student records fit on each page.
>
> 1.  What is the total number of pages required to store the table?
> 2.  Using the I/O cost model, what is the cost of finding a specific student's record if the only way to do so is to scan the entire table from beginning to end?
> 3.  Suppose we have an index that allows us to find the student's record by performing just 3 I/Os. Which approach is better, and by what factor?
>
> **Answer:**
>
> 1.  Total pages = Total Records / Records per Page = 10,000,000 / 50 = 200,000 pages.
> 2.  The cost of a full table scan is the number of pages in the table. The I/O cost is **200,000 I/Os**. This would be a sequential read.
> 3.  The index approach costs **3 I/Os**. These would likely be random reads. Even so, comparing the raw counts, the index is vastly superior. The scan is 200,000 / 3 ≈ 66,667 times more expensive in terms of page accesses. This is the difference between a query that runs in milliseconds and one that takes many minutes.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.099" chapter="3" section="3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations" kind="code" -->

### 3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations

Now let's apply this I/O cost model to our BuzzDB implementation. The model gives us a vocabulary to analyze the performance of our own code. The fundamental I/O operations in BuzzDB are handled by the `StorageManager`, which provides methods to move pages between memory and the database file on disk.

The two key methods are `load` and `flush`.

```cpp
// in StorageManager
std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage> load(uint16_t page_id) {
    fileStream.seekg(page_id * PAGE_SIZE, std::ios::beg);
    auto page = std::make_unique<SlottedPage>();
    fileStream.read(page->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE);
    // ...
    return page;
}

void flush(uint16_t page_id) {
    size_t page_offset = page_id * PAGE_SIZE;        
    fileStream.seekp(page_offset, std::ios::beg);
    fileStream.write(pages[page_id]->page_data.get(), PAGE_SIZE);        
    fileStream.flush();
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.100" chapter="3" section="3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations" kind="code" -->

In our model, each call to `load(page_id)` represents **one read I/O**. The `seekg` function call positions the file pointer to the start of the requested page, and `read` transfers the data. Similarly, each call to `flush(page_id)` represents **one write I/O**. It seeks to the correct position and writes the page's contents back to the file. These two methods are the primitive operations whose costs we want to count.

With these primitives defined, we can analyze more complex operations. Consider the `scanTableToBuildIndex` method in BuzzDB. This function is designed to read every tuple in the table to construct an in-memory index.

```cpp
// in BuzzDB
void scanTableToBuildIndex(){
    // ...
    for (size_t page_itr = 0; page_itr < sm.num_pages; page_itr++) {
        char* page_buffer = sm.pages[page_itr]->page_data.get();
        // ... process all tuples in the page ...
    }
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.101" chapter="3" section="3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations" kind="prose" -->

The logic here is a straightforward loop that iterates from the first page (`page_itr = 0`) to the last (`sm.num_pages - 1`). In each iteration, it accesses the data for one page. Assuming the `sm.pages` vector was populated by loading each page from disk, this operation performs a full **table scan**.

According to our I/O cost model, the cost of this scan is simply the number of pages in the table.

*Cost<sub>scanTableToBuildIndex</sub> = `sm.num_pages` I/Os*

This is a linear scan. If the table doubles in size, the I/O cost of this operation also doubles. Furthermore, because the pages are accessed in order of their `page_id` (0, 1, 2, ...), this will translate to a highly efficient *sequential I/O* pattern at the physical disk level, assuming the operating system has laid out the file contiguously. This is the most efficient way possible to read the entire contents of a file.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.102" chapter="3" section="3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations" kind="list" -->

Now consider a different operation: inserting a single new tuple and making it durable. The process might involve:

1.  Loading the target page into memory (if it's not already there).
2.  Modifying the page in memory to add the new tuple.
3.  Flushing the modified page back to disk to ensure the change is permanent.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch03.103" chapter="3" section="3.4.4 Analyzing BuzzDB Operations" kind="prose" -->

If the page must be loaded first, the operation costs two I/Os: one `load` and one `flush`. If the page is already in a memory buffer (a topic we will explore in detail later), the only I/O cost to make the write durable is the single `flush` operation. So, the cost of a single, durable insert is **1 write I/O**. If we were to insert 1,000 tuples into 1,000 different pages, this could require 1,000 separate, random write I/Os, which our model has shown to be a very expensive pattern.

By adopting this simple model of counting page transfers, we have gained a powerful tool. We can now look at any function in our database, from a simple insert to a complex query-processing algorithm, and ask the most important performance question: "How many I/Os does this take?" This question will guide our design of more advanced features, from buffer management to indexing and query optimization, as we strive to build a system that is not just correct, but fast.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.001" chapter="4" section="Chapter 4. Pages, Records, and File Organization" kind="prose" -->

# Chapter 4. Pages, Records, and File Organization

This chapter explores how a database moves beyond simple in-memory lists to organize data durably on disk. We'll dissect the internal structure of a data page and see how records are laid out, stored, and managed efficiently within files.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.002" chapter="4" section="4.1 From In--Memory Vectors to On-Disk Pages" kind="prose" -->

## 4.1 From In--Memory Vectors to On-Disk Pages

At its heart, a database table is a collection of records. If you were asked to build a simple table from scratch in a language like C++, your first instinct would likely be to use a standard library container. A dynamic array, like `std::vector`, seems like a perfect fit. It can grow as new records are added, it provides fast access to elements by their position, and it manages its own memory. This is a reasonable and effective strategy for data that lives entirely in memory for the duration of a program's execution.

However, a database management system (DBMS) has a much stricter requirement: **durability**. The data must survive program crashes, reboots, and power outages. This means the canonical copy of the data must live on persistent storage, like a solid-state drive or a hard disk. The system can't just load everything into memory at startup and save it all at shutdown. It must work with data on disk, bringing pieces of it into memory only when needed.

This fundamental shift from an in-memory-first to a disk-first worldview changes everything. The structures that are efficient and convenient for in-memory work are often deeply unsuited for the world of persistent storage. In this world, data is organized into fixed-size blocks called **pages**, which are the smallest unit of transfer between disk and memory. A typical page size is 4 KB, 8 KB, or 16 KB. The challenge is no longer just "how do we store a list of records?" but "how do we arrange records within a fixed-size page so that we can read, write, insert, and delete them efficiently, both on disk and in memory?"

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.005" chapter="4" section="4.1 From In--Memory Vectors to On-Disk Pages" kind="prose" -->

To see why our in-memory intuitions can lead us astray, we will examine an early, simple implementation of a page in BuzzDB. This version uses the very `std::vector` we first considered, revealing the subtle but critical problems that arise when a memory-centric design is tasked with managing persistent data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.006" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="code" -->

### 4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples

Let's look at BuzzDB's initial attempt to model a page of data. The `Page` class is designed to hold a collection of `Tuple` objects, up to a fixed `PAGE_SIZE` limit. The core of its implementation is a standard C++ vector:

```cpp
class Page {
public:
    size_t used_size = 0;
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Tuple>> tuples;
    // ... methods ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.007" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="code" -->

This design is straightforward. The `tuples` vector holds smart pointers to individual tuple objects, and `used_size` tracks the total size of the tuple data to ensure we don't exceed the page's capacity. Adding a new tuple is simple: the `addTuple` method checks if there's enough space and, if so, calls `tuples.push_back()`. For appending records, this is perfectly efficient.

The trouble begins when we need to delete a record. The `deleteTuple` method takes the index of the tuple to be removed and performs the deletion in two steps: it updates the `used_size` and then erases the element from the vector.

```cpp
void deleteTuple(size_t index) {
    // ... bounds check ...

    // Update used_size
    auto& tuple = tuples[index];
    used_size -= tuple->getSize();

    // Remove tuple from page
    auto it = tuples.begin();
    tuples.erase(it + index);
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.008" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="code" -->

The line `tuples.erase(it + index)` hides a significant amount of work. A `std::vector` is implemented as a contiguous block of memory. When an element is removed from the middle, the vector must maintain this contiguity. To do so, it shifts every single element that came after the deleted one to the left, filling the gap.

Imagine a page containing 100 tuples. If we delete the tuple at index 0, the vector must copy the remaining 99 tuples one position earlier in memory. This is an operation whose cost is proportional to the number of elements that need to be moved.

Let's trace this. Suppose our `tuples` vector in memory looks like this, where `T0` through `T4` are pointers to our tuples:

```
Initial State (deleting T1 at index 1):
Index:    0    1    2    3    4
        +----+----+----+----+----+
Vector: | T0 | T1 | T2 | T3 | T4 |
        +----+----+----+----+----+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.009" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="list" -->

Calling `deleteTuple(1)` triggers `tuples.erase(tuples.begin() + 1)`. The vector performs the following work:

1.  Destroys the object at index 1 (`T1`).
2.  Copies the element from index 2 to index 1.
3.  Copies the element from index 3 to index 2.
4.  Copies the element from index 4 to index 3.
5.  Updates its internal size from 5 to 4.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.010" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="code" -->

```
Final State:
Index:    0    1    2    3
        +----+----+----+----+
Vector: | T0 | T2 | T3 | T4 |
        +----+----+----+----+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.011" chapter="4" section="4.1.1 The Problem with a Simple List of Tuples" kind="prose" -->

This shifting is expensive, but it's only half the problem. The real issue is that this entire model is disconnected from the on-disk reality. The `std::vector` is a purely in-memory abstraction. To make the deletion permanent, the entire, modified page must be written back to the file. The `write` method in this version of BuzzDB does exactly that: it iterates through the *current* state of the in-memory vector and serializes each tuple to a file.

This design forces a costly choice: either our deletions are not durable, or every single deletion requires rewriting an entire 4 KB or 8 KB page to disk, even to remove a tiny 10-byte record.

A more disk-friendly approach avoids physically moving data. Instead of `erase`, we could simply mark the record as invalid. We could add a small header to each record on the page that contains a "valid" bit. A deletion would then become an O(1) operation: find the record and flip its bit from 1 to 0. The data remains in place, but the system knows to ignore it. The space it occupies can be reclaimed later, perhaps when a new record of a similar size needs to be inserted. This "tombstone" approach is far more suitable for page-based storage, as it minimizes the amount of I/O needed to perform small modifications.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.012" chapter="4" section="4.1.2 The Durability Dilemma" kind="code" -->

### 4.1.2 The Durability Dilemma

The conceptual inefficiency of the `std::vector` design leads to a critical, show-stopping bug related to durability. Because the in-memory representation is so different from a format that can be efficiently modified on disk, the v010 BuzzDB implementation doesn't even try to persist changes. The `deleteTuple` method modifies the in-memory `Page` object, but it never writes those changes back to the file.

The `main` function of the program demonstrates this failure perfectly:

```cpp
   304	    // Deserialize from disk
   305	    auto loadedPage = Page::deserialize(filename);
   306	
   307	    // PROBLEM: Deletion only in memory, not on disk
   308	    loadedPage->deleteTuple(0);
   309	
   310	    // Deserialize again from disk -- page unchanged
   311	    auto loadedPage2 = Page::deserialize(filename);
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.013" chapter="4" section="4.1.2 The Durability Dilemma" kind="list" -->

Let's walk through what happens at runtime:

1.  **Line 305**: `Page::deserialize` is called. It opens the file, reads the number of tuples, and then reads each tuple's data, constructing a new `Page` object in memory. Let's say the file contains three tuples: (Alice, 100), (Bob, 200), (Charlie, 300). The `loadedPage->tuples` vector now holds these three records.
2.  **Line 308**: `loadedPage->deleteTuple(0)` is called. The code finds the first tuple, (Alice, 100), and removes it from the in-memory vector. The `loadedPage->tuples` vector now contains only two records: (Bob, 200) and (Charlie, 300). The on-disk file, however, has not been touched. It still contains all three original records.
3.  **Line 311**: `Page::deserialize` is called *again*. It opens the very same file, which is still in its original state. It reads the tuple count (three) and proceeds to load (Alice, 100), (Bob, 200), and (Charlie, 300) into a *second* `Page` object, `loadedPage2`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.014" chapter="4" section="4.1.2 The Durability Dilemma" kind="prose" -->

From the program's perspective, the tuple for Alice has magically reappeared. The deletion was an illusion, a temporary change to a local, in-memory copy of the data. This violates the core promise of a database.

To fix this, one might be tempted to add a call to `page->write()` at the end of `deleteTuple`. While this would make the deletion durable, it would do so at an enormous performance cost. As we saw, `write` serializes the entire vector. Deleting one tuple would mean rewriting the whole page to disk. If you deleted 100 separate tuples, you would rewrite the entire page 100 times!

This dilemma reveals a foundational principle of database storage design: the in-memory format of a page must closely mirror its on-disk layout. The page should be treated as a block of bytes that can be read from disk into a memory buffer, modified directly in that buffer, and then written back to disk. An abstraction like `std::vector`, which hides the byte-level layout and encourages expensive, whole-object rewrites, is fundamentally at odds with this principle.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.015" chapter="4" section="4.1.3 Goals for a Page Format" kind="table" -->

### 4.1.3 Goals for a Page Format

The failures of the simple vector-based approach teach us what a robust on-disk page format must achieve. We can distill our observations into a set of clear design goals that will guide us toward a better solution.

| Feature | Pros (v010 `std::vector` approach) | Cons (v010 `std::vector` approach) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Simplicity** | Easy to implement and understand using standard library components. | Hides the complexity of on-disk layout, leading to incorrect assumptions about performance and durability. |
| **Deletion** | — | Inefficient in-memory operation (O(N) data shifting). Requires rewriting the entire page to persist. |
| **Insertion** | Efficient for appends (`push_back`). | Requires rewriting the entire page to persist any change. |
| **Space Mgmt** | Handled automatically in memory by the vector. | Poor on-disk space reuse after deletions. Leads to fragmentation unless the entire page is rewritten. |
| **Durability** | — | Not durable by default. Operations are in-memory only. Persisting changes is inefficient (full page rewrite). |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.016" chapter="4" section="4.1.3 Goals for a Page Format" kind="list" -->

Based on these shortcomings, we can define the goals for a professional-grade page format:

1.  **Efficient Record Operations:** Inserts, updates, and especially deletes of records should be fast. A deletion should not require shifting large amounts of data within the page. It should be an O(1) operation in terms of page modification, though finding the record might take longer.
2.  **Good Space Utilization:** The format must be able to reclaim the space freed by deleted records. When a new record is inserted, the page should be able to use any available free space "holes" to avoid growing the file unnecessarily. This minimizes wasted space, or *internal fragmentation*.
3.  **Support for Variable-Length Data:** Real-world data is rarely fixed-size. A page format must elegantly handle records of different lengths without creating large pockets of unusable space or requiring expensive reorganization.
4.  **Direct On-Disk Mapping:** The in-memory data structure for a page should be a direct reflection of its on-disk byte layout. This allows the database to read a page from disk into a memory buffer, operate on the bytes in that buffer, and write the buffer back to disk with minimal translation overhead.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.017" chapter="4" section="4.1.3 Goals for a Page Format" kind="quote" -->

These goals point toward a structure that is more deliberate and lower-level than a generic container like `std::vector`. We need to manage the bytes within the page ourselves, keeping track of where records are, where the free space is, and how many records we have. In the next section, we will examine the **slotted page** architecture, a classic and widely-used design that directly addresses all of these goals.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> 1.  **Performance Cost:** Suppose a page is 4096 bytes. It is currently holding 200 tuples, each of which is 20 bytes long. Using the v010 `Page` implementation, you call `deleteTuple(0)`. Approximately how many bytes of tuple data must be shifted within the in-memory `std::vector` to fill the gap? What if you called `deleteTuple(199)` (the last tuple) instead?
>
> 2.  **Design Fix:** How would you modify the v010 `Page` class to fix the durability bug where deletions are not saved to disk? Write down the one or two lines of code you would add and identify which method they would go in. What is the primary performance drawback of your fix?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.018" chapter="4" section="4.2 The Slotted Page: A Flexible Page Layout" kind="prose" -->

## 4.2 The Slotted Page: A Flexible Page Layout

In our initial, simplified database, we treated a page of data much like an in-memory `std::vector`. This was a convenient starting point, allowing us to `push_back` new records and manage them with familiar tools. However, this convenience hides significant problems that arise the moment we move from a transient, in-memory model to a persistent, on-disk one. A database must be able to store records of varying sizes—think of a user profile with a short username versus one with a long bio—and it must handle insertions and deletions efficiently, even in the middle of a massive file.

The `std::vector` approach fails on both counts. First, to handle variable-sized records, our `vector` stored pointers (`std::unique_ptr<Tuple>`), but memory addresses are meaningless once the program terminates and the data is written to disk. We need a way to manage raw bytes directly. Second, deleting an element from the middle of a vector is notoriously inefficient. An operation like `vector::erase` requires shifting every subsequent element to close the gap, an operation that translates into a cascade of expensive disk I/O. Imagine deleting a single 100-byte record and having to rewrite the next 4 kilobytes of data just to keep the array contiguous.

To build a robust storage manager, we need a page format designed from the ground up for on-disk life. It must be able to manage variable-sized records within a fixed-size page and support fast, localized deletions without catastrophic performance penalties. The industry-standard solution to this challenge is a page layout known as the **slotted page**. This design introduces a small amount of overhead in the form of a directory, but in return, it provides the flexibility and performance necessary for a real database system.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.019" chapter="4" section="4.2 The Slotted Page: A Flexible Page Layout" kind="code" -->

#### `SlottedPage` in `14-buzzdb.cpp:166-186`

The definitions for the `Slot` struct and the `SlottedPage` class, including its constructor which initializes the slot directory.

```cpp
166	struct Slot {
   167	    bool empty = true;                 // Is the slot empty?    
   168	    uint16_t offset = INVALID_VALUE;    // Offset of the slot within the page
   169	    uint16_t length = INVALID_VALUE;    // Length of the slot
   170	};
   171	
   172	// Slotted Page class
   173	class SlottedPage {
   174	public:
   175	    std::unique_ptr<char[]> page_data = std::make_unique<char[]>(PAGE_SIZE);
   176	    size_t metadata_size = sizeof(Slot) * MAX_SLOTS;
   177	
   178	    SlottedPage(){
   179	        // Empty page -> initialize slot array inside page
   180	        Slot* slot_array = reinterpret_cast<Slot*>(page_data.get());
   181	        for (size_t slot_itr = 0; slot_itr < MAX_SLOTS; slot_itr++) {
   182	            slot_array[slot_itr].empty = true;
   183	            slot_array[slot_itr].offset = INVALID_VALUE;
   184	            slot_array[slot_itr].length = INVALID_VALUE;
   185	        }
   186	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.020" chapter="4" section="4.2 The Slotted Page: A Flexible Page Layout" kind="code" -->

#### `SlottedPage::addTuple` in `14-buzzdb.cpp:188-252`

The implementation of tuple insertion in a slotted page, showing how it finds an empty slot and copies serialized data into the page buffer.

```cpp
188	    // Add a tuple, returns true if it fits, false otherwise.
   189	    bool addTuple(std::unique_ptr<Tuple> tuple) {
   190	
   191	        // Serialize the tuple into a char array
   192	        auto serializedTuple = tuple->serialize();
   193	        size_t tuple_size = serializedTuple.size();
   194	
   195	        //std::cout << "Tuple size: " << tuple_size << " bytes\n";
   196	        assert(tuple_size == 38);
   197	
   198	        // Check for first slot with enough space
   199	        size_t slot_itr = 0;
   200	        Slot* slot_array = reinterpret_cast<Slot*>(page_data.get());        
   201	        for (; slot_itr < MAX_SLOTS; slot_itr++) {
   202	            if (slot_array[slot_itr].empty == true and 
   203	                slot_array[slot_itr].length >= tuple_size) {
   204	                break;
   205	            }
   206	        }
   207	        if (slot_itr == MAX_SLOTS){
   208	            //std::cout << "Page does not contain an empty slot with sufficient space to store the tuple.";
   209	            return false;
   210	        }
   211	
   212	        // Identify the offset where the tuple will be placed in the page
   213	        // Update slot meta-data if needed
   214	        slot_array[slot_itr].empty = false;
   215	        size_t offset = INVALID_VALUE;
   216	        if (slot_array[slot_itr].offset == INVALID_VALUE){
   217	            if(slot_itr != 0){
   218	                auto prev_slot_offset = slot_array[slot_itr - 1].offset;
   219	                auto prev_slot_length = slot_array[slot_itr - 1].length;
   220	                offset = prev_slot_offset + prev_slot_length;
   221	            }
   222	            else{
   223	                offset = metadata_size;
   224	            }
   225	
   226	            slot_array[slot_itr].offset = offset;
   227	        }
   228	        else{
   229	            offset = slot_array[slot_itr].offset;
   230	        }
   231	
   232	        if(offset + tuple_size >= PAGE_SIZE){
   233	            slot_array[slot_itr].empty = true;
   234	            slot_array[slot_itr].offset = INVALID_VALUE;
   235	            return false;
   236	        }
   237	
   238	        assert(offset != INVALID_VALUE);
   239	        assert(offset >= metadata_size);
   240	        assert(offset + tuple_size < PAGE_SIZE);
   241	
   242	        if (slot_array[slot_itr].length == INVALID_VALUE){
   243	            slot_array[slot_itr].length = tuple_size;
   244	        }
   245	
   246	        // Copy serialized data into the page
   247	        std::memcpy(page_data.get() + offset, 
   248	                    serializedTuple.c_str(), 
   249	                    tuple_size);
   250	
   251	        return true;
   252	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch04.021" chapter="4" section="4.2 The Slotted Page: A Flexible Page Layout" kind="code" -->

#### `SlottedPage::deleteTuple` in `14-buzzdb.cpp:254-266`

The implementation of tuple deletion, which simply marks a slot as empty. This is a key contrast to the inefficient vector-based deletion in v010.

```cpp

   255	        Slot* slot_array = reinterpret_cast<Slot*>(page_data.get());
   256	        size_t slot_itr = 0;
   257	        for (; slot_itr < MAX_SLOTS; slot_itr++) {
   258	            if(slot_itr == index and
   259	               slot_array[slot_itr].empty == false){
   260	                slot_array[slot_itr].empty = true;
   261	                break;
   262	               }
   263	        }
   264	
   265	        //std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));
   266	    }
```

#### `Page` in `10-buzzdb.cpp:148-221`

The v010 Page class, which uses a std::vector to store tuples. This simple design is used to motivate the need for a more robust on-disk format.
