<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.111" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="code" -->

### 5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple

One of the most fundamental database operations is inserting a new record. In BuzzDB, this is handled by the `try_to_insert` method, which finds a page with enough free space and adds a new tuple to it. Let's compare how this operation was implemented in v014, before the buffer manager, with its implementation in v015, after the buffer manager was integrated.

In v014, the `BuzzDB` class directly owned a `StorageManager` instance. This `StorageManager` was responsible for loading the entire table from disk into a `std::vector` of `Page` objects upon startup.

```cpp
// v014 BuzzDB class definition
class BuzzDB {
public:
    // ...
    StorageManager sm;
    // ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.112" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="code" -->

When `try_to_insert` needed to access a page, it simply indexed into this public vector:

```cpp
// v014 try_to_insert snippet
status = sm.pages[page_itr]->addTuple(std::move(newTuple));
if (status == true){
    sm.flush(page_itr);
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.113" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="code" -->

This code is direct and easy to understand, but it's built on a shaky foundation. The expression `sm.pages[page_itr]` assumes that all pages are resident in memory and directly accessible. If the database file contains more pages than can fit in RAM, this design simply won't work. Furthermore, after the tuple is added, the code must explicitly tell the `StorageManager` to `flush` that specific page back to disk to make the change durable.

Now, consider the v015 implementation. The `BuzzDB` class has undergone a significant architectural change. It no longer owns a `StorageManager`; instead, it owns a `BufferManager`.

```cpp
// v015 BuzzDB class definition
class BuzzDB {
public:
    // ...
    BufferManager buffer_manager;
    // ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.114" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="code" -->

This change propagates to the `try_to_insert` method. The logic of finding a page and adding a tuple remains the same, but the mechanism for accessing the page is completely different.

```cpp
// v015 try_to_insert snippet
auto& page = buffer_manager.getPage(page_itr);

status = page->addTuple(std::move(newTuple));
if (status == true){
    buffer_manager.flushPage(page_itr);
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.115" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="code" -->

Let's look at the two versions side-by-side to appreciate the change.

```diff
--- a/14-buzzdb.cpp
+++ b/15-buzzdb.cpp
-            status = sm.pages[page_itr]->addTuple(std::move(newTuple));
-            if (status == true){
-                sm.flush(page_itr);
-            }
+            auto& page = buffer_manager.getPage(page_itr);
+
+            status = page->addTuple(std::move(newTuple));
+            if (status == true){
+                buffer_manager.flushPage(page_itr);
+            }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.116" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="list" -->

The call to `sm.pages[page_itr]` has been replaced by `buffer_manager.getPage(page_itr)`. This is not just a renaming. The new call is a request, not a direct memory access. When `getPage` is called, the `BufferManager` performs a complex sequence of actions that we explored in the previous section:

1.  It checks if the requested page is already in one of its buffer pool frames.
2.  If it is (a cache hit), it pins the page and returns a reference to it.
3.  If it is not (a cache miss), it finds a victim frame to evict (using its LRU policy), writes the victim to disk if it's dirty, reads the requested page from disk into the newly freed frame, pins the new page, and returns a reference.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.117" chapter="5" section="5.5.1 Before and After: Inserting a Tuple" kind="prose" -->

The client code in `try_to_insert` is completely shielded from this complexity. It simply asks for a page and receives one. The responsibility for I/O, caching, and memory management is now neatly encapsulated within the `BufferManager`. Similarly, the call to `sm.flush` is replaced by `buffer_manager.flushPage`. The `BufferManager` is now the sole component responsible for writing pages to disk, ensuring that all I/O operations are managed centrally.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.118" chapter="5" section="5.5.2 Impact on Table Scans" kind="table" -->

### 5.5.2 Impact on Table Scans

The benefits of the buffer manager are clear for single-page operations like our tuple insertion example. But what happens when an operation needs to access many different pages in a short amount of time? A full table scan, where the system reads every page of a table in sequence, is a perfect test case. This operation is common for queries without a suitable index, for building a new index, or for performing aggregate calculations.

In BuzzDB, the `scanTableToBuildIndex` method performs exactly this kind of sequential scan. It iterates through every page ID from 0 to `N-1`, where `N` is the total number of pages in the table, requesting each page from the buffer manager to read its tuples. Let's analyze the performance of this access pattern (`P_0, P_1, P_2, ... P_{N-1}`) when the table is larger than the buffer pool.

Consider a scenario with a buffer pool that can hold 4 pages (i.e., it has 4 frames) and a table that occupies 10 pages on disk. The `scanTableToBuildIndex` method will request pages 0 through 9 in order. Let's trace the state of the buffer pool, which uses an LRU replacement policy.

| Step | Page Request | Buffer Pool State (MRU → LRU) | Hit/Miss | Page Evicted |
| :--- | :----------- | :---------------------------- | :------- | :----------- |
| 1    | `P_0`        | `[P_0]`                       | Miss     | —            |
| 2    | `P_1`        | `[P_1, P_0]`                  | Miss     | —            |
| 3    | `P_2`        | `[P_2, P_1, P_0]`             | Miss     | —            |
| 4    | `P_3`        | `[P_3, P_2, P_1, P_0]`        | Miss     | —            |
| 5    | `P_4`        | `[P_4, P_3, P_2, P_1]`        | Miss     | `P_0`        |
| 6    | `P_5`        | `[P_5, P_4, P_3, P_2]`        | Miss     | `P_1`        |
| 7    | `P_6`        | `[P_6, P_5, P_4, P_3]`        | Miss     | `P_2`        |
| 8    | `P_7`        | `[P_7, P_6, P_5, P_4]`        | Miss     | `P_3`        |
| 9    | `P_8`        | `[P_8, P_7, P_6, P_5]`        | Miss     | `P_4`        |
| 10   | `P_9`        | `[P_9, P_8, P_7, P_6]`        | Miss     | `P_5`        |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.119" chapter="5" section="5.5.2 Impact on Table Scans" kind="prose" -->

The result is startling: every single page access is a cache miss. The hit rate is 0%. This phenomenon is known as **sequential flooding**. The stream of new, sequentially accessed pages constantly pushes out older pages from the cache. By the time `P_4` is read, `P_0` is the least recently used and is evicted to make room. By the time `P_5` is read, `P_1` is evicted, and so on. Each page is read from disk, used exactly once, and then evicted just before the next page in the sequence is evicted.

The LRU policy, which is highly effective for workloads with good temporal locality (where recently accessed items are likely to be accessed again soon), performs at its worst with this kind of sequential scan. The scan has no temporal locality; each page is accessed once and not needed again for the duration of the scan. The buffer manager churns through pages, performing a disk I/O for every single request, offering no performance benefit over reading directly from the file system.

This pathological behavior for LRU is a well-known problem in database systems. It demonstrates that a "one size fits all" replacement policy is not always optimal. Real-world systems often employ more sophisticated strategies to mitigate sequential flooding. Some systems detect long sequential scans and use a different replacement policy, such as Most Recently Used (MRU), for the pages involved. Others might allocate a small, separate portion of the buffer pool specifically for these scans to avoid polluting the main cache used by other queries. While BuzzDB's current LRU implementation is vulnerable to this issue, its new architecture makes it possible to experiment with and implement these more advanced policies in the future, a topic we will return to in a later chapter.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.120" chapter="5" section="5.5.3 The Benefits of Abstraction" kind="prose" -->

### 5.5.3 The Benefits of Abstraction

The transition from a simple, memory-bound `StorageManager` to a disk-aware `BufferManager` is a pivotal moment in BuzzDB's development. While our analysis of table scans shows that our initial replacement policy has flaws, the architectural benefits of the new design are immense and far-reaching. They touch on correctness, scalability, and maintainability.

First, the `BufferManager` provides a powerful **encapsulation of complexity**. Managing memory, scheduling disk I/O, and ensuring that pages are written back correctly when they are "dirty" are all complex, error-prone tasks. By centralizing this logic within a single component, we reduce the chance of bugs elsewhere in the system. Client code like `try_to_insert` no longer needs to be aware of these details. It operates at a higher level of abstraction, simply requesting the data it needs. This separation of concerns is a hallmark of robust software design.

Second, the new architecture is built for **scalability**. The v014 design had a hard physical limit: the database could be no larger than the machine's RAM. The `BufferManager` shatters this limit. BuzzDB can now process tables that are orders of magnitude larger than the available memory. Performance will depend on the size of the buffer pool and the effectiveness of the replacement policy, but the system is no longer fundamentally constrained. The work of performance tuning is now focused on improving the intelligence of the `BufferManager`, not on rewriting the entire database engine.

Finally, this change promotes **modularity and maintainability**. Because the `BufferManager` presents a clean, stable interface (`getPage`, `flushPage`, etc.), its internal implementation can be changed without affecting the rest of the system. If we decide to replace the LRU policy with a more advanced CLOCK or 2Q algorithm, the code in `try_to_insert` and `scanTableToBuildIndex` remains identical. This modularity makes the system easier to understand, debug, and extend over time.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.121" chapter="5" section="5.5.3 The Benefits of Abstraction" kind="prose" -->

By routing all page requests through a central manager, we have laid the foundation for a true multi-user database system. The `BufferManager` is not just a cache; it is the gatekeeper for all data, a critical component that will enable us to add features like concurrency control and recovery in the future.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch05.122" chapter="5" section="5.5.3.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.001" chapter="6" section="Chapter 6. Replacement Policies and Working Sets" kind="prose" -->

# Chapter 6. Replacement Policies and Working Sets

A simple 'one-size-fits-all' memory management strategy can cripple database performance. This chapter explores how to design a flexible buffer manager by separating the eviction policy from the page-caching mechanism, allowing the system to adapt to different query workloads.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.002" chapter="6" section="6.1 The Limits of a Single Strategy" kind="prose" -->

## 6.1 The Limits of a Single Strategy

A database buffer manager acts as the gatekeeper between the fast, expensive world of main memory and the slow, cavernous realm of disk storage. Its mission is simple to state but complex to execute: keep the most useful data pages in memory to minimize costly disk I/O. When a query requests a page, the buffer manager first checks its in-memory cache, the buffer pool. If the page is present—a "hit"—it can be handed over to the query executor almost instantly. If the page is not in memory—a "miss"—the manager must read it from disk, an operation thousands of times slower.

This process is straightforward until the buffer pool fills up. When a new page must be loaded from disk into a full pool, the buffer manager faces a critical decision: which page currently in memory should be evicted to make room? The logic governing this choice is called the **replacement policy**. It is the heart of the buffer manager's intelligence, and its effectiveness directly impacts the entire system's performance.

The ideal policy would be clairvoyant, evicting the page that will not be needed for the longest time in the future. Since predicting the future is impossible, system designers rely on heuristics that use past behavior to guess future needs. One of the most venerable and intuitive heuristics is the **Least Recently Used (LRU)** policy. It operates on a simple, powerful assumption: pages that have been accessed recently are likely to be accessed again soon. Therefore, when a page must be evicted, LRU chooses the one that has gone the longest without being used.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.004" chapter="6" section="6.1 The Limits of a Single Strategy" kind="prose" -->

For many application workloads, this is a remarkably effective strategy. Yet, as we will see, the structured and often repetitive nature of database query processing can create access patterns that turn LRU's simple assumption into a critical performance liability. A single, rigidly implemented policy, even a classic one like LRU, is often not enough.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.005" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="code" -->

### 6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy

In our first iteration of BuzzDB, the buffer manager's design directly embeds the LRU policy into its core logic. The choice of replacement strategy is not a configurable parameter; it is an inseparable part of the `BufferManager` class itself. This tight coupling is a common starting point in system design, but it reveals its limitations when we need more flexibility.

Let's examine the key components of the v015 `BufferManager` to see how this hardcoded policy works. The manager uses two primary data structures to track the pages in the buffer pool:

```cpp
private:
    using PageID = uint16_t;
    using PageList = std::list<std::pair<PageID, std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>>>;
    using PageMap = std::unordered_map<PageID, typename PageList::iterator>;

    StorageManager storage_manager;
    PageList lruList;
    PageMap pageMap;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.006" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="list" -->

1.  `lruList`: A `std::list` of pairs, where each pair contains a page ID and a pointer to the actual page data. This list maintains the pages in LRU order. The front of the list holds the most recently used page, and the back holds the least recently used page.
2.  `pageMap`: A `std::unordered_map` that maps a page ID to an iterator pointing to that page's entry in the `lruList`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.007" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="code" -->

This two-structure approach is a classic solution to a common trade-off. A linked list like `std::list` is excellent for reordering elements efficiently—we can move a node from the middle to the front in constant time. However, finding an element in a list requires a linear scan, which is far too slow. A hash map like `std::unordered_map` provides fast, near-constant-time lookups. By storing list iterators in the map, we get the best of both worlds: fast lookups via the map, followed by fast reordering via the list.

The entire LRU logic is orchestrated within the `getPage` method. When a page is requested, the manager first checks the `pageMap`.

```cpp
std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>& getPage(int page_id) {
    auto it = pageMap.find(page_id);
    if (it != pageMap.end()) {
        // Page is in the buffer pool (a hit)
        touch(it->second);
        return it->second->second;
    }
    // ... logic for a miss
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.008" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="code" -->

If the page is found (a buffer hit), the manager calls a helper method, `touch`, before returning the page. The `touch` method is responsible for updating the page's status to "most recently used."

```cpp
void touch(typename PageList::iterator it) {
    // Move page to front of list
    lruList.splice(lruList.begin(), lruList, it); 
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.009" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="code" -->

This single line is the core of the LRU bookkeeping on a cache hit. The `std::list::splice` operation is a highly efficient way to move a node from one position in a list to another. It takes the element pointed to by the iterator `it` and moves it to the beginning of `lruList`, all without allocating or deallocating memory. This action perfectly implements the LRU rule: upon access, a page becomes the most recently used.

If the requested page is not in the `pageMap` (a buffer miss), the manager must load it from disk. But first, it checks if the buffer pool is full.

```cpp
    // ... continuing getPage after a miss
    if (lruList.size() >= MAX_PAGES_IN_MEMORY) {
        evict();
    }

    auto page = storage_manager.load(page_id);
    lruList.emplace_front(page_id, std::move(page));
    pageMap[page_id] = lruList.begin();

    return lruList.begin()->second;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.010" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="code" -->

If the pool is full, the `evict` method is called. This method's job is to remove the least recently used page. Given our data structure, this page is always the one at the very back of the `lruList`.

```cpp
void evict() {
    auto last = lruList.end();
    last--; // Get an iterator to the last element
    int evictedPageId = last->first;

    storage_manager.flush(evictedPageId, pageMap[evictedPageId]->second);

    pageMap.erase(evictedPageId);
    lruList.pop_back();
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.011" chapter="6" section="6.1.1 A Hardcoded Policy" kind="prose" -->

The `evict` method identifies the victim page, flushes its contents to disk to ensure durability, and then removes it from both the `pageMap` and the `lruList`. Once space is freed (or if there was space to begin with), the new page is loaded from disk, placed at the front of the `lruList` (making it the new most recently used page), and an entry for it is added to the `pageMap`.

This implementation is clean, correct, and efficient for an LRU policy. However, the policy itself is an assumption baked into every line of the code. The methods are named `touch` and `evict`, but they could have been named `moveToFrontOfLruList` and `evictFromBackOfLruList`. There is no way to ask the `BufferManager` to, for example, evict the *most* recently used page or a randomly selected page without rewriting the class. This lack of abstraction is a ticking time bomb, set to go off when the database encounters a workload that violates LRU's fundamental assumptions.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.012" chapter="6" section="6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan" kind="prose" -->

### 6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan

The central assumption of LRU is **temporal locality**: if a page is accessed, it is likely to be accessed again in the near future. This holds true for many patterns, such as repeatedly accessing a user's profile data or looking up items in a B-Tree index. But what about a query that needs to read every single row in a large table?

Consider a simple SQL query: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales;`. To answer this, the database must perform a **sequential scan**, reading every page of the `sales` table from beginning to end. This access pattern is the nemesis of LRU. When scanning a table, the system reads page 1, then page 2, then page 3, and so on. After reading page `i`, it is immediately done with it and moves on to page `i+1`. Page `i` has no temporal locality; it is not likely to be needed again soon, if ever, during this query.

When a sequential scan operates on a table larger than the buffer pool, a pathological behavior known as **sequential flooding** (or sequential pollution) occurs. The pages from the scan systematically march through the buffer pool, entering at the "most recently used" end and pushing every other page towards the "least recently used" end, until they are evicted. In the process, they flush out potentially valuable pages—like index nodes or metadata pages that have high temporal locality—to make room for scan pages that will be used exactly once.

Let's trace this disaster with a concrete example. Imagine a buffer pool with only four frames and a query that needs to scan a table spanning pages P1 through P7.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.013" chapter="6" section="6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan" kind="list" -->

The initial state of the buffer pool is empty.

`Buffer Pool (MRU -> LRU): [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]`

1.  **Request P1 (Miss):** P1 is loaded from disk and placed at the front.
    `[P1]`
2.  **Request P2 (Miss):** P2 is loaded.
    `[P2, P1]`
3.  **Request P3 (Miss):** P3 is loaded.
    `[P3, P2, P1]`
4.  **Request P4 (Miss):** P4 is loaded. The buffer pool is now full.
    `[P4, P3, P2, P1]`

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.014" chapter="6" section="6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan" kind="list" -->

So far, we have had four misses, which is expected when warming up a cold cache. The problem begins with the next request.

5.  **Request P5 (Miss):** The pool is full. The `evict` method is called. The LRU page is P1, at the back of the list. P1 is evicted, and P5 is loaded at the front.
    `[P5, P4, P3, P2]` (Evicted P1)
6.  **Request P6 (Miss):** The pool is full. The LRU page is now P2. P2 is evicted, and P6 is loaded.
    `[P6, P5, P4, P3]` (Evicted P2)
7.  **Request P7 (Miss):** The pool is full. The LRU page is P3. P3 is evicted, and P7 is loaded.
    `[P7, P6, P5, P4]` (Evicted P3)

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.015" chapter="6" section="6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan" kind="table" -->

The table below summarizes the churn.

| Request | Buffer Pool State (MRU → LRU) | Hit/Miss | Evicted Page |
| :------ | :---------------------------- | :------- | :----------- |
| P1      | `[P1]`                        | Miss     | -            |
| P2      | `[P2, P1]`                    | Miss     | -            |
| P3      | `[P3, P2, P1]`                | Miss     | -            |
| P4      | `[P4, P3, P2, P1]`            | Miss     | -            |
| P5      | `[P5, P4, P3, P2]`            | Miss     | P1           |
| P6      | `[P6, P5, P4, P3]`            | Miss     | P2           |
| P7      | `[P7, P6, P5, P4]`            | Miss     | P3           |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.016" chapter="6" section="6.1.2 When LRU Fails: The Sequential Scan" kind="prose" -->

After the pool fills, every single request results in a miss and an eviction. The hit rate for this portion of the scan is 0%. The buffer pool is doing little more than streaming pages from disk to the CPU, providing almost no caching benefit. Worse, if P1, P2, or P3 were important index pages needed by another concurrent query, they have been needlessly flushed from memory. The sequential scan has polluted the cache with pages that have no reuse value.

This failure mode is a direct consequence of the hardcoded logic in our v015 `BufferManager`. The `touch` method dutifully moves every single scan page to the front of the `lruList`, guaranteeing that they will displace older, potentially more valuable pages. The `evict` method then obediently removes the page at the back, which is exactly the wrong thing to do when the pages at the front have no chance of being reused. The implementation correctly executes a policy that is fundamentally mismatched to the workload.

This single, dramatic failure case demonstrates that a "one size fits all" approach to buffer replacement is insufficient for a general-purpose database system. The system needs to be more intelligent. It could try to detect a sequential scan and treat its pages differently, perhaps by placing them at the LRU end of the list immediately so they are the first to be evicted. Or, it could employ a different policy altogether, one that is more resistant to this kind of pollution.

To enable any of these more advanced solutions, we must first break the tight coupling between the buffer management mechanism and the replacement policy. Our next step will be to refactor the `BufferManager` to delegate the replacement decisions to a separate, swappable strategy object. This will transform our buffer manager from a rigid, single-purpose tool into a flexible framework capable of adapting to the diverse and demanding access patterns of real-world database workloads.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.020" chapter="6" section="6.2 The Strategy Pattern: Separating Mechanism from Policy" kind="prose" -->

## 6.2 The Strategy Pattern: Separating Mechanism from Policy

In our previous exploration of buffer management, we saw a system with a single, fixed approach to page replacement. The BuzzDB v015 `BufferManager` implemented a Least Recently Used (LRU) policy, and this logic was woven directly into its core methods. This design is simple and effective for a specific goal, but it carries a significant hidden cost: inflexibility. What if we discover that for a particular workload, a simple First-In, First-Out (FIFO) policy performs better? Or what if we want to experiment with a more sophisticated algorithm that considers both recency and frequency of access?

With the v015 design, implementing such a change would require invasive surgery on the `BufferManager` class itself. We would need to rip out the `std::list` that tracks the LRU order, replace it with a different data structure, and rewrite the `touch` and `evict` methods to implement the new logic. Changing the policy would mean changing the manager. This tight coupling of the *what* (evicting a page) with the *how* (the specific LRU algorithm) makes the system brittle and difficult to extend.

This is a classic software design challenge. We have a stable component—the buffer manager's mechanism for mapping page IDs to memory frames and handling I/O—and a variable component—the policy for choosing a victim page. The key to a more robust and extensible system is to separate these two concerns. We need a way to define a family of interchangeable eviction algorithms and allow the buffer manager to use one without being permanently tied to its implementation. This is precisely the problem that the **Strategy design pattern** is designed to solve. By encapsulating the eviction algorithm in a separate object, we can transform the `BufferManager` from a component that *is* an LRU manager into a component that *has* a replacement policy, whatever that policy may be.

```cpp
   443	    BufferManager(): policy(std::make_unique<FifoPolicy>()) {}
   444	
   445	    std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>& getPage(int page_id) {
   446	        auto it = pageMap.find(page_id);
   447	        if (it != pageMap.end()) {
   448	            policy->touch(page_id);
   449	            return pageMap.find(page_id)->second;
   450	        }
   451	
   452	        if (pageMap.size() >= MAX_PAGES_IN_MEMORY) {
   453	            auto evictedPageId = policy->evict();
   454	            if(evictedPageId != INVALID_VALUE){
   455	                std::cout << "Evicting page " << evictedPageId << "\n";
   456	                storage_manager.flush(evictedPageId, 
   457	                                      pageMap[evictedPageId]);
   458	            }
   459	        }
   460	
   461	        auto page = storage_manager.load(page_id);
   462	        policy->touch(page_id);
   463	        std::cout << "Loading page: " << page_id << "\n";
   464	        pageMap[page_id] = std::move(page);
   465	        return pageMap[page_id];
   466	    }
   467	
   468	    void flushPage(int page_id) {
   469	        //std::cout << "Flush page " << page_id << "\n";
   470	        storage_manager.flush(page_id, pageMap[page_id]);
   471	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.024" chapter="6" section="6.2.1 An Interface for Eviction" kind="code" -->

### 6.2.1 An Interface for Eviction

The first step in decoupling the policy from the mechanism is to define a clear contract. What, at a minimum, must any replacement policy be able to do? The `BufferManager` needs to interact with a policy in two fundamental ways. First, it needs to inform the policy whenever a page is accessed, as this is the primary signal used by most algorithms. Second, when the buffer pool is full and a new page must be loaded, the manager needs to ask the policy which existing page should be evicted.

BuzzDB v016 introduces this contract as a C++ abstract base class named `Policy`. It is a concise and powerful declaration of these two essential responsibilities.

```cpp
class Policy {
public:
    virtual void touch(PageID page_id) = 0;
    virtual PageID evict() = 0;
    virtual ~Policy() = default;
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.025" chapter="6" section="6.2.1 An Interface for Eviction" kind="list" -->

This interface is the cornerstone of the new design. Let's break down its components:

*   **`virtual void touch(PageID page_id) = 0;`**: This is a pure virtual function that serves as a notification. When the `BufferManager` handles a request for a page that is already in the buffer pool (a cache hit), or when it loads a new page from disk, it will call `touch()` and pass the corresponding `page_id`. It is up to the concrete policy implementation to decide what to do with this information. An LRU policy would use this signal to mark the page as "most recently used." A Least Frequently Used (LFU) policy might increment a counter associated with the page. A simple FIFO policy might ignore this call entirely for pages that are already resident.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.026" chapter="6" section="6.2.1 An Interface for Eviction" kind="list" -->

*   **`virtual PageID evict() = 0;`**: This is the second pure virtual function, representing a direct request. When the `BufferManager` needs to free up a frame, it calls `evict()`. The policy is expected to consult its internal state—which it maintains based on the history of `touch()` calls—and return the `PageID` of the page it has selected as the victim.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.027" chapter="6" section="6.2.1 An Interface for Eviction" kind="prose" -->

The most elegant aspect of this `Policy` interface is what it leaves out. Notice that it knows nothing about `SlottedPage` objects, file handles, or the `StorageManager`. It doesn't deal with memory pointers or the actual contents of a page. Its entire world consists of `PageID`s, which are just simple integers. This strict separation of concerns is critical. The `Policy`'s job is not to *manage* pages but to *reason about* which page is the best candidate for eviction based on a history of accesses. The `BufferManager` retains the responsibility for the mechanical tasks of flushing the victim page's data to disk and deallocating its memory frame. This clean division of labor makes both components simpler and easier to understand.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.028" chapter="6" section="6.2.2 A Refactored Buffer Manager" kind="code" -->

### 6.2.2 A Refactored Buffer Manager

With the `Policy` contract in place, we can now refactor the `BufferManager` to delegate eviction decisions. Comparing the implementation in v015 with the one in v016 reveals a dramatic shift in responsibility.

First, let's look at the private members of the v015 `BufferManager`:

```cpp
// From 15-buzzdb.cpp
private:
    using PageList = std::list<std::pair<PageID, std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>>>;
    using PageMap = std::unordered_map<PageID, typename PageList::iterator>;

    StorageManager storage_manager;
    PageList lruList;
    PageMap pageMap;

    void touch(typename PageList::iterator it) { /* ... */ }
    void evict() { /* ... */ }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.029" chapter="6" section="6.2.2 A Refactored Buffer Manager" kind="code" -->

Here, the LRU logic is an integral part of the class. The `lruList` directly stores the page data, ordered by recency. The `touch` and `evict` methods are private helpers that directly manipulate this list. The policy is baked in.

Now, consider the private members of the refactored v016 `BufferManager`:

```cpp
// From 16-buzzdb.cpp
private:
    using PageMap = std::unordered_map<PageID, std::unique_ptr<SlottedPage>>;

    StorageManager storage_manager;
    PageMap pageMap;
    std::unique_ptr<Policy> policy;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.030" chapter="6" section="6.2.2 A Refactored Buffer Manager" kind="prose" -->

The change is striking. The `lruList` is gone. The private `touch` and `evict` methods are also gone. In their place is a single new member: `std::unique_ptr<Policy> policy`. The `BufferManager` no longer maintains its own complex data structure for tracking usage order. Instead, it holds a smart pointer to a `Policy` object. This object will now encapsulate all the state and logic required for the chosen replacement strategy.

This fundamental architectural change is most apparent in the `getPage` method, the workhorse of the buffer manager. Let's compare its logic side-by-side.

| BuzzDB v015 `getPage` (LRU hardcoded) - | BuzzDB v016 `getPage` (Policy delegated) -

-----------------------------------------------------------------

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.031" chapter="6" section="6.2.2 A Refactored Buffer Manager" kind="prose" -->

| **On a cache hit (page is in memory):** - | `touch(it->second);` - | `policy->touch(page_id);` - | The manager calls its own private `touch` method, which directly manipulates the internal `lruList`. - | The manager calls the `touch` method on its `policy` object, delegating the task of recording the access. - | **When space is needed (cache miss and pool is full):** - | `evict();` - | `auto evictedPageId = policy->evict();` - | The manager calls its own private `evict` method. This method finds the last element in `lruList`, flushes it to disk, and then removes it from both the list and the map. - | The manager calls `evict` on its `policy` object. It receives a `PageID` in return and then performs the mechanical actions of flushing and removing that page from its `pageMap`. |

This delegation is the heart of the Strategy pattern. The `BufferManager` no longer needs to know *how* the victim was chosen; it only needs to know *which* victim was chosen. It trusts the `policy` object to handle the decision-making process correctly.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.032" chapter="6" section="6.2.3 The Power of Polymorphism" kind="code" -->

### 6.2.3 The Power of Polymorphism

The true benefit of this new architecture comes from C++'s support for polymorphism. The `BufferManager` holds a `std::unique_ptr<Policy>`, a pointer to the abstract base class. This means it can hold an instance of *any* concrete class that inherits from `Policy` and implements its pure virtual functions.

For example, we can now create separate classes for each replacement algorithm:

```cpp
// A FIFO policy that uses a queue to track arrival order
class FifoPolicy : public Policy {
private:
    std::list<PageID> fifo_queue;
public:
    void touch(PageID page_id) override {
        // On first load, add to queue. Subsequent touches are ignored.
        // (Implementation details would go here)
    }
    PageID evict() override {
        // Return and remove the page at the front of the queue.
        // (Implementation details would go here)
    }
};

// A new LRU policy, now in its own class
class LruPolicy : public Policy {
private:
    std::list<PageID> lru_list;
    std::unordered_map<PageID, std::list<PageID>::iterator> lru_map;
public:
    void touch(PageID page_id) override {
        // Move page to the front of the list.
        // (Implementation details would go here)
    }
    PageID evict() override {
        // Return and remove the page at the back of the list.
        // (Implementation details would go here)
    }
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.033" chapter="6" section="6.2.3 The Power of Polymorphism" kind="code" -->

The `BufferManager` can be configured to use any of these policies at runtime, without changing a single line of its own code. In the v016 implementation, the choice is made in the constructor:

```cpp
// From 16-buzzdb.cpp
BufferManager(): policy(std::make_unique<FifoPolicy>()) {}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.034" chapter="6" section="6.2.3 The Power of Polymorphism" kind="list" -->

By simply changing this one line to `std::make_unique<LruPolicy>()`, we could switch the entire database's eviction strategy. This is a profound improvement. It allows for:

1.  **Experimentation:** Database developers can easily implement and benchmark different policies to find the best fit for expected workloads.
2.  **Configuration:** A database administrator could potentially select a policy from a configuration file when the system starts, tuning the database for its specific use case (e.g., transactional vs. analytical workloads).
3.  **Maintainability:** The logic for each policy is isolated in its own class, making it easier to debug, test, and reason about. A bug in the `LruPolicy` will not affect the `FifoPolicy` or the `BufferManager` itself.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.035" chapter="6" section="6.2.3 The Power of Polymorphism" kind="prose" -->

This separation of mechanism (the `BufferManager`) from policy (the `Policy` implementations) is a hallmark of mature, well-engineered systems. It replaces a rigid, monolithic design with a flexible, component-based architecture that is prepared for future evolution. The next step, of course, is to build out these concrete policy classes and see how their different internal behaviors affect the overall performance of the system.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.036" chapter="6" section="6.2.3.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

#### 6.2.3.1 Check Your Understanding

1.  **Design:** Imagine you want to implement a "Random" eviction policy, which simply picks a random page to evict when space is needed. What internal data structure(s) would a `RandomPolicy` class need to maintain? How would you implement its `touch` and `evict` methods?
2.  **Analysis:** In the v016 `BufferManager::getPage` method, there is a check: `if(evictedPageId != INVALID_VALUE)`. This implies that `policy->evict()` might sometimes indicate that no page should be evicted. Under what circumstances would a policy implementation correctly return an "invalid" page ID?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.037" chapter="6" section="6.3 Implementing Classic Policies" kind="prose" -->

## 6.3 Implementing Classic Policies

The Strategy pattern gives us a powerful architectural tool: it separates the *mechanism* of buffer management from the *policy* of page replacement. The `BufferManager` is now a neutral arbiter, responsible for pinning pages, tracking dirty status, and coordinating with the disk. When it needs to make a value judgment—"which page should I sacrifice to make room for a new one?"—it delegates that decision to a `Policy` object. This design is clean, extensible, and testable.

But this clean separation pushes the complexity elsewhere. We have traded a monolithic `BufferManager` for a simpler one that relies on a potentially complex `Policy` implementation. Now, we must confront the details of that implementation. What does it actually take to build a policy like Least Recently Used (LRU)? The core idea is simple: when you need to evict a page, choose the one that has gone the longest without being accessed. The intuition is that pages used recently are likely to be used again soon, a principle known as temporal locality.

Executing this simple idea efficiently under pressure is a classic data structures problem. A buffer pool might handle thousands of requests per second. For every single request that "touches" a page, the policy must update its internal state to record that this page is now the *most* recently used. When an eviction is needed, it must be able to identify the *least* recently used page almost instantly. A naive implementation, perhaps scanning a list of all pages in the buffer to find the one with the oldest timestamp, would be disastrously slow. The cost of managing the policy cannot be allowed to dominate the cost of the actual database work. This is the central tension: the policy must be smart, but it must also be fast.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.039" chapter="6" section="6.3.1 The Recency Principle: An Efficient LRU" kind="code" -->

### 6.3.1 The Recency Principle: An Efficient LRU

To implement the LRU policy, we need a data structure that can satisfy two conflicting demands. First, on every page access, we must be able to take a given `PageID`, find it among all the pages currently in the buffer, and promote it to "most recently used" status. This suggests a data structure optimized for fast lookups, like a hash map. Second, when we need to evict a page, we must be able to find the "least recently used" page just as quickly. This suggests a data structure that maintains a strict order, like a queue or a list.

Using either one alone is insufficient. A simple list or vector would require a linear scan (an O(N) operation, where N is the number of pages in the buffer) to find a page before it could be moved. A hash map provides O(1) average-case lookup, but it offers no inherent ordering; we cannot ask it "which key was inserted earliest or accessed least recently?"

The classic and highly efficient solution is to use both. BuzzDB's `LruPolicy` demonstrates this pattern perfectly. It combines a doubly-linked list, which maintains the strict ordering of pages from most- to least-recently used, with a hash map that provides immediate access to any page's position within that list.

```cpp
class LruPolicy : public Policy {
private:
    // List to keep track of the order of use
    std::list<PageID> lruList;

    // Map to find a page's iterator in the list efficiently
    std::unordered_map<PageID, std::list<PageID>::iterator> map;

    size_t cacheSize;
// ...
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.040" chapter="6" section="6.3.1 The Recency Principle: An Efficient LRU" kind="code" -->

The `lruList` is the heart of the ordering mechanism. We will treat its front (`lruList.begin()`) as the Most Recently Used (MRU) end and its back (`lruList.back()`) as the Least Recently Used (LRU) end. The `map` is the key to efficiency. It doesn't just tell us *if* a page is in the list; it stores a `PageID` as its key and a `std::list<PageID>::iterator` as its value. This iterator is a direct pointer to the node for that `PageID` within the `lruList`. This allows us to jump directly to a node in the list in O(1) time, without having to traverse the list from the beginning.

Let's trace the logic of the two main `Policy` methods, `touch` and `evict`.

The `touch` method is called by the `BufferManager` every time a page is accessed. Its job is to update the recency ordering.

```cpp
bool touch(PageID page_id) override {
    bool found = false;
    // If page already in the list, remove it
    if (map.find(page_id) != map.end()) {
        found = true;
        lruList.erase(map[page_id]);
        map.erase(page_id);            
    }

    // If cache is full, evict
    if(lruList.size() == cacheSize){
        evict();
    }

    if(lruList.size() < cacheSize){
        // Add the page to the front of the list
        lruList.emplace_front(page_id);
        map[page_id] = lruList.begin();
    }

    return found;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.041" chapter="6" section="6.3.1 The Recency Principle: An Efficient LRU" kind="code" -->

When `touch(page_id)` is called, it first checks the `map`. If the `page_id` is found, it's a "hit"—the page is already in the buffer. Because this page has just been accessed, it must become the new MRU page. The implementation achieves this by first completely removing the page from its current position. It uses the iterator from the map (`map[page_id]`) to erase the element from the `lruList` in O(1) time, and then removes the corresponding entry from the `map`. The code then proceeds as if it were a new page, adding it to the front of the list and updating the map. This two-step process of remove-then-add is a simple way to guarantee the page ends up at the MRU position.

If the `page_id` is not found in the map, it's a "miss." The page needs to be loaded into the buffer. Before adding it, the policy checks if the buffer is full (`lruList.size() == cacheSize`). If it is, an existing page must be evicted by calling `evict()`. Finally, the new `page_id` is added to the front of the `lruList` (the MRU position) and an iterator to its new location is stored in the `map`.

The `evict` method is simpler. Its single responsibility is to identify and remove the LRU page.

```cpp
PageID evict() override {
    // Evict the least recently used page
    PageID evictedPageId = INVALID_VALUE;
    if(lruList.size() != 0){
        evictedPageId = lruList.back();
        map.erase(evictedPageId);
        lruList.pop_back();
    }
    return evictedPageId;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.042" chapter="6" section="6.3.1 The Recency Principle: An Efficient LRU" kind="prose" -->

By our convention, the LRU page is always at the back of the list. The method retrieves its `PageID` using `lruList.back()`, removes it from the `map`, and then removes it from the list using `pop_back()`. All of these are O(1) operations. The combination of the list and map ensures that the core operations of the LRU policy—promotion on access and eviction of the least-used—are performed in constant time.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.043" chapter="6" section="6.3.1.1 A Worked Example" kind="table" -->

#### 6.3.1.1 A Worked Example

To see how these data structures interact, let's trace a sequence of page accesses with a buffer pool of size 4. The access sequence is: **1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 6**.

The state of the `lruList` is shown with the MRU page on the left and the LRU page on the right.

| Access | Hit/Miss | Action | `lruList` State (MRU -> LRU) | `map` Contents |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Miss | Add 1 | `[1]` | `{1: iter_to_1}` |
| **2** | Miss | Add 2 | `[2, 1]` | `{1:..., 2:...}` |
| **3** | Miss | Add 3 | `[3, 2, 1]` | `{1:..., 2:..., 3:...}` |
| **1** | Hit | Promote 1 | `[1, 3, 2]` | `{1:..., 2:..., 3:...}` |
| **4** | Miss | Add 4 | `[4, 1, 3, 2]` | `{1:..., 2:..., 3:..., 4:...}` |
| **2** | Hit | Promote 2 | `[2, 4, 1, 3]` | `{1:..., 2:..., 3:..., 4:...}` |
| **5** | Miss | Evict 3, Add 5 | `[5, 2, 4, 1]` | `{1:..., 2:..., 4:..., 5:...}` |
| **6** | Miss | Evict 1, Add 6 | `[6, 5, 2, 4]` | `{2:..., 4:..., 5:..., 6:...}` |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.044" chapter="6" section="6.3.1.1 A Worked Example" kind="list" -->

Let's break down a few key steps:

- **Access 1:** A hit on page 1. It was previously the third-most-recently used page. The policy finds it in the map, removes it from its old position in the list, and re-inserts it at the front. The new order is `[1, 3, 2]`.
- **Access 4:** A miss, but the buffer is not yet full. Page 4 is added to the front, becoming the new MRU page. The buffer is now at capacity.
- **Access 5:** A miss, and the buffer is full. The `evict()` method is called. It looks at the back of the list, `[2, 4, 1, 3]`, and identifies page 3 as the LRU victim. Page 3 is removed from both data structures. Then, page 5 is added to the front.
- **Access 6:** Another miss with a full buffer. The LRU page is now page 1. It is evicted, and page 6 is brought in as the new MRU page.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.045" chapter="6" section="6.3.1.1 A Worked Example" kind="prose" -->

This trace shows the dynamism of the LRU policy. It constantly reorders pages based on access, ensuring that "hot" pages like 1 and 2 stay in the buffer, while "cold" pages like 3 are quickly identified as candidates for eviction.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.046" chapter="6" section="6.3.2 A Simpler Baseline: First-In, First-Out" kind="prose" -->

### 6.3.2 A Simpler Baseline: First-In, First-Out

The dual-structure implementation of LRU is effective, but it carries a certain complexity. Is it always necessary? To appreciate why this effort is worthwhile, it helps to compare it to a much simpler policy: First-In, First-Out (FIFO).

As its name implies, FIFO ignores all information about how frequently or recently a page has been used. It tracks only one thing: arrival time. The page that has been in the buffer for the longest period is always the first to be evicted. This is analogous to a checkout line at a grocery store; the first person in line is the first to be served, regardless of how many items they have.

A FIFO policy can be implemented with a single, simple data structure: a queue. When a new page is brought into the buffer, it is added to the back of the queue. When an eviction is needed, the page at the front of the queue is removed. Unlike LRU, a "hit" on a page already in the buffer requires no action at all; the page's position in the queue does not change.

Let's reconsider our previous access sequence (**1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, 6**) with a 4-frame buffer managed by a FIFO policy.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.047" chapter="6" section="6.3.2 A Simpler Baseline: First-In, First-Out" kind="table" -->

| Access | Hit/Miss | Action | Buffer State (Front -> Back) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | Miss | Add 1 | `[1]` |
| **2** | Miss | Add 2 | `[1, 2]` |
| **3** | Miss | Add 3 | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| **1** | Hit | No change | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| **4** | Miss | Add 4 | `[1, 2, 3, 4]` |
| **2** | Hit | No change | `[1, 2, 3, 4]` |
| **5** | Miss | Evict 1, Add 5 | `[2, 3, 4, 5]` |
| **6** | Miss | Evict 2, Add 6 | `[3, 4, 5, 6]` |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.048" chapter="6" section="6.3.2 A Simpler Baseline: First-In, First-Out" kind="prose" -->

The outcome is starkly different. When page 5 needs to be loaded, FIFO evicts page 1. Why? Because page 1 was the first one to arrive. It doesn't matter that page 1 was accessed more recently than pages 2 and 3. Its fate was sealed the moment it entered the buffer. Similarly, when page 6 arrives, page 2 is evicted because it is now the oldest resident.

The weakness of FIFO is that it conflates arrival time with importance. A core data page that is accessed constantly by many queries might be evicted simply because it was loaded at the start of the database's uptime. LRU, by contrast, would recognize this page's frequent use and keep it resident in the buffer. While FIFO is simple to implement and has very low overhead, its simplistic logic often leads to poor hit rates in real-world database workloads, which exhibit strong temporal locality. It serves as a useful baseline for appreciating the intelligence of more sophisticated policies.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.049" chapter="6" section="6.3.3 The Cost of Perfection: Approximating LRU with Clock" kind="prose" -->

### 6.3.3 The Cost of Perfection: Approximating LRU with Clock

The LRU implementation in BuzzDB is a textbook example of an efficient, "true" LRU policy. For every page access, it perfectly updates its internal ordering to reflect that the touched page is now the most recently used. However, this perfection comes at a price. Every `touch` operation, whether a hit or a miss, requires modifications to both the list and the map. In a highly concurrent system, these data structures would need to be protected by a lock or other synchronization primitive, and the constant manipulation could become a point of contention.

For this reason, many operating systems and database systems opt for an approximation of LRU that offers a better balance between performance and accuracy. The most famous of these is the **Clock algorithm**, also known as the second-chance algorithm.

The Clock algorithm avoids the overhead of reordering a list on every access. Instead, it arranges the buffer frames in a conceptual circle and uses a single "reference bit" for each frame. A pointer, or "clock hand," cycles through the frames.

The algorithm works as follows:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.050" chapter="6" section="6.3.3 The Cost of Perfection: Approximating LRU with Clock" kind="list" -->

1.  **Arrangement:** All buffer frames are treated as a circular array. A clock hand points to one of the frames, which is the next candidate for eviction.
2.  **Reference Bit:** Each frame has a reference bit, initially set to 0.
3.  **On Page Access:** When a page in a frame is accessed (a hit), its reference bit is set to 1. This is a very cheap operation—just flipping a single bit in memory. No pointers are moved, and no nodes are reordered.
4.  **On Page Fault (Eviction):** When a new page must be loaded into a full buffer, the system needs to find a victim. The clock hand begins to sweep across the frames from its current position:
    -   If the hand points to a frame whose reference bit is 1, the system sees this as a sign of recent use. It gives the page a "second chance" by flipping the reference bit back to 0 and advancing the clock hand to the next frame.
    -   If the hand points to a frame whose reference bit is 0, this page is the victim. It has not been referenced since the last time the clock hand swept past it. The new page is loaded into this frame, the frame's reference bit is set to 1 (as it has just been used), and the clock hand is advanced to the next position.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.051" chapter="6" section="6.3.3 The Cost of Perfection: Approximating LRU with Clock" kind="code" -->

The following figure illustrates the state of a 4-frame buffer managed by the Clock algorithm.

```
     Buffer Frames (Circular)

          [F1 (R=1)]
        /            \
     [F4 (R=0)]      [F2 (R=0)] <-- Clock Hand
        \            /
          [F3 (R=1)]
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.052" chapter="6" section="6.3.3 The Cost of Perfection: Approximating LRU with Clock" kind="prose" -->

In this scenario, the clock hand is currently pointing at Frame 2. If an eviction were needed, the system would inspect F2. Since its reference bit (R) is 0, the page in F2 would be evicted immediately. The new page would be loaded, its bit set to 1, and the hand would move to F3. If, however, the hand were pointing at F1, it would see the reference bit is 1. It would flip the bit to 0, advance the hand to F2, and then inspect F2 as the next candidate.

The Clock algorithm is a clever compromise. It approximates LRU by dividing pages into two simple groups: those used recently (R=1) and those not used recently (R=0). It doesn't maintain the perfect, fine-grained ordering of a true LRU policy, but it avoids the expensive data structure manipulation on every hit. The only time the system does significant work is during an eviction, and even then, the work is a bounded scan rather than a complex shuffle of pointers. While BuzzDB implements a true LRU policy, understanding the Clock algorithm is crucial, as its low-overhead approach has made it a mainstay in practical systems for decades.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.055" chapter="6" section="6.4 Beyond LRU: The Two-Queue Policy" kind="prose" -->

## 6.4 Beyond LRU: The Two-Queue Policy

The Strategy pattern has given us a clean separation between the buffer manager's mechanics and its page replacement policy. This is a powerful design, but it doesn't change the fundamental behavior of the policies themselves. As we saw with the Least Recently Used (LRU) policy, a simple and intuitive heuristic can have significant, and sometimes disastrous, performance implications. The core weakness of LRU is its single-minded focus on recency. It assumes that any page accessed recently is important, and any page that hasn't been accessed in a while is not.

This assumption breaks down spectacularly in the face of a common database operation: the sequential scan. Imagine a query that needs to read every record in a large `students` table to calculate the average GPA. If this table spans thousands of pages—far more than can fit in the buffer pool—the scan will systematically read one page after another. With an LRU policy, each new page brought in for the scan evicts the least recently used page. If the buffer pool has `N` frames, after reading the first `N` pages of the table, the buffer is full. When the `(N+1)`-th page is requested, the *first* page of the scan is evicted. This continues for the entire scan.

The result is what's known as **sequential flooding**. The scan effectively flushes the entire buffer pool, replacing every page that was there before—index root pages, frequently accessed user profiles, system catalog data—with the final pages of the `students` table. These are the very pages that are *least* likely to be needed again soon. The scan, a single, low-value operation in terms of data reuse, has polluted the cache and destroyed its carefully curated working set. To recover, the database must slowly rebuild its hot set through a series of expensive disk reads. This is the price of LRU's simplicity: it cannot distinguish between a one-time access and a genuinely popular page.

### 6.4.1 A Tale of Two Queues

To solve the sequential flooding problem, we need a policy that can differentiate between fleeting, single-use pages and pages with demonstrated, lasting value. The policy needs a memory of access *frequency*, not just recency. This is the motivation behind the **Two-Queue (2Q)** replacement policy. Instead of one list tracking all pages, 2Q partitions the buffer pool into two logical groups, managed by two separate queues.

The core idea is to treat new pages with suspicion. When a page is first read from disk, it isn't immediately considered valuable. It's placed on a "probationary" queue. Only if that page is accessed a *second* time while it's still in the buffer is it "promoted" to a protected status. This design elegantly separates the transient traffic of a sequential scan from the repeated hits on truly "hot" data.

BuzzDB's `TwoQPolicy` implements this strategy using two internal lists:

1.  `FIFO`: A queue for new, "cold" pages that have only been accessed once. It's managed with a First-In, First-Out discipline. Think of this as the buffer's waiting room.
2.  `LRU`: A list for "hot" pages that have been accessed at least twice. It's managed with a standard Least Recently Used discipline. This is the VIP section.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.058" chapter="6" section="6.4.1 A Tale of Two Queues" kind="code" -->

The movement of a page between these two lists, and ultimately out of the buffer, follows a clear lifecycle:

```
                                     ┌──────────────────┐
                                     │ Page Re-Accessed │
                                     └─────────┬────────┘
                                               │
                                               ▼
┌────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│ New Page   ├────►│ FIFO Queue     ├────►│ LRU List     │
│ from Disk  │     │ (Cold / New)   │     │ (Hot / Proven) │
└────────────┘     └───────┬────────┘     └──────┬───────┘
                           │                     │
                           │ Evicted First       │ Evicted Second
                           │ (if not promoted)   │ (if FIFO is empty)
                           ▼                     ▼
                         ┌───┴───┐             ┌───┴───┐
                         │ EVICT │             │ EVICT │
                         └───────┘             └───────┘
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.059" chapter="6" section="6.4.1 A Tale of Two Queues" kind="prose" -->

When a page is first requested, it enters the back of the `FIFO` queue. If the buffer is full, an eviction must occur. The 2Q policy's first choice for a victim is the page at the front of the `FIFO` queue—the one that has been in the probationary area the longest without being re-accessed. This is the crucial defense against scan pollution. Pages from a sequential scan will enter the `FIFO` queue and be pushed out by later pages in the same scan, never getting a chance to disturb the hot pages.

If a page in the `FIFO` queue is accessed again, the policy recognizes its value. The page is promoted to the `LRU` list, marking it as hot. From then on, any subsequent access to that page will simply move it to the front of the `LRU` list, just as in a standard LRU policy. Evictions only target the `LRU` list when the `FIFO` queue is completely empty. This simple partitioning protects the working set of frequently used pages while allowing transient data to flow through a separate channel.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.060" chapter="6" section="6.4.2 Tracing 2Q's Logic" kind="code" -->

### 6.4.2 Tracing 2Q's Logic

The logic for managing these two queues is encapsulated in the `touch` and `evict` methods of BuzzDB's `TwoQPolicy`. Let's examine how they work together to protect the buffer pool.

The `TwoQPolicy` class maintains the two lists and a hash map for quick lookups:

```cpp
class TwoQPolicy : public Policy {
private:
    size_t cacheSize;

    std::list<PageID> FIFO; // Read-once pages (FIFO)
    std::list<PageID> LRU;  // Hot pages (LRU)

    std::unordered_map<PageID, std::list<PageID>::iterator> pageMap;
    // ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.061" chapter="6" section="6.4.2 Tracing 2Q's Logic" kind="code" -->

The `touch` method is called by the `BufferManager` every time a page is accessed. Its job is to update the policy's internal state based on this access.

```cpp
bool touch(PageID page_id) {
    bool found = false;
    // Check if page is already in cache
    if (pageMap.find(page_id) != pageMap.end()) {
        found = true;
        auto it = pageMap[page_id];

        // If it's in FIFO, move to LRU
        if (std::find(FIFO.begin(), FIFO.end(), page_id) != FIFO.end()) {
            FIFO.erase(it);
            LRU.push_front(page_id);
            pageMap[page_id] = LRU.begin();
        } else {
            // If it's in LRU, move to the front
            LRU.erase(it);
            LRU.push_front(page_id);
            pageMap[page_id] = LRU.begin();
        }
    } else {
        // If cache is full, evict
        if (FIFO.size() + LRU.size() >= cacheSize) {
            evict();
        }

        // Add page to FIFO
        FIFO.push_back(page_id);
        pageMap[page_id] = std::prev(FIFO.end());
    }
    return found;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.062" chapter="6" section="6.4.2 Tracing 2Q's Logic" kind="code" -->

The logic follows two main paths. If the page is already in the buffer (`pageMap.find(page_id) != pageMap.end()`), the policy must decide if this is a promotion or a simple refresh. The code checks if the page exists in the `FIFO` list. If so, this is the page's second touch, and it gets promoted: it's erased from `FIFO` and added to the front of `LRU`. If it's not in `FIFO`, it must already be in `LRU`, so it's just moved to the front of `LRU` to mark it as most-recently-used.

If the page is not in the buffer, it's a new arrival. The policy first checks if the buffer is full. If `FIFO.size() + LRU.size() >= cacheSize`, it calls `evict()` to make room. Then, the new page is placed at the back of the `FIFO` queue, beginning its probationary period.

The `evict` method contains the other half of the policy's intelligence:

```cpp
PageID evict() {
    PageID evictedPageId = INVALID_VALUE;
    if (!FIFO.empty()) {
        evictedPageId = FIFO.front();
        FIFO.pop_front();
        pageMap.erase(evictedPageId);
    } else {
        evictedPageId = LRU.back();
        LRU.pop_back();
        pageMap.erase(evictedPageId);
    }
    return evictedPageId;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.063" chapter="6" section="6.4.2 Tracing 2Q's Logic" kind="prose" -->

The logic is direct and powerful. It first checks if the `FIFO` queue has any pages. If it does, the victim is the page at the very front—the one that arrived earliest and has not been re-accessed. Only if the `FIFO` queue is empty does the policy fall back to evicting the least-recently-used page from the back of the `LRU` list.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.064" chapter="6" section="6.4.2.1 Worked Example: Surviving a Scan" kind="list" -->

#### 6.4.2.1 Worked Example: Surviving a Scan

Let's trace the same scenario that caused sequential flooding in LRU and see how 2Q handles it. Assume a buffer pool with a `cacheSize` of 5.

Our workload consists of two phases:

1.  **Warm-up:** A series of accesses establishes a hot set: `A, B, C, B, A`.
2.  **Scan:** A sequential scan reads new pages: `P1, P2, P3, P4, P5`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.065" chapter="6" section="6.4.2.1 Worked Example: Surviving a Scan" kind="table" -->

The table below shows the state of the `FIFO` and `LRU` lists after each access. The front of each list is on the left.

| Access | Action | `FIFO` Queue (Cold) | `LRU` List (Hot) | Evicted | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `A` | New page | `[A]` | `[]` | - | A enters probation. |
| `B` | New page | `[A, B]` | `[]` | - | B enters probation. |
| `C` | New page | `[A, B, C]` | `[]` | - | C enters probation. |
| `B` | Re-access | `[A, C]` | `[B]` | - | B is promoted to hot. |
| `A` | Re-access | `[C]` | `[A, B]` | - | A is promoted to hot. |
| `P1` | New page | `[C, P1]` | `[A, B]` | - | P1 enters probation. |
| `P2` | New page | `[C, P1, P2]` | `[A, B]` | - | P2 enters probation. Buffer is now full (3+2=5). |
| `P3` | New page | `[P1, P2, P3]` | `[A, B]` | `C` | Buffer full. `evict()` removes `C` from `FIFO`. `P3` added. |
| `P4` | New page | `[P2, P3, P4]` | `[A, B]` | `P1` | Buffer full. `evict()` removes `P1` from `FIFO`. `P4` added. |
| `P5` | New page | `[P3, P4, P5]` | `[A, B]` | `P2` | Buffer full. `evict()` removes `P2` from `FIFO`. `P5` added. |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.066" chapter="6" section="6.4.2.1 Worked Example: Surviving a Scan" kind="prose" -->

At the end of this sequence, the buffer contains `{P3, P4, P5}` in the `FIFO` queue and, crucially, `{A, B}` in the `LRU` list. The sequential scan pages (`P1` through `P5`) flowed through the `FIFO` queue, pushing each other out. The genuinely hot pages, `A` and `B`, remained safe and untouched in the protected `LRU` list. The 2Q policy successfully weathered the scan, preserving the valuable working set. This is a dramatic improvement over a simple LRU policy, which would have ended with a buffer containing only `{P1, P2, P3, P4, P5}`.

The 2Q policy is not without its own complexities. The original academic proposal includes parameters to control the relative sizes of the queues, allowing database administrators to tune the policy. BuzzDB's implementation uses a simplified model where the queues can grow dynamically, but the core principle remains the same. Furthermore, in a high-performance system, one might optimize the check for a page's location. The `std::find` on the `FIFO` list in `touch` is an O(N) operation. A more complex implementation could store a bit or a pointer in the `pageMap`'s value to indicate which queue a page belongs to, making the check an O(1) operation.

Even with these simplifications, BuzzDB's `TwoQPolicy` is a significant step up from basic LRU. It introduces the idea that not all data access is equal. By creating a simple probationary system, it protects the long-term value of the buffer pool from the transient needs of a single query, leading to more stable and predictable performance under mixed workloads.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.067" chapter="6" section="6.4.2.2 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

#### 6.4.2.2 Check Your Understanding

1.  **Performance Bottleneck:** In the `touch` method of BuzzDB's `TwoQPolicy`, the line `std::find(FIFO.begin(), FIFO.end(), page_id)` performs a linear scan to see if a page is in the cold queue. If the `FIFO` queue contains thousands of pages, this could become a performance issue. How could you modify the `TwoQPolicy`'s data structures to determine which list a page belongs to in O(1) time?
2.  **Workload Analysis:** Consider a workload that exclusively consists of large, non-repeating sequential scans where each scan touches more pages than the buffer pool's capacity. How would the 2Q policy's performance compare to a simple LRU policy under these conditions? What would be the state of the `FIFO` and `LRU` lists?
3.  **Policy Tuning:** The original 2Q algorithm proposed splitting the buffer into three sections: `A_in` (a FIFO queue), `A_out` (a list of identifiers of recently evicted pages from `A_in`), and `A_m` (the main LRU-managed hot section). A page was only promoted to `A_m` if it was re-accessed after being evicted from `A_in`. How does this differ from BuzzDB's implementation, and what kind of access pattern might it handle more effectively?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch06.068" chapter="6" section="6.5 Measuring What Matters: Simulating Policy Performance" kind="prose" -->

## 6.5 Measuring What Matters: Simulating Policy Performance

Theoretical discussions about "recency" and "frequency" are essential for understanding the design of replacement policies, but they can only take us so far. To truly grasp the impact of choosing LRU over 2Q, or any policy over another, we need to see how they perform under pressure. What happens when a real sequence of page requests hits the buffer manager? Which policy will yield a higher hit rate, and by how much? Answering these questions with confidence requires empirical evidence.

Running a full database system with a complex application workload just to measure the buffer hit rate is often impractical. The performance of the system as a whole is influenced by countless factors: query optimization, lock contention, disk I/O speed, and more. Isolating the effect of a single component—the replacement policy—can be like trying to hear a whisper in a crowded stadium.

A common and powerful technique in systems development is to build a focused simulator or test harness. Instead of running the entire database, we can lift the component we care about, in this case, the `Policy` objects, and drive them with a controlled, repeatable sequence of inputs. This allows us to observe their behavior in isolation, compare them fairly, and understand their strengths and weaknesses on specific workloads. BuzzDB v018 does exactly this, replacing the complex, unpredictable life of a database server with a simple, direct simulation.

```cpp
   386	private:
   387	    // List to keep track of the order of use
   388	    std::list<PageID> lruList;
   389	
   390	    // Map to find a page's iterator in the list efficiently

   392

   401	
   402	        bool found = false;

   404	        if (map.find(page_id) != map.end()) {
   405	            found = true;
   406	            lruList.erase(map[page_id]);
   407	            map.erase(page_id);            
   408	        }
   409	
   410	        // If cache is full, evict
   411	        if(lruList.size() == cacheSize){

   414
```
