<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.029" chapter="10" section="10.2 Indexing Spatial Data: R-Trees" kind="prose" -->

The core problem is that one-dimensional indexes cannot comprehend two-dimensional proximity. A B+ Tree on latitude has no idea which points are close together by longitude, and vice-versa. To efficiently query spatial data, we need an index that groups objects by their proximity in two (or more) dimensions simultaneously. This is the fundamental pressure that led to the development of spatial indexes like the R-Tree.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.030" chapter="10" section="10.2.1 The R-Tree: A Hierarchy of Rectangles" kind="list" -->

### 10.2.1 The R-Tree: A Hierarchy of Rectangles

The R-Tree's core insight is to group nearby objects into a hierarchy of bounding boxes. Instead of ordering data along a single line, it organizes it by spatial containment. The fundamental building block is the **Minimum Bounding Rectangle (MBR)**, which is the smallest rectangle, aligned with the coordinate axes, that completely encloses a set of objects.

An R-Tree is a height-balanced tree, much like a B+ Tree, but its structure is based on these MBRs:

*   **Leaf Nodes:** Contain entries that point to the actual data objects. For point data, the MBR of a leaf entry is simply the point itself. For geometric shapes like polygons, the MBR is the bounding box of that shape.
*   **Internal Nodes:** Contain entries that consist of an MBR and a pointer to a child node. The MBR in an internal node entry completely encloses all the MBRs in the child node it points to.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.031" chapter="10" section="10.2.1 The R-Tree: A Hierarchy of Rectangles" kind="code" -->

This structure creates a nested hierarchy. The MBR of the root node encloses the entire dataset. Its children are smaller MBRs that partition the space, and their children partition the space further, until the leaf nodes are reached, which contain the data objects themselves. Unlike a B+ Tree, where the ranges in an internal node are ordered and do not overlap, the MBRs in an R-Tree node can and often do overlap. This is a crucial distinction that influences how the tree is built and queried.

Let's visualize this. Imagine we are indexing the locations of several landmarks in a city park.

```
      +----------------------------------------------------+
      | Root MBR (R1)                                      |
      | +----------------------+  +----------------------+ |
      | | Internal MBR (A1)    |  | Internal MBR (B1)    | |
      | |                      |  |                      | |
      | | +-------+  +-------+ |  | +-------+  +-------+ | |
      | | | L1    |  | L2    | |  | | L3    |  | L4    | | |
      | | |  .a   |  |   .d  | |  | |  .f   |  |  .h   | | |
      | | | .b .c |  | .e    | |  | |    .g |  |       | | |
      | | +-------+  +-------+ |  | +-------+  +-------+ | |
      | +----------------------+  +----------------------+ |
      +----------------------------------------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.032" chapter="10" section="10.2.1 The R-Tree: A Hierarchy of Rectangles" kind="code" -->

In this figure, points `a`, `b`, and `c` are grouped into a leaf-level MBR `L1`. Points `d` and `e` are in `L2`. These two leaf MBRs, `L1` and `L2`, are then grouped together under a larger internal MBR, `A1`. Similarly, points `f`, `g`, and `h` are grouped into leaves `L3` and `L4`, which are contained by internal MBR `B1`. Finally, at the top level, the root node's MBR, `R1`, contains both `A1` and `B1`.

In BuzzDB, this structure is captured by two simple structs in `z-rtree.cpp`:

```cpp
struct Entry {
    Rect mbr;
    Node* child;   // nullptr for leaf entries
    int   id;      // payload id if leaf; undefined for internal
    Entry(const Rect& r, Node* c, int id=-1) : mbr(r), child(c), id(id) {}
};

struct Node {
    bool isLeaf;
    vector<Entry> entries;
    Node* parent = nullptr;
    // ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.033" chapter="10" section="10.2.1 The R-Tree: A Hierarchy of Rectangles" kind="prose" -->

An `Entry` holds the `mbr` and a union-like pair of pointers: a `child` `Node` pointer if it's in an internal node, or a data `id` if it's in a leaf. The `Node` itself is a container for a `vector` of these entries and a boolean flag, `isLeaf`, to distinguish its level in the tree. This elegant design directly models the conceptual hierarchy of nested rectangles.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.034" chapter="10" section="10.2.2 Insertion: Minimizing Enlargement and Splitting Nodes" kind="prose" -->

### 10.2.2 Insertion: Minimizing Enlargement and Splitting Nodes

Building an R-Tree involves inserting new objects one by one. Each insertion requires two key decisions: which leaf node should hold the new object, and what to do if that leaf node becomes full. The quality of these decisions determines the performance of the tree, as a well-structured tree with tight, non-overlapping MBRs will prune searches much more effectively.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.035" chapter="10" section="10.2.2.1 Choosing a Subtree" kind="code" -->

#### 10.2.2.1 Choosing a Subtree

To insert a new object, we start at the root and traverse down to a leaf. At each internal node, we must decide which of its children to descend into. The goal is to place the new object in a subtree where it "fits" best. The most common heuristic, and the one used by BuzzDB, is to **choose the child whose MBR requires the least area enlargement** to include the new object's MBR. If there's a tie, we break it by choosing the child with the MBR of the smallest area. This greedy strategy aims to keep MBRs as small and tight as possible.

BuzzDB's `chooseSubtree` method implements this logic. It iterates through the entries of the current node and calculates the cost of adding the new rectangle `r` to each child's MBR.

```cpp
// from RTree::chooseSubtree in z-rtree.cpp
for (int i=0;i<(int)cur->entries.size();++i) {
    const Rect& mbr = cur->entries[i].mbr;
    float enl = mbr.enlargement(r);
    float area = mbr.area();
    // ...
    if (enl < bestEnl ||
        (enl == bestEnl && area < bestArea) ||
        // ... tie-break further by entry count
    ) {
        best = i; bestEnl = enl; bestArea = area;
    }
}
cur = cur->entries[best].child;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.036" chapter="10" section="10.2.2.1 Choosing a Subtree" kind="prose" -->

The code finds the `enlargement` needed for each child's `mbr`. It keeps track of the `best` candidate seen so far, prioritizing minimum enlargement (`bestEnl`), then minimum area (`bestArea`), and finally, as a last resort, the child with fewer entries. This process repeats until a leaf node is reached. The new entry is then added to this leaf.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.037" chapter="10" section="10.2.2.2 Splitting Overfull Nodes" kind="list" -->

#### 10.2.2.2 Splitting Overfull Nodes

After adding the new entry, the leaf node might have more than the maximum allowed number of entries (a parameter often denoted as `M`). When a node overflows, it must be split into two, just like in a B+ Tree. The original entries, plus the new one, must be distributed between the two new nodes. The parent of the split node must then be updated to reflect this change, which may cause the parent to split, and so on up the tree.

Splitting an R-Tree node is far more complex than splitting a B+ Tree node. With a B+ Tree, we can simply find the median key and divide the entries cleanly. In multiple dimensions, there is no single, obvious ordering. The goal of a split is to create two new groups of entries whose MBRs are as small as possible and have as little overlap as possible. A bad split can lead to large, overlapping MBRs that degrade query performance, as queries will be forced to explore both branches.

Many algorithms exist for splitting a node. BuzzDB implements a classic one called **Quadratic Split**. The name comes from its O(n²) complexity in the number of entries being split. The algorithm works as follows:

1.  **Pick Seeds:** First, find the two entries that are "worst" to have in the same group and make them the seeds of the two new nodes. A good way to do this is to find the pair of entries that would create the largest MBR if grouped together. Placing them in separate nodes from the start encourages a good partition.
2.  **Distribute Remaining Entries:** Iteratively assign the remaining entries to one of the two new groups. To decide where to place an entry, the algorithm can use various heuristics. BuzzDB's `quadraticSplit` picks the unassigned entry that has the strongest preference for one group over the other. It calculates the area enlargement required to add the entry to each group's MBR. The entry with the largest *difference* between these two enlargement costs is chosen next and assigned to the group that it enlarges the least. This heuristic prioritizes the most "obvious" assignments first.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.038" chapter="10" section="10.2.2.2 Splitting Overfull Nodes" kind="code" -->

Let's look at the core assignment loop in `quadraticSplit`:

```cpp
// from RTree::quadraticSplit in z-rtree.cpp
float bestDiff = -1.0f; int bestIdx = -1; int bestGroup = -1;
for (int i=0;i<(int)E.size();++i) if (!taken[i]) {
    float gain0 = cov0.enlargement(E[i].mbr);
    float gain1 = cov1.enlargement(E[i].mbr);
    float diff = fabs(gain0 - gain1);
    // ... logic to pick a group 'g'
    if (diff > bestDiff) { bestDiff = diff; bestIdx = i; bestGroup = g; }
}
// ... assign entry bestIdx to bestGroup
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.039" chapter="10" section="10.2.2.2 Splitting Overfull Nodes" kind="prose" -->

The code calculates `gain0` and `gain1`, the enlargement costs for adding entry `i` to group 0 and group 1, respectively. It then finds the entry with the maximum `diff` between these costs and assigns it. This process repeats until all entries are distributed. The algorithm also includes logic to enforce a minimum fill factor (`m`), ensuring that neither of the new nodes is nearly empty, which maintains the tree's balance and storage efficiency.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.040" chapter="10" section="10.2.3 Spatial Queries: Window and Nearest-Neighbor" kind="prose" -->

### 10.2.3 Spatial Queries: Window and Nearest-Neighbor

Once an R-Tree is built, it can efficiently answer spatial queries. The hierarchical structure of MBRs allows the query processor to quickly prune large portions of the search space that could not possibly contain results.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.041" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.1 Window Queries" kind="list" -->

#### 10.2.3.1 Window Queries

The most fundamental R-Tree operation is the window query, which finds all objects that intersect a given query rectangle. The search algorithm is a straightforward recursive descent:

1.  Start at the root node.
2.  For each `Entry` in the current node, test if its `mbr` intersects the query rectangle.
3.  If an entry's MBR does **not** intersect the query rectangle, that entry and its entire subtree can be ignored. This is the pruning step that gives the R-Tree its power.
4.  If an entry's MBR **does** intersect the query rectangle:
    *   If the current node is an internal node, recursively call the search function on the child node pointed to by the entry.
    *   If the current node is a leaf node, test the object itself (represented by its MBR in the entry) against the query rectangle. If it intersects, add the object's ID to the result set.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.042" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.1 Window Queries" kind="code" -->

Let's trace a window query on our earlier park map example. Suppose we are searching for landmarks within the query window `Q`.

```
      +----------------------------------------------------+
      | Root MBR (R1)                                      |
      | +----------------------+  +----------------------+ |
      | | Internal MBR (A1)    |  | Internal MBR (B1)    | |
      | |      +-------+       |  |                      | |
      | |      |   Q   |       |  | +-------+  +-------+ | |
      | | +----|--+  +-|-----+ |  | | L3    |  | L4    | | |
      | | | L1 |  |  | L2    | |  | |  .f   |  |  .h   | | |
      | | | .b |c |  | .e    | |  | |    .g |  |       | | |
      | | +----|--+  +-------+ |  | +-------+  +-------+ | |
      | +------|---------------+  +----------------------+ |
      +--------|-------------------------------------------+
               +-------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.043" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.1 Window Queries" kind="list" -->

1.  **Root:** The query starts at the root `R1`. The query window `Q` intersects `R1`, so we examine its children.
2.  **Internal Node Level:** The root's children are `A1` and `B1`.
    *   `Q` intersects `A1`. We must descend into the node represented by `A1`.
    *   `Q` does **not** intersect `B1`. The entire subtree under `B1`, including leaves `L3` and `L4` and points `f`, `g`, and `h`, is pruned from the search. We never even look at it.
3.  **Leaf Level:** We are now at the node for `A1`. Its children are leaves `L1` and `L2`.
    *   `Q` intersects `L1`. We examine the points within `L1`. Point `c` is inside `Q`, so it is added to our results. Points `a` and `b` are outside.
    *   `Q` intersects `L2`. We examine the points within `L2`. Point `e` is inside `Q`, so it is added. Point `d` is outside.
4.  **Result:** The query returns points `{c, e}`. By pruning the entire `B1` branch, we avoided checking half of the data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.044" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.1 Window Queries" kind="prose" -->

BuzzDB's `windowQuery` method is a clean, recursive implementation of this exact logic.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.045" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Search" kind="prose" -->

#### 10.2.3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Search

Another common spatial query is the *k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN)* search, which finds the `k` objects closest to a given query point. For example, "find the 3 closest hospitals to my location."

This is more complex than a window query because the search area is not fixed; it is defined by the distance to the k-th closest neighbor we've found so far. A simple traversal could miss the true nearest neighbor if it happens to be in a subtree whose MBR is slightly farther away than another MBR.

The canonical algorithm for kNN on an R-Tree uses a priority queue to guide the search. The priority queue stores nodes to visit, ordered by the minimum possible distance (`minDist`) from the query point to the node's MBR.

The search proceeds as follows:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.046" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Search" kind="list" -->

1.  Initialize a priority queue and add the root node with a distance of 0.
2.  Initialize a list to store the `k` best results found so far.
3.  While the priority queue is not empty, pop the entry with the smallest distance. Let this be `(dist, node)`.
4.  If `dist` is greater than the distance to the k-th best result found so far, we can stop. Any remaining nodes in the queue are guaranteed to be even farther away.
5.  If `node` is an internal node, calculate the `minDist` from the query point to the MBR of each of its children. Add each child to the priority queue with its corresponding `minDist`.
6.  If `node` is a leaf node, calculate the actual distance from the query point to each object within it. Update the list of `k` best results if any of these objects are closer.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.047" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Search" kind="code" -->

BuzzDB's `kNearest` method demonstrates this pattern. It uses a `std::priority_queue` to manage the search frontier and maintains a `best` vector of results.

```cpp
// from RTree::kNearest in z-rtree.cpp
priority_queue<QItem, vector<QItem>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);
// ...
pq.emplace(0.0f, root);
while(!pq.empty()) {
    auto [bound, node] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
    if (bound > kth) break; // Pruning step

    if (node->isLeaf) {
        // ... calculate actual distances and update best results
    } else {
        for (auto& e : node->entries) {
            float b = e.mbr.minDist(q);
            if (b <= kth) pq.emplace(b, e.child); // Add promising children
        }
    }
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.048" chapter="10" section="10.2.3.2 k-Nearest Neighbor Search" kind="prose" -->

The key is the pruning condition. The variable `kth` stores the distance to the current k-th nearest neighbor. When we pop a node from the queue whose minimum possible distance (`bound`) is already greater than `kth`, we know that nothing in that node's subtree can possibly be among the top `k` results, so we can terminate the search early. Similarly, when considering children of an internal node, we only add a child to the queue if its MBR's minimum distance (`b`) is less than or equal to `kth`. This "best-first" search strategy efficiently hones in on the closest neighbors.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.049" chapter="10" section="10.2.4 Beyond 2D: The Curse of Dimensionality" kind="code" -->

### 10.2.4 Beyond 2D: The Curse of Dimensionality

The R-Tree concept is not limited to two dimensions. The MBR can be generalized to a multi-dimensional hyper-rectangle, allowing R-Trees to index data in 3D, 4D, or even hundreds of dimensions. BuzzDB's experimental `z-ndrtree.cpp` shows this generalization, defining a `Point` using a `std::vector<float>` to hold an arbitrary number of coordinates.

```cpp
// from z-ndrtree.cpp
struct Point {
    std::vector<float> coordinates;
    // ...
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.050" chapter="10" section="10.2.4 Beyond 2D: The Curse of Dimensionality" kind="quote" -->

However, as the number of dimensions (`d`) grows, the performance of R-Trees and similar spatial indexes tends to degrade dramatically. This phenomenon is known as the **Curse of Dimensionality**.

In a high-dimensional space, the volume of a hyper-rectangle grows exponentially with `d`. This has a counter-intuitive consequence: nearly all of the volume is concentrated in the "corners." As a result, MBRs must stretch to cover their enclosed points, and they end up including vast amounts of empty space. These bloated MBRs are very likely to overlap with each other, even if the data points they contain are far apart.

When MBRs overlap heavily, the R-Tree's pruning power vanishes. A query window is likely to intersect most of the MBRs at each level of the tree, forcing the search algorithm to visit nearly every node. The search degenerates from an efficient logarithmic-time operation into a slow linear scan of the entire dataset. For this reason, R-Trees are typically most effective for data with a small number of dimensions, usually not more than a handful. For the high-dimensional vector data common in modern machine learning applications, such as word embeddings or image feature vectors, different indexing structures are required, which we will explore in a later chapter.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> You are designing a system to store and query satellite images of Earth. Each image is associated with a geographic footprint—the rectangular area on the globe that it covers. Your system needs to support queries like, "Find all images that overlap with this specific region of interest."
>
> Would an R-Tree be a good choice for indexing these images by their geographic footprint? Why or why not?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.051" chapter="10" section="10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries" kind="prose" -->

## 10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries

The B+ Tree is a master of one-dimensional order. It can efficiently answer questions about ranges of numbers, alphabetical sequences of strings, or chronological series of dates. But what happens when data lives in more than one dimension, as with spatial coordinates, or when it lacks a clear, sortable structure altogether, as with free-form text? A B+ Tree can index a text column, but its utility is limited. It can quickly find all strings that *start with* a certain prefix using a query like `WHERE comment LIKE 'database%'`, because that aligns with its sorted nature. It is far less helpful for finding all comments that *contain* the word 'database' anywhere within them. A full table scan is often the only option.

This kind of "full-text search" is a cornerstone of modern applications, from web search engines to document management systems. Users expect to find documents not just by a single keyword, but by combinations of words, or by words that appear close to one another. To support these queries efficiently, databases employ specialized index structures designed for the unique challenges of unstructured text. Instead of imposing a single order on entire documents, these indexes deconstruct the text into its constituent parts—the words—and build a map from those words back to their locations. This process, known as inversion, is the key to unlocking fast and flexible text search.

In this section, we will explore two fundamental structures for text indexing. First, the inverted index, the workhorse of full-text search, which allows for rapid keyword lookups and proximity queries. Second, we will examine the trie, a tree-based structure optimized for prefix matching, which powers features like autocomplete. By looking at BuzzDB's implementations, we will see how these indexes turn the messy, unstructured world of text into a highly organized and queryable resource.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.052" chapter="10" section="10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries" kind="code" -->

#### `InvertedIndex::index` in `z-inverted-index.cpp:31-33`

The core data structure of the inverted index: a map from a term (string) to its posting list. The posting list is itself a map from a document ID to a vector of positions where the term appears.

```cpp
31	    // Map from word to a map of document ID to positions in the document
    32	    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::unordered_map<int, std::vector<int>>> index;
    33	    std::vector<std::string> documents;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.053" chapter="10" section="10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries" kind="code" -->

#### `InvertedIndex::proximitySearch` in `z-inverted-index.cpp:60-101`

Implements a proximity search by retrieving the posting lists for two words and checking for documents where their positions are within a given distance `k` of each other.

```cpp
60	    std::unordered_set<int> proximitySearch(const std::string &word1, const std::string &word2, int k) {
    61	        std::unordered_set<int> result;
    62	        std::string lowerWord1 = toLower(word1);
    63	        std::string lowerWord2 = toLower(word2);
    64	
    65	        if (index.find(lowerWord1) != index.end() && index.find(lowerWord2) != index.end()) {
    66	            for (const auto &entry1 : index[lowerWord1]) {
    67	                int docID = entry1.first;
    68	                
    69	                if (index[lowerWord2].find(docID) != index[lowerWord2].end()) {
    70	                    const auto &positions1 = entry1.second;
    71	                    const auto &positions2 = index[lowerWord2].at(docID);
    72	
    73	                    // Print the positions for debugging
    74	                    std::cout << "Doc ID: " << docID << "\n";
    75	                    std::cout << "Positions of \"" << word1 << "\": ";
    76	                    for (int pos : positions1) {
    77	                        std::cout << pos << " ";
    78	                    }
    79	                    std::cout << "\nPositions of \"" << word2 << "\": ";
    80	                    for (int pos : positions2) {
    81	                        std::cout << pos << " ";
    82	                    }
    83	                    std::cout << std::endl;
    84	
    85	                    for (int pos1 : positions1) {
    86	                        for (int pos2 : positions2) {
    87	                            if (std::abs(pos1 - pos2) <= k) {
    88	                                result.insert(docID);
    89	                                break;  // No need to check further once a match is found
    90	                            }
    91	                        }
    92	                        if (result.find(docID) != result.end()) {
    93	                            break;  // Stop checking other positions if a match is already found
    94	                        }
    95	                    }
    96	                }
    97	            }
    98	        }
    99	
   100	        return result;
   101	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.054" chapter="10" section="10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries" kind="code" -->

#### `PatriciaTrie::insertHelper` in `z-trie.cpp:18-64`

Shows the insertion logic for a Patricia trie (radix trie). It highlights the key operation: when a new word partially matches an existing edge, the edge is split to create a new internal node.

```cpp
18	    void insertHelper(PatriciaNode* node, const std::string& word, size_t index, int value) {
    19	
    20	        std::cout << "[insertHelper] Word: '" << word << "', Index: " << index << "\n";
    21	
    22	        if (index == word.length()) {
    23	            node->isEndOfWord = true;
    24	            node->value = value;  // Store the value when the word ends
    25	            return;
    26	        }
    27	
    28	        std::string remaining = word.substr(index);
    29	        for (auto& child : node->children) {
    30	            const std::string& key = child.first;
    31	            PatriciaNode* childNode = child.second;
    32	
    33	            size_t commonLength = 0;
    34	            while (commonLength < key.length() && commonLength < remaining.length() &&
    35	                   key[commonLength] == remaining[commonLength]) {
    36	                commonLength++;
    37	            }
    38	
    39	            if (commonLength > 0) {
    40	                if (commonLength < key.length()) {
    41	                    // Split the child's key
    42	                    std::string newKey = key.substr(0, commonLength);
    43	                    std::string oldKey = key.substr(commonLength);
    44	
    45	                    std::cout << "[insertHelper] Splitting Key: '" << key << "' into '" << newKey << "' and '" << oldKey << "'\n";
    46	
    47	                    PatriciaNode* newChildNode = new PatriciaNode();
    48	                    newChildNode->children[oldKey] = childNode;
    49	                    node->children[newKey] = newChildNode;
    50	                    node->children.erase(key);
    51	
    52	                    childNode = newChildNode;                    
    53	                }
    54	
    55	                insertHelper(childNode, word, index + commonLength, value);
    56	                return;
    57	            }
    58	        }
    59	
    60	        std::cout << "REMAINING: " << remaining << "\n";
    61	
    62	        node->children[remaining] = new PatriciaNode();
    63	        insertHelper(node->children[remaining], word, word.length(), value);
    64	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.055" chapter="10" section="10.3 Indexing Text: Inverted Indexes and Tries" kind="code" -->

#### `BinaryPatriciaTrie::insertHelper` in `z-trie-bitset.cpp:37-85`

Adapts the Patricia trie concept to binary data (integers). Instead of character strings, edges represent compressed paths of bits, demonstrating the generality of the trie structure.

```cpp
37	    // Insert helper to recursively insert a key
    38	    PatriciaNode* insertHelper(PatriciaNode* node, int key, int value, int bitIndex) {
    39	        if (node == nullptr) {
    40	            node = new PatriciaNode(key, bitIndex);
    41	            node->isEndOfWord = true;
    42	            node->value = value;
    43	            return node;
    44	        }
    45	
    46	        // Calculate the common prefix between the current node's key part and the new key
    47	        int commonLength = commonPrefixLength(node->keyPart, key, bitIndex);
    48	
    49	        // If we have a full match (all bits match), proceed with the insertion
    50	        if (commonLength == bitIndex) {
    51	            node->isEndOfWord = true;
    52	            node->value = value;
    53	            return node;
    54	        }
    55	
    56	        // If the current node fully matches the existing key (key divergence happens at a lower level)
    57	        if (commonLength == node->skip) {
    58	            bool bit = getBit(key, bitIndex - node->skip);
    59	            if (bit == 0) {
    60	                node->left = insertHelper(node->left, key, value, bitIndex - node->skip - 1);
    61	            } else {
    62	                node->right = insertHelper(node->right, key, value, bitIndex - node->skip - 1);
    63	            }
    64	        } else {
    65	            // Partial match, need to split the current node
    66	            PatriciaNode* newInternalNode = new PatriciaNode(key, commonLength);
    67	
    68	            // Set up the new internal node
    69	            bool bit = getBit(node->keyPart, commonLength);
    70	            if (bit == 0) {
    71	                newInternalNode->left = node;
    72	                newInternalNode->right = new PatriciaNode(key, bitIndex - commonLength);
    73	                newInternalNode->right->isEndOfWord = true;
    74	                newInternalNode->right->value = value;
    75	            } else {
    76	                newInternalNode->right = node;
    77	                newInternalNode->left = new PatriciaNode(key, bitIndex - commonLength);
    78	                newInternalNode->left->isEndOfWord = true;
    79	                newInternalNode->left->value = value;
    80	            }
    81	            return newInternalNode;
    82	        }
    83	
    84	        return node;
    85	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.056" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="prose" -->

### 10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases

Imagine you are looking for a specific concept in a large reference book. You wouldn't read it from cover to cover. Instead, you would turn to the index at the back. The book's index lists important terms in alphabetical order, and for each term, it provides the page numbers where that term appears. This is a physical example of an inverted index. It inverts the natural structure of the book (pages containing words) into a map from words back to pages.

A database's inverted index operates on the same principle. It treats each document (or row, or text field) as a "page" and each word as a "term." The index is a dictionary structure that maps each term to a list of all documents that contain it. This list is called a **posting list**.

A simple posting list might just contain document IDs. For the query "find all documents containing 'SQL'", the system would look up 'sql' in its dictionary, retrieve the corresponding posting list `[doc_3, doc_8, doc_42]`, and return those documents. This is already a massive improvement over a table scan.

However, we can make the index more powerful by storing more information in the posting lists. A common enhancement is to also record the *position* of each term within the document—for example, 'sql' appears in `doc_3` as the 5th and 21st words. This positional information is crucial for handling more sophisticated queries, such as finding documents where 'database' and 'systems' appear near each other.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.057" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="code" -->

BuzzDB's implementation of an inverted index reveals this structure clearly. The core of the index is a C++ `std::unordered_map`, a hash map that provides fast key-value lookups.

```cpp
// Map from word to a map of document ID to positions in the document
std::unordered_map<std::string, std::unordered_map<int, std::vector<int>>> index;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.058" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="list" -->

Let's break down this nested type definition:

1.  `std::unordered_map<std::string, ...>`: This is the main dictionary. The key is a `std::string`, representing a term (e.g., "database").
2.  `... std::unordered_map<int, ...>>`: The value associated with each term is another map. This map is the posting list. Its key is an `int`, representing the document ID.
3.  `... std::vector<int>>`: The value associated with each document ID is a vector of integers. This vector stores the 0-indexed positions where the term appears in that document.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.059" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="table" -->

To make this concrete, consider the following three simple documents:

| Doc ID | Content                                       |
| :----- | :-------------------------------------------- |
| 1      | "Database systems are the best systems."      |
| 2      | "A query processor is part of a database."    |
| 3      | "Relational systems use a structured query."  |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.060" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="table" -->

After tokenizing (splitting into words), lowercasing, and removing common "stop words" like "are", "the", and "a", BuzzDB would build the following inverted index from these documents:

| Term        | Posting List (Map of DocID -> Positions)                               |
| :---------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "database"  | `{ 1: [0], 2: [6] }`                                                   |
| "systems"   | `{ 1: [1, 4], 3: [1] }`                                                |
| "best"      | `{ 1: [3] }`                                                           |
| "query"     | `{ 2: [1], 3: [5] }`                                                   |
| "processor" | `{ 2: [2] }`                                                           |
| "is"        | `{ 2: [3] }`                                                           |
| "part"      | `{ 2: [4] }`                                                           |
| "of"        | `{ 2: [5] }`                                                           |
| "relational"| `{ 3: [0] }`                                                           |
| "use"       | `{ 3: [2] }`                                                           |
| "structured"| `{ 3: [4] }`                                                           |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.061" chapter="10" section="10.3.1 The Inverted Index: A Concordance for Databases" kind="prose" -->

With this structure in place, finding all documents containing "systems" is a single hash map lookup. The result is the map `{ 1: [1, 4], 3: [1] }`, from which we can easily extract the document IDs: 1 and 3. The real power of this index, however, emerges when we start combining these lists to answer more complex questions.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.062" chapter="10" section="10.3.2 Querying with Posting Lists: Intersections and Proximity" kind="list" -->

### 10.3.2 Querying with Posting Lists: Intersections and Proximity

Once the inverted index is built, it can serve a variety of queries. The simplest is a single-term query, which we've seen is just a dictionary lookup. More interesting are multi-term queries. For a boolean query like "find documents containing 'database' AND 'systems'", the process is straightforward:

1.  Retrieve the posting list for "database": `{ 1: [0], 2: [6] }`.
2.  Retrieve the posting list for "systems": `{ 1: [1, 4], 3: [1] }`.
3.  Find the intersection of the document IDs present in both lists. The document IDs for "database" are {1, 2}. The document IDs for "systems" are {1, 3}. The intersection is {1}.
4.  The result is Document 1.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.063" chapter="10" section="10.3.2 Querying with Posting Lists: Intersections and Proximity" kind="code" -->

This intersection operation is fundamental to processing text queries. Efficient algorithms for intersecting sorted lists of document IDs (often using a merge-join-like approach) are a key optimization in large-scale search systems.

The positional information in BuzzDB's index unlocks an even more powerful type of query: the proximity search. A user might want to find documents where 'structured' and 'query' appear within, say, two words of each other. This is a much stronger signal of relevance than just finding a document that contains both words somewhere. BuzzDB's `proximitySearch` method implements exactly this logic.

Let's trace a call to `proximitySearch("structured", "query", 2)` using the index from our example.

```cpp
std::unordered_set<int> proximitySearch(const std::string &word1, const std::string &word2, int k) {
    std::unordered_set<int> result;
    // ... words are lowercased ...

    if (index.find(lowerWord1) != index.end() && index.find(lowerWord2) != index.end()) {
        // Both words exist in the index.
        // For "structured", index[lowerWord1] is { 3: [4] }
        // For "query", index[lowerWord2] is { 2: [1], 3: [5] }

        for (const auto &entry1 : index[lowerWord1]) {
            int docID = entry1.first; // First (and only) iteration: docID = 3

            if (index[lowerWord2].find(docID) != index[lowerWord2].end()) {
                // Does the posting list for "query" contain docID 3? Yes.

                const auto &positions1 = entry1.second; // positions1 = [4]
                const auto &positions2 = index[lowerWord2].at(docID); // positions2 = [5]

                for (int pos1 : positions1) { // Outer loop: pos1 = 4
                    for (int pos2 : positions2) { // Inner loop: pos2 = 5
                        if (std::abs(pos1 - pos2) <= k) { // is abs(4 - 5) <= 2? Yes, 1 <= 2.
                            result.insert(docID); // Add 3 to the result set.
                            break; // Found a match in this doc, no need to check other positions.
                        }
                    }
                    if (result.find(docID) != result.end()) {
                        break; // Stop checking positions for pos1 if doc is already added.
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return result; // Returns {3}
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.064" chapter="10" section="10.3.2 Querying with Posting Lists: Intersections and Proximity" kind="prose" -->

The code first performs the intersection of document IDs. It iterates through all documents containing the first word (`for (const auto &entry1 ...)`). For each of these documents, it checks if the second word's posting list also contains that document ID (`if (index[lowerWord2].find(docID) ...)`).

Only if a document contains *both* words does it proceed to the expensive part: the nested loop over positions. This is a critical performance detail. The algorithm avoids comparing positions for documents that couldn't possibly satisfy the query. Inside the nested loops, the core logic `std::abs(pos1 - pos2) <= k` checks if the distance between the two words is within the specified proximity `k`. The two `break` statements are simple but effective optimizations: once a single pair of positions satisfies the proximity constraint for a given document, that document is added to the results, and the inner loops can terminate early for that document. There's no need to find *all* proximity matches if we only care about *whether* one exists.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.065" chapter="10" section="10.3.3 Tries for Prefix Search and Autocomplete" kind="prose" -->

### 10.3.3 Tries for Prefix Search and Autocomplete

Inverted indexes are excellent for finding documents based on whole words, but they are not well-suited for another common text operation: prefix matching. Applications like search bars, code editors, and command-line shells often provide "autocomplete" or "type-ahead" suggestions. As a user types `databa`, the system should suggest `database`. A B+ Tree can handle this, but it involves string comparisons at each level of the tree. A more natural and often more efficient structure for this task is the **trie** (from "re*trie*val", often pronounced "try").

A trie, also known as a prefix tree, is a tree structure where each path from the root to a node represents a prefix. In a simple character trie, each node might have an array of pointers, one for each character in the alphabet (e.g., 26 for English letters). To insert the word "team", you would start at the root, follow the 't' pointer to a child node, then the 'e' pointer from there, and so on. The final node, corresponding to the full word "team", would be marked with a special flag to indicate it's the end of a valid word.

The key advantage of a trie is that the time to search for a word (or check if a prefix exists) is proportional to the length of the word or prefix, not the number of words in the dictionary. To find all words starting with "data", you simply traverse the trie along the path `d-a-t-a`. All words in the subtree rooted at that final node are your results.

However, this simple trie structure has a significant drawback: it can be very space-inefficient. If you insert the word "database", you create a chain of eight nodes, many of which may have only a single child. If no other word in your dictionary starts with "databas", then seven of those nodes are just wasteful intermediate steps.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.066" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="list" -->

### 10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie

To combat the space inefficiency of simple tries, a more compact variant called a **Patricia Trie** (or **Radix Trie**) is used. The core idea is to compress any chain of single-child nodes into a single edge. Instead of edges representing single characters, they represent sequences of characters.

When a new word is inserted, one of three things can happen:

1.  The new word's prefix matches an existing path, and the word extends beyond it. A new edge is simply added.
2.  The new word is a prefix of an existing word. The node where the new word ends is marked as an end-of-word node.
3.  The new word shares a prefix with an existing edge but then diverges. This is the most interesting case: the existing edge must be **split** into two. A new internal node is created at the point of divergence.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.067" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="code" -->

BuzzDB's `PatriciaTrie` implementation showcases this splitting logic in its `insertHelper` method. Let's trace the insertion of a few words to see how the trie evolves.

**1. Insert "team"** The trie is initially empty. The word "team" is added as a single edge from the root.

```
(root)
  |
  +-- "team" --> (node1, isEnd=true)
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.068" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="list" -->

**2. Insert "test"** The `insertHelper` starts at the root. It compares the new word "test" with the existing edges.

- It finds the edge labeled "team".
- It calculates the length of the common prefix between "test" and "team", which is "te" (length 2).
- The code detects that a split is necessary because the common length (2) is less than the edge's key length (4).

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.069" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="code" -->

The `insertHelper` logic executes the split:

```cpp
// commonLength = 2, key = "team"
if (commonLength < key.length()) { // 2 < 4 is true
    // Split the child's key
    std::string newKey = key.substr(0, commonLength); // "te"
    std::string oldKey = key.substr(commonLength);   // "am"

    // Create a new internal node for the "te" prefix
    PatriciaNode* newChildNode = new PatriciaNode();

    // The original child (node1) is now a child of this new node,
    // reached via the remainder of its old key, "am".
    newChildNode->children[oldKey] = childNode; // childNode is node1

    // The new node is attached to the parent (root) under the common prefix "te".
    node->children[newKey] = newChildNode;

    // The old edge "team" is removed from the root.
    node->children.erase(key);

    // ... recursive call continues from the new node to insert "st" ...
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.070" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="code" -->

After the split and the insertion of the remainder "st", the trie looks like this:

```
(root)
  |
  +-- "te" --> (node2, isEnd=false)
                |
                +-- "am" --> (node1, isEnd=true)  // Remainder of "team"
                |
                +-- "st" --> (node3, isEnd=true)  // Remainder of "test"
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.071" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="list" -->

The single edge "team" has been replaced by a new internal node `node2` representing the prefix "te", with two branches leading to the unique suffixes "am" and "st".

**3. Insert "tea"**

- The helper traverses from the root down the "te" edge to `node2`.
- The remaining part of the word to insert is "a".
- At `node2`, it compares "a" with the outgoing edges "am" and "st".
- It finds a common prefix of length 1 ("a") with the "am" edge.
- Another split is required! The "am" edge is split into "a" and "m".

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.072" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="code" -->

The final structure becomes:

```
(root)
  |
  +-- "te" --> (node2, isEnd=false)
                |
                +-- "a" --> (node4, isEnd=true)   // "tea" ends here
                |   |
                |   +-- "m" --> (node1, isEnd=true) // Remainder of "team"
                |
                +-- "st" --> (node3, isEnd=true)  // Remainder of "test"
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.073" chapter="10" section="10.3.4 Compressing Tries: The Patricia Trie" kind="prose" -->

Now, the node `node4` is marked as `isEnd=true` because "tea" is a valid word, and it also has a child edge "m" that completes the word "team". This compact structure efficiently stores the shared prefixes while only creating branches where the words diverge.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.074" chapter="10" section="10.3.5 From Strings to Bits" kind="code" -->

### 10.3.5 From Strings to Bits

The concept of a Patricia Trie is not limited to character strings. The "alphabet" used to build the tree can be anything, as long as the keys can be seen as a sequence of symbols from that alphabet. A powerful generalization is to treat keys as sequences of bits, where the alphabet is simply {0, 1}. This allows tries to index integers, IP addresses, or any other data that has a fixed-size binary representation.

BuzzDB's `BinaryPatriciaTrie` demonstrates this principle. It applies the exact same logic of compressing paths and splitting nodes, but it operates on the bits of an integer key. Instead of edges labeled with substrings, its nodes effectively represent a decision point: "at this bit position, does the key have a 0 or a 1?". The path compression is handled by storing a `skip` value in each node, indicating how many bits are shared along the path to it.

The `insertHelper` for the binary version mirrors its string-based counterpart:

```cpp
// Partial match, need to split the current node
PatriciaNode* newInternalNode = new PatriciaNode(key, commonLength);

// Set up the new internal node
bool bit = getBit(node->keyPart, commonLength);
if (bit == 0) {
    newInternalNode->left = node;
    newInternalNode->right = new PatriciaNode(key, bitIndex - commonLength);
    // ...
} else {
    newInternalNode->right = node;
    newInternalNode->left = new PatriciaNode(key, bitIndex - commonLength);
    // ...
}
return newInternalNode;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.075" chapter="10" section="10.3.5 From Strings to Bits" kind="quote" -->

Here, `commonPrefixLength` calculates how many of the most significant bits are shared between the new key and the key represented by the current node. When a split is needed (`commonLength` is less than the number of bits skipped to reach the current node), a `newInternalNode` is created. The next bit in the *existing* key (`getBit(node->keyPart, commonLength)`) determines whether the old node goes to the left (0) or right (1) child of the new internal node. The new key's path is then attached to the other child.

This demonstrates the abstract power of the trie. Whether dealing with characters in a word or bits in an integer, the fundamental algorithm of finding the point of divergence and creating a new branch remains the same. This makes it a versatile tool for specialized indexing tasks beyond simple text search.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> 1.  **Index Size.** Consider the inverted index from the first subsection. If you add a fourth document, "Database query languages are powerful," which terms from the existing index will have their posting lists updated? Which new terms will be added to the index dictionary? Roughly how does the size of an inverted index grow in relation to the number of documents and the number of unique words?
>
> 2.  **Trie Insertion.** Starting with the final Patricia Trie from our example (containing "team", "test", and "tea"), draw the state of the trie after inserting the word "ten". Which existing edge is split? What are the labels of the new edges created?
>
> 3.  **Design Choice.** You are designing a product catalog database. The `products` table has a `description` column (long text) and a `product_code` column (e.g., 'SKU-123-ABC'). Users need to be able to search for products by keywords in the description and also be able to type the beginning of a product code to get suggestions. Would you use an inverted index, a Patricia Trie, or a B+ Tree for each of these columns? Justify your choices.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.076" chapter="10" section="10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search" kind="prose" -->

## 10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search

The previous section explored how specialized indexes like inverted files and tries can conquer the unstructured world of text by finding exact matches for keywords. We saw that the challenge was not ordering, but rather mapping from a sparse set of terms to the documents that contain them. We now turn to a different kind of unstructured data, one that has become central to modern artificial intelligence and data analysis: the high-dimensional vector.

Imagine you are building a music recommendation service. When a user listens to a song, you want to suggest others that have a similar "vibe"—perhaps a similar tempo, instrumentation, or mood. Or consider an e-commerce platform where a user can upload a photo of a chair they like and ask the system to find similar-looking chairs in its catalog. In both cases, the core problem is defining and searching for "similarity." How can a database quantify the "vibe" of a song or the "style" of a chair?

The answer lies in a technique called *embedding*. Modern machine learning models, particularly deep neural networks, have a remarkable ability to act as universal translators. They can take a complex object—a song's audio waveform, an image's pixels, a paragraph of text—and convert it into a dense list of numbers called a **vector embedding**. In BuzzDB, this is represented by the simple but powerful `Point` struct, which is just a wrapper around a `std::vector<float>`.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.077" chapter="10" section="10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search" kind="code" -->

#### `Node` in `z-hnsw.cpp:57-63`

Defines the HNSW graph node, which contains a point and a multi-level list of neighbors. `neighbors[i]` stores the connections for this node at layer `i` of the hierarchy.

```cpp
57	struct Node {
    58	    Point point;
    59	    std::vector<std::vector<Node*>> neighbors;
    60	
    61	    explicit Node(const Point& pt, int maxLevel) 
    62	        : point(pt), neighbors(maxLevel + 1) {}
    63	};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.078" chapter="10" section="10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search" kind="code" -->

#### `HNSW::insertNode` in `z-hnsw.cpp:96-119`

Shows the HNSW insertion process. A new node is inserted from the top layer down, performing a `searchLayer` at each level to find its nearest neighbors and establish connections.

```cpp
96	    void insertNode(Node* newNode) {
    97	        if (graph.nodes.empty()) {
    98	            graph.nodes.push_back(newNode);
    99	            graph.entrance = newNode;
   100	            return;
   101	        }
   102	
   103	        Node* enterPoint = graph.entrance;
   104	        int level = maxLevel;
   105	
   106	        // Ensure layer access is within bounds
   107	        int effectiveLevel = std::min(static_cast<int>(newNode->neighbors.size()) - 1, level);
   108	        for (int lc = level; lc > effectiveLevel; --lc) {
   109	            enterPoint = searchLayer(enterPoint, newNode->point, lc, 1).top().second;
   110	        }
   111	
   112	        for (int lc = effectiveLevel; lc >= 0; --lc) {
   113	            auto topCandidates = searchLayer(enterPoint, newNode->point, lc, efConstruction);
   114	            selectNeighbors(newNode, topCandidates, lc);
   115	        }
   116	
   117	        maxLevel = std::max(maxLevel, effectiveLevel);
   118	        graph.nodes.push_back(newNode);
   119	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.079" chapter="10" section="10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search" kind="code" -->

#### `HNSW::searchLayer` in `z-hnsw.cpp:121-156`

Implements the greedy search algorithm within a single layer of the HNSW graph. It explores neighbors to find the `ef` points closest to the query, forming the candidate set for the next layer down.

```cpp
121	    std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>> searchLayer(Node* enterPoint, const Point& point, int level, int ef) {
   122	        std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>> topCandidates;
   123	        std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>, std::vector<std::pair<float, Node*>>, std::greater<>> candidates;
   124	        std::unordered_map<Node*, bool> visited;
   125	
   126	        float lowerBound = euclideanDistance(point, enterPoint->point);
   127	        candidates.emplace(lowerBound, enterPoint);
   128	        topCandidates.emplace(lowerBound, enterPoint);
   129	        visited[enterPoint] = true;
   130	
   131	        while (!candidates.empty()) {
   132	            auto currPair = candidates.top();
   133	            float dist = currPair.first;
   134	            Node* currNode = currPair.second;
   135	            candidates.pop();
   136	
   137	            if (dist > lowerBound) break;
   138	
   139	            for (Node* neighbor : currNode->neighbors[level]) {
   140	                if (!visited[neighbor]) {
   141	                    visited[neighbor] = true;
   142	                    float d = euclideanDistance(point, neighbor->point);
   143	                    if (topCandidates.size() < static_cast<size_t>(ef) || d < lowerBound) {
   144	                        candidates.emplace(d, neighbor);
   145	                        topCandidates.emplace(d, neighbor);
   146	                        if (topCandidates.size() > static_cast<size_t>(ef)) {
   147	                            topCandidates.pop();
   148	                            lowerBound = topCandidates.top().first;
   149	                        }
   150	                    }
   151	                }
   152	            }
   153	        }
   154	
   155	        return topCandidates;
   156	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.082" chapter="10" section="10.4 Indexing High-Dimensional Vectors for Similarity Search" kind="prose" -->

These vectors are not just random numbers. They are carefully constructed so that their geometric relationships in a high-dimensional space mirror the semantic relationships of the original objects. Two songs with a similar vibe will have their embedding vectors located close to each other in this space. Two visually similar chairs will likewise have their vectors clustered together. The problem of finding "similar items" is thus transformed into a geometric one: given a query vector, find its *nearest neighbors* in a massive dataset of other vectors. This is known as a **k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN)** search.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.083" chapter="10" section="10.4.1 Why Exact Methods Fail: The Curse of Dimensionality Revisited" kind="list" -->

### 10.4.1 Why Exact Methods Fail: The Curse of Dimensionality Revisited

Our first instinct might be to apply the spatial indexing techniques we've seen before. An R-Tree, for example, is excellent at indexing two- or three-dimensional geographic data. It partitions space with minimum bounding rectangles (MBRs) and can quickly prune entire regions that do not overlap with a query window. Why not just extend this to the 128, 512, or even 1536 dimensions common in modern vector embeddings?

The reason this fails is a counter-intuitive but fundamental problem in high-dimensional geometry known as the **curse of dimensionality**. As the number of dimensions (`d`) increases, the volume of the space grows exponentially (`Volume ∝ L^d`). The data points we have, even if there are millions of them, become incredibly sparse, like a few grains of sand in an ever-expanding universe.

This sparsity has several bizarre and debilitating consequences for indexing:

1.  **Distance Concentration:** In high dimensions, the distance between any two randomly chosen points becomes almost the same. The concept of a "close" neighbor and a "far" neighbor begins to lose its meaning. The ratio of the distance to the nearest neighbor and the farthest neighbor approaches 1, making it difficult to discriminate between points based on distance.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.084" chapter="10" section="10.4.1 Why Exact Methods Fail: The Curse of Dimensionality Revisited" kind="list" -->

2.  **Ineffective Partitioning:** For an index like an R-Tree to be effective, its MBRs must partition the space cleanly, allowing the search algorithm to discard large parts of the dataset. In high dimensions, any MBR that contains even a small cluster of points must be extended so far in every other dimension that it ends up overlapping with almost every other MBR. A query for a point near the edge of an MBR will force the search to visit not just one or two neighboring boxes, but a huge fraction of all the boxes in the tree.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.085" chapter="10" section="10.4.1 Why Exact Methods Fail: The Curse of Dimensionality Revisited" kind="prose" -->

The result is that the index ceases to be a shortcut. The search algorithm spends all its time navigating a complex tree structure only to conclude that it must visit nearly every data point anyway. The performance of the index search degrades until it is no better—and often worse, due to overhead—than a simple, brute-force sequential scan of every vector in the database. For datasets with millions or billions of vectors, this is computationally infeasible.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.086" chapter="10" section="10.4.2 The ANN Trade-off: Good Enough is Better than Perfect" kind="prose" -->

### 10.4.2 The ANN Trade-off: Good Enough is Better than Perfect

If an exact k-NN search is prohibitively slow, we are faced with a critical engineering trade-off. What if we could design an index that was incredibly fast but didn't guarantee finding the *absolute* closest neighbors? What if, instead, it guaranteed finding a set of neighbors that were *very likely* to be the correct ones? This is the core idea behind **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)** search.

For applications like music recommendation or image search, this trade-off is not just acceptable; it's ideal. If a user is looking for a chair similar to one in a photo, they don't care if the system returns the 1st, 2nd, and 5th most similar chairs instead of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. The results are, for all practical purposes, just as good. The user gets a relevant, high-quality response in milliseconds instead of minutes.

The quality of an ANN search is often measured by **recall**. Recall@k is the proportion of the true top-k nearest neighbors that are returned by the approximate search.

`Recall@k = | (True top-k neighbors) ∩ (Returned k neighbors) | / k`

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.087" chapter="10" section="10.4.2 The ANN Trade-off: Good Enough is Better than Perfect" kind="prose" -->

An ANN index might achieve a recall of 99% while being 100 to 1000 times faster than an exact, brute-force search. This is the trade-off that makes similarity search practical at scale. There are many algorithms for building ANN indexes—including quantization-based methods and tree-based methods—but one of the most successful and widely used is a graph-based approach called Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW).

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.088" chapter="10" section="10.4.3 HNSW: A Multi-Layer Navigable Graph" kind="list" -->

### 10.4.3 HNSW: A Multi-Layer Navigable Graph

The HNSW algorithm organizes data points into a special kind of proximity graph. In this graph, the nodes are the vectors themselves, and an edge between two nodes means they are close to each other in the vector space. A naive search would involve starting at a random node and "walking" through the graph, always moving to the neighbor closest to the query vector until a local minimum is reached. This is better than a full scan, but it can easily get stuck in a region of the graph that is far from the true nearest neighbor.

The key innovation of HNSW is its **hierarchical** structure. Instead of one flat graph, HNSW builds a series of graphs in layers.

*   **Layer 0:** This is the base layer and contains every single data point. The graph here is dense, with each node connected to a number of its closest neighbors.
*   **Higher Layers (1, 2, 3, ...):** Each higher layer is a sparse subgraph of the one below it. A node from Layer `i` is promoted to Layer `i+1` with a certain probability. This means Layer 1 contains a random subset of the nodes from Layer 0, Layer 2 contains a subset of Layer 1, and so on. The highest layers are extremely sparse.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.089" chapter="10" section="10.4.3 HNSW: A Multi-Layer Navigable Graph" kind="code" -->

The edges in the higher, sparser layers act as "expressways" for navigating the vector space. A search can quickly traverse long distances across the graph at a high layer before descending to the lower, denser layers for fine-grained refinement.

This multi-layer structure is directly visible in the BuzzDB implementation of an HNSW node. The `Node` struct contains not just the vector data (`Point`) but also a vector of vectors to store its neighbor lists at each level of the hierarchy.

```cpp
// from z-hnsw.cpp
struct Node {
    Point point;
    std::vector<std::vector<Node*>> neighbors;

    explicit Node(const Point& pt, int maxLevel) 
        : point(pt), neighbors(maxLevel + 1) {}
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.090" chapter="10" section="10.4.3 HNSW: A Multi-Layer Navigable Graph" kind="code" -->

Here, `neighbors[0]` holds the list of `Node*` pointers for the dense base layer, `neighbors[1]` holds the list for the sparser layer above it, and so on, up to the maximum level this particular node exists in.

We can visualize this structure with a simple one-dimensional analogy. Imagine our points are laid out on a line. A search for point `G` starting from `A` would be slow at the base layer. But with the hierarchy, the search can take a long-range link from `A` to `E` at a higher layer, getting much closer to the target in a single step.

```
Layer 2:  A -----------------------------------> E

           |                                      |
           v                                      v
Layer 1:  A <---------> C <--------------------> E

           |             |                        |
           v             v                        v
Layer 0:  A <-> B <-> C <-> D <-> E <-> F <-> G
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.091" chapter="10" section="10.4.3 HNSW: A Multi-Layer Navigable Graph" kind="prose" -->

This layered approach allows HNSW to combine the best of two worlds: fast, long-distance traversal using the sparse upper layers, and precise, short-distance searching using the dense lower layers.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.092" chapter="10" section="10.4.4 HNSW Search and Insertion" kind="prose" -->

### 10.4.4 HNSW Search and Insertion

With the multi-layer graph in place, the search and insertion algorithms become an elegant process of descending through the hierarchy.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.093" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.1 The Search Algorithm" kind="list" -->

#### 10.4.4.1 The Search Algorithm

A k-NN search in HNSW proceeds as follows:

1.  **Enter at the Top:** The search begins at a fixed entry point in the sparsest, topmost layer of the graph.
2.  **Greedy Search Downwards:** At the current layer, the algorithm greedily traverses the graph. From the current node, it examines its neighbors and moves to the one that is closest to the query vector. This continues until it reaches a local minimum—a node where no neighbor is closer to the query.
3.  **Drop and Refine:** The node found at the end of the search in layer `i` becomes the entry point for the search in layer `i-1`.
4.  **Repeat:** This process of greedy search followed by dropping to the next layer is repeated until the search reaches the dense base layer (Layer 0).
5.  **Final Search:** At Layer 0, a more exhaustive search is performed, exploring a larger set of candidate nodes to produce the final list of `k` nearest neighbors.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.094" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.1 The Search Algorithm" kind="code" -->

The core of this process within a single layer is implemented in BuzzDB's `HNSW::searchLayer` method. This function is the workhorse of both search and insertion.

```cpp
// from z-hnsw.cpp
std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>> 
searchLayer(Node* enterPoint, const Point& point, int level, int ef) {
    // ...
    std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>> topCandidates; // Max-heap for best results
    std::priority_queue<std::pair<float, Node*>, ..., std::greater<>> candidates; // Min-heap for visit list
    std::unordered_map<Node*, bool> visited;

    float lowerBound = euclideanDistance(point, enterPoint->point);
    candidates.emplace(lowerBound, enterPoint);
    topCandidates.emplace(lowerBound, enterPoint);
    visited[enterPoint] = true;

    while (!candidates.empty()) {
        // ...
        Node* currNode = candidates.top().second;
        candidates.pop();

        if (currNode's distance > lowerBound) break; // Pruning

        for (Node* neighbor : currNode->neighbors[level]) {
            if (!visited[neighbor]) {
                visited[neighbor] = true;
                float d = euclideanDistance(point, neighbor->point);
                if (topCandidates.size() < ef || d < lowerBound) {
                    candidates.emplace(d, neighbor);
                    topCandidates.emplace(d, neighbor);
                    if (topCandidates.size() > ef) {
                        topCandidates.pop();
                        lowerBound = topCandidates.top().first;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return topCandidates;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.095" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.1 The Search Algorithm" kind="list" -->

Let's break down this critical function. It maintains two main data structures:

*   `candidates`: A min-priority queue that acts as a "to-do list" of nodes to visit, ordered by their distance to the query point. We always explore the most promising (closest) node next.
*   `topCandidates`: A max-priority queue that holds the `ef` best nodes found so far. `ef` is a crucial tuning parameter, the "effective search factor." It determines the size of the dynamic candidate list. A larger `ef` leads to a more accurate but slower search.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.096" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.1 The Search Algorithm" kind="prose" -->

The `while` loop drives the search. It pulls the closest unvisited node from `candidates`. The distance to the farthest node in `topCandidates` is stored in `lowerBound`. If the closest node in our visit list (`candidates`) is already farther away than the farthest node in our result set (`topCandidates`), there's no hope of finding a better candidate by exploring from it, so we can stop the search early (`if (dist > lowerBound) break;`). This is a key optimization. For each neighbor of the current node, we calculate its distance. If it's better than the worst candidate in our result set, we add it to both queues and update `lowerBound`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.097" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.2 The Insertion Algorithm" kind="list" -->

#### 10.4.4.2 The Insertion Algorithm

Inserting a new node into an HNSW graph cleverly uses the search algorithm itself. To find the right place for a new node and connect it to its neighbors, the system must first find where that node *would* belong.

The `HNSW::insertNode` method in BuzzDB shows this process clearly.

1.  **Assign a Level:** First, a new node is assigned a random maximum level `L`. It will be inserted into all layers from 0 to `L`.
2.  **Find Entry Points:** The algorithm starts at the global entry point of the entire graph (at the very top layer) and performs a `searchLayer` to find the closest node. It descends layer by layer until it reaches level `L`, the new node's top level.
3.  **Find and Connect Neighbors:** From level `L` down to 0, the algorithm performs a more thorough search at each layer using `searchLayer`. The goal is to find the `efConstruction` nearest neighbors to the new node *at that layer*. `efConstruction` is a build-time parameter analogous to the query-time `ef`.
4.  **Establish Links:** After finding the best neighbors, the `selectNeighbors` function (not shown) is called to create the actual edges in the graph, connecting the new node to its neighbors and, in some cases, neighbors to the new node.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.098" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.2 The Insertion Algorithm" kind="code" -->

```cpp
// from z-hnsw.cpp
void insertNode(Node* newNode) {
    // ... handle empty graph ...
    Node* enterPoint = graph.entrance;
    int level = maxLevel;
    int effectiveLevel = newNode->neighbors.size() - 1;

    // 1. Search from global top layer down to the new node's top layer
    //    to find the best entry point for the real insertion.
    for (int lc = level; lc > effectiveLevel; --lc) {
        enterPoint = searchLayer(enterPoint, newNode->point, lc, 1).top().second;
    }

    // 2. For each level the new node belongs to (from its top down to 0)...
    for (int lc = effectiveLevel; lc >= 0; --lc) {
        // 3. ...find its nearest neighbors at that level.
        auto topCandidates = searchLayer(enterPoint, newNode->point, lc, efConstruction);
        // 4. ...and connect it into the graph.
        selectNeighbors(newNode, topCandidates, lc);
    }
    // ...
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch10.099" chapter="10" section="10.4.4.2 The Insertion Algorithm" kind="prose" -->

This "search-then-connect" strategy ensures that the graph maintains its high-quality structure. New nodes are intelligently woven into the existing hierarchy, creating new shortcuts and pathways that will benefit future queries. The quality of the index—and therefore its query performance and accuracy—is determined almost entirely by how well this insertion process builds a robust, navigable graph.
