<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.024" chapter="13" section="13.2 Implementing Aggregation with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

#### `HashAggregationOperator::FieldVectorHasher` in `41-buzzdb.cpp:943-979`

The custom hasher required to use a vector of Field objects as a key in an std::unordered_map, demonstrating a key implementation detail for grouping.

```cpp
943	    struct FieldVectorHasher {
   944	        std::size_t operator()(const std::vector<Field>& fields) const {
   945	            std::size_t hash = 0;
   946	            for (const auto& field : fields) {
   947	                std::hash<std::string> hasher;
   948	                std::size_t fieldHash = 0;
   949	
   950	                // Depending on the type, hash the corresponding data
   951	                switch (field.type) {
   952	                    case INT: {
   953	                        // Convert integer data to string and hash
   954	                        int value = *reinterpret_cast<const int*>(field.data.get());
   955	                        fieldHash = hasher(std::to_string(value));
   956	                        break;
   957	                    }
   958	                    case FLOAT: {
   959	                        // Convert float data to string and hash
   960	                        float value = *reinterpret_cast<const float*>(field.data.get());
   961	                        fieldHash = hasher(std::to_string(value));
   962	                        break;
   963	                    }
   964	                    case STRING: {
   965	                        // Directly hash the string data
   966	                        std::string value(field.data.get(), field.data_length - 1); // Exclude null-terminator
   967	                        fieldHash = hasher(value);
   968	                        break;
   969	                    }
   970	                    default:
   971	                        throw std::runtime_error("Unsupported field type for hashing.");
   972	                }
   973	
   974	                // Combine the hash of the current field with the hash so far
   975	                hash ^= fieldHash + 0x9e3779b9 + (hash << 6) + (hash >> 2);
   976	            }
   977	            return hash;
   978	        }
   979	    };
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.025" chapter="13" section="13.2 Implementing Aggregation with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

#### `HashAggregationOperator::updateAggregate` in `41-buzzdb.cpp:1068-1119`

The helper function that applies an incoming tuple's value to the running aggregate state for a group, handling functions like SUM, MAX, MIN, and COUNT.

```cpp
1068	    Field updateAggregate(const AggrFunc& aggrFunc, const Field& currentAggr, const Field& newValue) {
  1069	        if (currentAggr.getType() != newValue.getType()) {
  1070	            throw std::runtime_error("Mismatched Field types in aggregation.");
  1071	        }
  1072	
  1073	        switch (aggrFunc.func) {
  1074	            case AggrFuncType::COUNT: {
  1075	                if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::INT) {
  1076	                    // For COUNT, simply increment the integer value
  1077	                    int count = currentAggr.asInt() + 1;
  1078	                    return Field(count);
  1079	                }
  1080	                break;
  1081	            }
  1082	            case AggrFuncType::SUM: {
  1083	                if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::INT) {
  1084	                    int sum = currentAggr.asInt() + newValue.asInt();
  1085	                    return Field(sum);
  1086	                } else if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::FLOAT) {
  1087	                    float sum = currentAggr.asFloat() + newValue.asFloat();
  1088	                    return Field(sum);
  1089	                }
  1090	                break;
  1091	            }
  1092	            case AggrFuncType::MAX: {
  1093	                if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::INT) {
  1094	                    int max = std::max(currentAggr.asInt(), newValue.asInt());
  1095	                    return Field(max);
  1096	                } else if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::FLOAT) {
  1097	                    float max = std::max(currentAggr.asFloat(), newValue.asFloat());
  1098	                    return Field(max);
  1099	                }
  1100	                break;
  1101	            }
  1102	            case AggrFuncType::MIN: {
  1103	                if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::INT) {
  1104	                    int min = std::min(currentAggr.asInt(), newValue.asInt());
  1105	                    return Field(min);
  1106	                } else if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::FLOAT) {
  1107	                    float min = std::min(currentAggr.asFloat(), newValue.asFloat());
  1108	                    return Field(min);
  1109	                }
  1110	                break;
  1111	            }
  1112	            default:
  1113	                throw std::runtime_error("Unsupported aggregation function.");
  1114	        }
  1115	
  1116	        // Default case for unsupported operations or types
  1117	        throw std::runtime_error(
  1118	            "Invalid operation or unsupported Field type.");
  1119	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.026" chapter="13" section="13.2.1 Anatomy of the Aggregation Operator" kind="code" -->

### 13.2.1 Anatomy of the Aggregation Operator

The `HashAggregationOperator` is the workhorse for `GROUP BY` queries in BuzzDB. When the query planner builds an execution tree, it places this operator at a point where it can consume a stream of tuples and emit a new, smaller stream of aggregated results. To do its job, the operator needs to be configured with two key pieces of information: which columns define the groups, and what calculations to perform on each group.

This configuration is provided when the operator is created. The grouping columns are specified as a list of attribute indexes, and the aggregation tasks are defined using a simple C++ struct, `AggrFunc`:

```cpp
enum class AggrFuncType { COUNT, MAX, MIN, SUM };

struct AggrFunc {
    AggrFuncType func;
    size_t attr_index; // Index of the attribute to aggregate
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.027" chapter="13" section="13.2.1 Anatomy of the Aggregation Operator" kind="list" -->

This small structure elegantly captures the semantics of a SQL aggregate function. For a query like `SELECT department, SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department`, the planner would configure the `HashAggregationOperator` with:

- **Grouping Attributes**: An index pointing to the `department` column.
- **Aggregation Functions**: A list containing one `AggrFunc` where `func` is `AggrFuncType::SUM` and `attr_index` points to the `salary` column.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.028" chapter="13" section="13.2.1 Anatomy of the Aggregation Operator" kind="prose" -->

The central component of the `HashAggregationOperator`'s internal state is its hash table. In BuzzDB, this is an `std::unordered_map`. The map's key represents the grouping key, and its value holds the running state of all aggregate computations for that group. For a query grouping by one or more columns, the key is a `std::vector<Field>`, allowing for composite keys like `GROUP BY department, job_title`. The value is also a `std::vector<Field>`, where each element corresponds to the intermediate state of one of the requested aggregate functions. For example, if the query is `SELECT department, COUNT(*), SUM(salary) ...`, the value vector for the "Engineering" group might look like `{ Field(25), Field(2750000) }`, representing a count of 25 employees and a total salary of $2.75M so far.

This design—a hash table mapping grouping keys to a vector of aggregate states—is both flexible and efficient. It allows the operator to handle arbitrary grouping keys and multiple aggregate functions within a single pass over the input data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.029" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

### 13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table

The fundamental algorithm of the `HashAggregationOperator` is a classic example of stream processing. The operator pulls tuples one by one from its child operator and uses them to build its internal hash table. It doesn't produce any output tuples until its entire input has been consumed. Once the input stream is exhausted, the operator switches modes: subsequent calls to its `next()` method will iterate over the completed hash table and yield the final aggregated rows one at a time.

Let's trace this process with a concrete example. Consider the following query on a small `employees` table:

```sql
SELECT
    department,
    COUNT(*),
    SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.030" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="table" -->

The input tuples stream into the `HashAggregationOperator` as follows:

| name    | department  | salary |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| Alice   | Engineering | 90000  |
| Bob     | Sales       | 75000  |
| Charlie | Engineering | 110000 |
| Diana   | Sales       | 85000  |
| Eve     | Engineering | 95000  |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.031" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="list" -->

The operator's logic for each incoming tuple follows these steps:

1.  **Extract Grouping Key**: From the current tuple, construct the key for the hash table. In this case, the key is the value of the `department` column.
2.  **Probe Hash Table**: Look up this key in the internal hash table.
3.  **Update State**:
    *   If the key is **not found**, this is the first tuple for this group. A new entry is inserted into the hash table. The key is the department name, and the initial value is derived from this first tuple. For `COUNT(*)`, the initial state is `1`. For `SUM(salary)`, it's the salary from this tuple.
    *   If the key **is found**, the operator retrieves the existing aggregate state (the vector of running values) and updates it using the data from the new tuple. The count is incremented, and the new salary is added to the running sum.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.032" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

The following figure illustrates how the hash table evolves as each tuple is processed.

**After processing `(Alice, Engineering, 90000)`:** The "Engineering" key is new. An entry is created with an initial count of 1 and a sum of 90000.

```
          Hash Table
+----------------------------------+
| Key         | Value (count, sum) |
+==================================+
| Engineering | (1, 90000)         |
+----------------------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.033" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

**After processing `(Bob, Sales, 75000)`:** The "Sales" key is new. A second entry is created.

```
          Hash Table
+----------------------------------+
| Key         | Value (count, sum) |
+==================================+
| Engineering | (1, 90000)         |
| Sales       | (1, 75000)         |
+----------------------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.034" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="code" -->

**After processing `(Charlie, Engineering, 110000)`:** The "Engineering" key already exists. The operator retrieves its current value, `(1, 90000)`, and updates it. The new count is `1 + 1 = 2`, and the new sum is `90000 + 110000 = 200000`.

```
          Hash Table
+----------------------------------+
| Key         | Value (count, sum) |
+==================================+
| Engineering | (2, 200000)        |
| Sales       | (1, 75000)         |
+----------------------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.035" chapter="13" section="13.2.2 The Core Logic: Grouping with a Hash Table" kind="prose" -->

This process continues until all input tuples are consumed. The final state of the hash table will contain the complete, correct aggregate values for every group. At this point, the operator is ready to produce its output by simply iterating through the key-value pairs in the table.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.036" chapter="13" section="13.2.3 Hashing Complex Keys" kind="code" -->

### 13.2.3 Hashing Complex Keys

The core of hash aggregation relies on the O(1) average-time performance of hash table lookups. This performance, however, is not guaranteed. It depends entirely on the quality of the hash function—the algorithm used to convert a key into an integer index for the hash table's underlying array. A poor hash function can lead to many "collisions," where different keys map to the same index, forcing the hash table to fall back to a slower linear search.

In BuzzDB, the hash table key is a `std::vector<Field>`, which represents a composite grouping key (e.g., `GROUP BY department, region`). The C++ standard library does not provide a built-in hash function for `std::vector`, let alone a vector of a custom `Field` type. Therefore, BuzzDB must supply its own. This is the role of the `FieldVectorHasher`, a custom functor passed to the `std::unordered_map` to tell it how to handle our specific key type.

```cpp
struct FieldVectorHasher {
    std::size_t operator()(const std::vector<Field>& fields) const {
        std::size_t hash = 0;
        for (const auto& field : fields) {
            std::hash<std::string> hasher;
            std::size_t fieldHash = 0;

            // ... switch statement to hash individual fields ...
            switch (field.type) {
                // ... cases for INT, FLOAT, STRING ...
            }

            // Combine the hash of the current field with the hash so far
            hash ^= fieldHash + 0x9e3779b9 + (hash << 6) + (hash >> 2);
        }
        return hash;
    }
};
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.037" chapter="13" section="13.2.3 Hashing Complex Keys" kind="list" -->

The `operator()` method implements the hashing logic. It iterates through each `Field` in the key vector and performs two main steps:

1.  **Hash Individual Fields**: It first computes a hash for the individual field. The implementation uses a simple but effective strategy: it converts numeric types like `INT` and `FLOAT` to their string representation and then uses the standard library's string hasher. For `STRING` fields, it hashes the content directly. This approach provides a uniform way to get a hash value regardless of the field's underlying type.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.038" chapter="13" section="13.2.3 Hashing Complex Keys" kind="list" -->

2.  **Combine Hashes**: Simply adding the individual field hashes (`hash += fieldHash`) would be a poor combination strategy. For example, the keys `{'Sales', 'Q1'}` and `{'Q1', 'Sales'}` would produce the same final hash, leading to an incorrect collision. To avoid this, the hasher uses a more sophisticated formula to combine the accumulated hash (`hash`) with the hash of the current field (`fieldHash`):
    ```cpp
    hash ^= fieldHash + 0x9e3779b9 + (hash << 6) + (hash >> 2);
    ```
    This line is a well-known pattern for combining hash values, similar to the one used in Boost's `hash_combine` function. It uses bitwise operations (XOR `^`, left shift `<<`, right shift `>>`) and a large prime constant (`0x9e3779b9`, derived from the golden ratio) to thoroughly mix the bits of the new hash into the existing one. This ensures that the order of fields significantly impacts the final hash value, dramatically reducing the probability of collisions and helping maintain the hash table's excellent performance.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.039" chapter="13" section="13.2.4 Updating Aggregate State" kind="code" -->

### 13.2.4 Updating Aggregate State

Once the operator has used the grouping key to find the correct entry in its hash table, it must update the aggregate state. This logic is encapsulated in the `updateAggregate` helper function. This function is called for each aggregate function specified in the query (e.g., one call for `COUNT(*)`, another for `SUM(salary)`) every time a tuple for an existing group is processed.

The function's signature clearly defines its role:

```cpp
Field updateAggregate(const AggrFunc& aggrFunc, const Field& currentAggr, const Field& newValue);
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.040" chapter="13" section="13.2.4 Updating Aggregate State" kind="code" -->

It takes the definition of the aggregation (`aggrFunc`), the current running state for that aggregate (`currentAggr`), and the new value from the tuple being processed (`newValue`). It returns a new `Field` object containing the updated state.

The implementation is a `switch` statement that handles each type of aggregation:

```cpp
switch (aggrFunc.func) {
    case AggrFuncType::COUNT: {
        // For COUNT, simply increment the integer value
        int count = currentAggr.asInt() + 1;
        return Field(count);
    }
    case AggrFuncType::SUM: {
        if (currentAggr.getType() == FieldType::INT) {
            int sum = currentAggr.asInt() + newValue.asInt();
            return Field(sum);
        } // ... else if for FLOAT ...
    }
    // ... cases for MAX and MIN ...
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.041" chapter="13" section="13.2.4 Updating Aggregate State" kind="list" -->

Let's trace its execution for the `SUM(salary)` on the "Engineering" group.

-   **Initial State**: The hash table holds `(2, 200000)` for "Engineering". The `currentAggr` for the `SUM` is `Field(200000)`.
-   **New Tuple**: The tuple `(Eve, Engineering, 95000)` arrives. The `newValue` is `Field(95000)`.
-   **Function Call**: `updateAggregate` is called. Inside, the `SUM` case is triggered.
-   **Calculation**: It executes `currentAggr.asInt() + newValue.asInt()`, which is `200000 + 95000`.
-   **Return Value**: The function returns a new `Field(295000)`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.042" chapter="13" section="13.2.4 Updating Aggregate State" kind="prose" -->

This returned `Field` then replaces the old sum in the hash table's value vector for the "Engineering" key. The logic for `COUNT` is even simpler: it ignores the `newValue` entirely and just increments the `currentAggr` count. The `MAX` and `MIN` cases use `std::max` and `std::min` respectively to compare the current aggregate with the new value and return the appropriate result.

This clean separation of concerns—with `FieldVectorHasher` handling key creation and `updateAggregate` handling value updates—makes the core loop of the `HashAggregationOperator` clear and maintainable. It focuses on the high-level algorithm of probing and updating the hash table, delegating the complex details to these specialized helper components.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.043" chapter="13" section="13.2.4.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

#### 13.2.4.1 Check Your Understanding

1.  **Hash Function Quality**: What would happen to the performance of the `HashAggregationOperator` if the `FieldVectorHasher` simply summed the integer values of all fields? Consider a `GROUP BY` on two integer columns, `(colA, colB)`, where the input contains keys like `(10, 20)` and `(20, 10)`.
2.  **Initial State**: The `updateAggregate` function for `COUNT` increments the current value. What should the *initial* value be for a `COUNT` aggregate when a new group is seen for the first time? How does this differ from the initial value for `SUM`?
3.  **Memory Limitations**: BuzzDB's `HashAggregationOperator` builds its entire hash table in memory before producing any output. Describe a scenario (e.g., in terms of data size or the number of distinct groups) where this in-memory approach would fail. What might be an alternative strategy for a database to handle such a case?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.044" chapter="13" section="13.3 The Pipeline Breaker: A Blocking Operator" kind="prose" -->

## 13.3 The Pipeline Breaker: A Blocking Operator

Imagine a simple assembly line. A worker at the first station places a widget on a conveyor belt. The next worker inspects it for defects and, if it passes, sends it along. The final worker packages the approved widget. In this system, a finished product can roll off the line moments after the first widget is placed on it. The work is continuous, and the stations operate in parallel on different widgets. This is the essence of pipelining in a database query engine. Operators like filters (`WHERE`) and projections (`SELECT`) can often work this way. A `SelectOperator` can receive a tuple from a table scan, check if it matches a condition, and immediately pass it up to the next operator in the query plan if it does. It doesn't need to see all the other tuples in the table to decide about the current one.

Now, imagine the final station's task is different. Instead of packaging each widget, the worker's job is to find the single heaviest widget that came down the line all day. To do this, they can't just package the first one they see. They must wait for every single widget to arrive, weigh each one, and keep track of the heaviest one found so far. Only when the conveyor belt is empty and all widgets have been inspected can they confidently point to the heaviest one and send it to shipping. The flow has been stopped. The entire input must be consumed before a single output can be produced.

This second scenario is precisely what happens with certain database operations, most notably aggregation. An operator tasked with calculating `COUNT(*)` or `SUM(salary)` for different groups cannot produce the final count for the 'Sales' department after seeing only the first 'Sales' employee. It must process every single employee in the input to ensure no more 'Sales' staff are waiting to be counted. This requirement fundamentally changes the execution model. The operator must block the flow of data, consuming its entire input before producing its first result. For this reason, such operators are known as **blocking operators**, or more evocatively, **pipeline breakers**. They introduce a point in the query plan where the smooth, tuple-at-a-time flow of data is forced to halt and collect, a process known as materialization.

Source excerpts:

The open() method, which contains the core logic of the blocking operator. It consumes the entire input to build the hash table before any output can be produced.


<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.046" chapter="13" section="13.3.1 Pipelined vs. Blocking Execution" kind="code" -->

### 13.3.1 Pipelined vs. Blocking Execution

To visualize the difference, let's consider two query plans. A query plan is a tree of operators that the database executes to produce a result. Data flows upwards from the leaves (like table scans) to the root (the final output).

A simple, pipelined query like `SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000` might have a plan that looks like this:

```
      [Output]
         ^
         |
  [Project(name)]
         ^
         |
 [Select(salary > 100k)]
         ^
         |
   [Scan(employees)]
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.047" chapter="13" section="13.3.1 Pipelined vs. Blocking Execution" kind="code" -->

In this model, the `Scan` operator can fetch a single tuple for an employee. The `Select` operator immediately evaluates the `salary` and, if it's greater than 100,000, passes the tuple up to the `Project` operator. The `Project` operator extracts the `name` and sends it to the output. A result can appear almost as soon as the first matching employee is found. The data flows smoothly, like water through a pipe.

Now, consider a query with aggregation: `SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department`. This query requires a blocking operator.

```
      [Output]
         ^
         |
[HashAggregate(AVG(salary))]
         ^
         |
        ---  <-- Pipeline Break
         |
   [Scan(employees)]
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.048" chapter="13" section="13.3.1 Pipelined vs. Blocking Execution" kind="list" -->

The `HashAggregate` operator acts like a dam. The `Scan` operator begins sending employee tuples upwards, one by one. However, the `HashAggregate` operator does not immediately pass anything on. Instead, it consumes each tuple and uses it to build an internal data structure—in BuzzDB's case, a hash table—that tracks the running aggregate values for each department. It continues this process until the `Scan` operator signals that there are no more tuples. Only after the *entire* `employees` table has been processed can the `HashAggregate` operator begin to produce its output, sending the final `(department, average_salary)` tuples upwards.

This distinction is not merely academic; it has profound performance implications.

1.  **Latency to First Result**: In a pipelined plan, the user can start seeing results almost immediately. For a blocking operator, there is a potentially long delay between starting the query and seeing the first output tuple, as the operator must first process its entire input.
2.  **Memory Consumption**: A pipelined `Select` operator needs very little memory—just enough to hold the single tuple it's currently evaluating. A blocking `HashAggregationOperator`, however, must store the intermediate state for every group it has encountered. If a `GROUP BY` is performed on a column with high cardinality (many unique values), the internal hash table can grow very large, consuming significant memory. If this state exceeds available RAM, the system may need to spill intermediate data to disk, incurring a severe performance penalty.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.049" chapter="13" section="13.3.1 Pipelined vs. Blocking Execution" kind="prose" -->

The iterator model, with its `open()`, `next()`, and `close()` methods, provides a uniform interface for all operators, but its implementation for blocking operators is fundamentally different from that of pipelined ones. For a pipelined operator, `open()` performs minimal setup, and each call to `next()` pulls one tuple from its child, processes it, and yields a result. For a blocking operator, the division of labor is skewed: the `open()` method does almost all the work, and `next()` becomes a simple cursor over a pre-computed result set.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.050" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="code" -->

### 13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method

The heart of a blocking operator's implementation is its `open()` method. This is where the pipeline is broken and the input is fully materialized. Let's examine the `HashAggregationOperator::open` method in BuzzDB to see exactly how this is accomplished. When a parent operator calls `open()` on the `HashAggregationOperator`, it doesn't just get back a ready-to-go iterator; it triggers a complete computation.

The method begins with standard setup:

```cpp
   986	    void open() override {
   987	        input->open(); // Ensure the input operator is opened
   988	        output_tuples_index = 0;
   989	        output_tuples.clear();
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.051" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="code" -->

Line 987 is a standard part of the iterator model, recursively opening the child operator. Lines 988 and 989 prepare the operator's internal state for the results that will be generated. The real work starts with the declaration of the hash table.

```cpp
   992	        std::unordered_map<std::vector<Field>, std::vector<Field>, FieldVectorHasher> hash_table;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.052" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="code" -->

This `hash_table` is the core data structure. It will store the intermediate aggregate results. The key is a `std::vector<Field>`, representing the values of the `GROUP BY` columns for a given group (e.g., `{'Sales'}`). The value is another `std::vector<Field>`, which will hold the running state of the aggregate functions (e.g., `COUNT` and `SUM`).

The next block of code is the most critical part of the operator. It is the engine that consumes the input and builds the aggregate state.

```cpp
   994	        while (input->next()) {
   995	            const auto& tuple = input->getOutput();
   996	
   997	            // Extract group keys...
   998	            std::vector<Field> group_keys;
   999	            for (auto& index : group_by_attrs) {
  1000	                group_keys.push_back(*tuple[index]);
  1001	            }
  1002	
  1003	            // Process aggregation functions
  1004	            if (!hash_table.count(group_keys)) {
  1005	                // Initialize aggregate values for a new group
  1006	                std::vector<Field> aggr_values(aggr_funcs.size(), Field(0));
  1007	                hash_table[group_keys] = aggr_values;
  1008	            }
  1009	
  1010	            // Update aggregate values
  1011	            auto& aggr_values = hash_table[group_keys];
  1012	            for (size_t i = 0; i < aggr_funcs.size(); ++i) {
  1013	                aggr_values[i] = updateAggregate(aggr_funcs[i], aggr_values[i], *tuple[aggr_funcs[i].attr_index]);
  1014	            }
  1015	        }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.053" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="list" -->

The `while (input->next())` loop on line 994 is the pipeline break made manifest. This loop will not terminate until the child operator (`input`) has exhausted its entire result set. The call to `open()` will not return to its parent until this loop is finished. Inside the loop, for each tuple that arrives:

1.  **Key Extraction**: Lines 998-1001 construct the `group_keys` vector from the current tuple. This key will be used to look up the group in the `hash_table`.
2.  **Group Initialization**: Line 1004 checks if this is the first time we've seen this group. If `hash_table.count(group_keys)` is false, it means a new group has been found. Lines 1006-1007 initialize the aggregate values for this new group (e.g., setting initial counts and sums to zero) and insert it into the hash table.
3.  **Group Update**: Lines 1011-1014 handle the core aggregation logic. The code retrieves the current aggregate values for the group and calls `updateAggregate` for each aggregate function. This function takes the old value, the new value from the current tuple, and computes the updated aggregate value.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.054" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="table" -->

Let's trace this with a concrete example. Suppose our input is a stream of employee tuples and the query is `SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department`.

| Input Tuple | `group_keys` | `hash_table` State After Processing |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `('Alice', 'Sales')` | `{'Sales'}` | `{'Sales': [1]}` (New group, count initialized to 1) |
| `('Bob', 'Eng')` | `{'Eng'}` | `{'Sales': [1], 'Eng': [1]}` (New group) |
| `('Carol', 'Sales')` | `{'Sales'}` | `{'Sales': [2], 'Eng': [1]}` (Existing group, count incremented) |
| `('Dave', 'Eng')` | `{'Eng'}` | `{'Sales': [2], 'Eng': [2]}` (Existing group, count incremented) |
| `('Eve', 'HR')` | `{'HR'}` | `{'Sales': [2], 'Eng': [2], 'HR': [1]}` (New group) |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.055" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="code" -->

This process continues until `input->next()` returns `false`. At that point, the `hash_table` contains the complete, final aggregate values for every group in the entire dataset. The operator has successfully materialized the aggregation result in memory.

The final step within `open()` is to transform this internal representation into the standard tuple format that the parent operator expects.

```cpp
  1017	        // Prepare output tuples from the hash table
  1018	        for (const auto& entry : hash_table) {
  1019	            const auto& group_keys = entry.first;
  1020	            const auto& aggr_values = entry.second;
  1021	            Tuple output_tuple;
  1022	            // ... add group keys and aggregate values to output_tuple
  1029	            output_tuples.push_back(std::move(output_tuple));
  1030	        }
  1031	    }
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.056" chapter="13" section="13.3.2 Code Deep Dive: The `open()` Method" kind="prose" -->

This loop iterates over every key-value pair in the completed `hash_table`. For each entry, it constructs a final `Tuple` containing the group keys and the final aggregate values and adds it to the `output_tuples` member variable.

When the `open()` method finally returns control to its caller, the `output_tuples` vector holds the entire result set of the aggregation. The blocking work is complete.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.057" chapter="13" section="13.3.3 Producing the Final Result" kind="code" -->

### 13.3.3 Producing the Final Result

After the monumental effort within `open()`, the jobs of `next()` and `getOutput()` are remarkably simple. They no longer need to perform complex calculations or even interact with the child operator. Their role shifts from active computation to passively serving up the pre-computed results. This two-phase process—a "build" phase in `open()` and a "drain" phase in `next()`—is a classic pattern for implementing blocking operators within the iterator model.

A hypothetical `next()` method for our `HashAggregationOperator` would look something like this:

```cpp
// Hypothetical implementation based on the state set up in open()
bool next() override {
    if (output_tuples_index < output_tuples.size()) {
        output_tuples_index++;
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.058" chapter="13" section="13.3.3 Producing the Final Result" kind="code" -->

Each time the parent operator calls `next()`, the method simply checks if the `output_tuples_index` is still within the bounds of the `output_tuples` vector. If it is, it increments the index and returns `true`, signaling that a valid tuple is available. If the index has reached the end of the vector, it returns `false`, indicating that all results have been produced.

Similarly, the `getOutput()` method becomes a trivial lookup:

```cpp
// Hypothetical implementation
const Tuple& getOutput() const override {
    // Assumes next() was called and returned true
    return output_tuples[output_tuples_index - 1];
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.059" chapter="13" section="13.3.3 Producing the Final Result" kind="prose" -->

It simply returns a reference to the tuple at the current position in the `output_tuples` vector.

This separation of concerns is elegant. The complexity of aggregation is entirely encapsulated within the `open()` method. The `next()` and `getOutput()` methods adhere to the simple, non-blocking contract that the parent operator expects, even though the operator as a whole is blocking. The parent operator can pull tuples one at a time, unaware of the massive computation that occurred just to enable the first call to `next()` to succeed.

This design highlights the power and flexibility of the iterator model. It provides a uniform interface that can accommodate both streaming, pipelined operators and complex, blocking, materializing operators. Understanding this pattern is key to understanding how a database can compose simple building blocks into a powerful engine capable of executing complex analytical queries. The pipeline breaker, while disruptive to the flow of data, is an essential and powerful tool for set-oriented operations that are the foundation of relational query processing.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.060" chapter="13" section="13.3.3.1 Check Your Understanding" kind="list" -->

#### 13.3.3.1 Check Your Understanding

1.  **Memory Pressure:** The `HashAggregationOperator` builds its `hash_table` in memory. What are the potential consequences if the query involves grouping by a column with very high cardinality (e.g., a `user_id` column in a table with millions of unique users)? How might a production database system handle a situation where the hash table exceeds available RAM?
2.  **Extending Aggregates:** The provided code initializes aggregate values with `Field(0)`. This works well for `SUM` and can be adapted for `COUNT`. How would you need to change the state stored in the `hash_table`'s value (the `std::vector<Field>`) to correctly compute `AVG(salary)`? What information would the `updateAggregate` function need to maintain for each group?
3.  **Alternative Strategies:** Hash aggregation is not the only way to implement a `GROUP BY` clause. Another common strategy is sort-based aggregation, where the data is first sorted on the grouping keys. Once sorted, all tuples for a given group are contiguous, and aggregates can be computed with a single pass over the sorted data. Is a sort-based aggregation operator also a blocking operator? Why or why not?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.061" chapter="13" section="13.4 Assembling an Aggregation Query Plan" kind="prose" -->

## 13.4 Assembling an Aggregation Query Plan

In our journey so far, we have built a simple but effective query execution engine. Using a `ScanOperator` to read data from disk and a `SelectOperator` to filter it, we can answer basic questions that inspect individual records. For example, we can find all employees hired after a certain date or all sales transactions over a certain value. The operators work together in a clean, pipelined fashion: the `ScanOperator` produces a tuple, the `SelectOperator` consumes and evaluates it, and if it passes the filter, the tuple is immediately available as an output. This process repeats, one tuple at a time, until the data source is exhausted.

This tuple-at-a-time model is elegant and efficient for filtering, but it has a fundamental limitation. It cannot answer questions about the dataset as a whole. We can find *which* sales were large, but we cannot easily find the *total* sales for each product. We can list the employees in each department, but we cannot *count* how many there are. These operations—`SUM`, `COUNT`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`—are known as aggregate functions. They don't operate on a single tuple in isolation; they operate on groups of tuples, summarizing them into a single result.

To support aggregation, we need a new kind of operator, one that can consume many tuples and produce just a few. This operator must gather and hold onto information from all relevant input tuples before it can produce its final summary. In the previous section, we designed and built the `HashAggregationOperator` for this exact purpose. Now, we will see how this powerful new component fits into BuzzDB’s execution engine. By composing it with our existing operators, we can construct a query plan that goes beyond simple filtering to perform sophisticated, set-oriented analysis.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.064" chapter="13" section="13.4.1 From Filtering to Aggregation" kind="prose" -->

### 13.4.1 From Filtering to Aggregation

The beauty of the iterator model is its composability. A well-designed operator doesn't need to know the specific implementation of its children or its parent; it only needs to rely on the standard `open()`, `next()`, and `close()` interface. This allows us to "stack" operators to build increasingly complex query plans without rewriting the components.

Let's see this principle in action by comparing the query execution logic in BuzzDB before and after the introduction of the `HashAggregationOperator`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.065" chapter="13" section="13.4.1.1 The Plan Before: A Simple Filter" kind="code" -->

#### 13.4.1.1 The Plan Before: A Simple Filter

In an earlier version of BuzzDB, the `executeQuery` method implemented a straightforward scan-and-filter plan. Its goal was to read all tuples from a table, apply a predicate to filter out unwanted ones, and print the survivors.

The core of the execution logic looked like this:

```cpp
// From 39-buzzdb.cpp
// ... SelectOperator is created ...

selectOperator.open();
while (selectOperator.next()) {
    const auto& fields = selectOperator.getOutput();
    for (const auto& field_ptr : fields) {
        field_ptr->print();
        std::cout << " ";
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}
selectOperator.close();
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.066" chapter="13" section="13.4.1.1 The Plan Before: A Simple Filter" kind="prose" -->

This code is a direct implementation of the pipelined iterator model. The `SelectOperator` sits at the top of this simple plan. The `while` loop repeatedly calls `next()` on it, pulling one tuple at a time up through the operator tree. The `SelectOperator`, in turn, calls `next()` on its child, the `ScanOperator`, to get raw tuples from the disk. The flow is simple, memory usage is low (we only need to hold one tuple at a time), and results can be produced as soon as the first matching tuple is found.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.067" chapter="13" section="13.4.1.2 The Plan After: Adding Aggregation" kind="code" -->

#### 13.4.1.2 The Plan After: Adding Aggregation

Now, let's look at how `executeQuery` changes to support a `GROUP BY` query. The goal is no longer to print individual filtered tuples, but to group them by a specific attribute (e.g., a department ID) and compute an aggregate (e.g., the sum of salaries) for each group.

The new execution logic constructs a three-layer operator tree: `Scan -> Select -> Aggregate`.

```cpp
// From 41-buzzdb.cpp
// ... ScanOperator and SelectOperator are created ...

std::vector<AggrFunc> aggrFuncs{
    {AggrFuncType::SUM, 1}, // Summing the values of the second attribute
};

std::vector<size_t> groupByAttrs{0}; // Group by the first attribute

HashAggregationOperator hashAggregationOperator(selectOperator, groupByAttrs, aggrFuncs);

hashAggregationOperator.open(); // Prepare the operator, perform aggregations
while (hashAggregationOperator.next()) {
    const auto& aggregatedFields = hashAggregationOperator.getOutput(); // Get aggregated results

    std::cout << "Key: ";
    aggregatedFields[0]->print();
    std::cout << ", Value: ";
    aggregatedFields[1]->print();
    std::cout << "\n";
}
hashAggregationOperator.close(); // Cleanup
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.068" chapter="13" section="13.4.1.2 The Plan After: Adding Aggregation" kind="prose" -->

Comparing the two versions reveals the power of composition. The `ScanOperator` and `SelectOperator` remain completely unchanged. We simply introduce the `HashAggregationOperator` as a new parent, wrapping the `selectOperator`.

Notice the key structural change in the execution loop. The client code—the `while` loop—no longer interacts with `selectOperator`. Instead, it treats `hashAggregationOperator` as the root of the plan. It calls `open()`, `next()`, and `close()` on this new top-level operator. The `HashAggregationOperator` is now responsible for driving the execution of its children. The `selectOperator` is still doing the exact same work as before, but now it serves tuples to the aggregation operator instead of directly to the client. This plug-and-play capability is the hallmark of a flexible, extensible query execution engine.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.069" chapter="13" section="13.4.2 Tracing the Data Flow" kind="prose" -->

### 13.4.2 Tracing the Data Flow

While the *interface* for all operators is the same, the internal *behavior* of the `HashAggregationOperator` creates a profoundly different data flow. The `Scan` and `Select` operators are pure "pipelining" operators; they process tuples one by one without needing to see the entire dataset. The `HashAggregationOperator`, however, is a **blocking operator**, also known as a **pipeline breaker**. It must consume its *entire* input before it can produce its first row of output. To calculate the total sum for a group, it must first see every single member of that group.

This blocking nature divides the query execution into two distinct phases: a materialization phase where the operator builds its internal state, and an output phase where it emits the final results.

Let's trace the execution of our `Scan -> Select -> Aggregate` plan to see how this works. Imagine our query is analyzing a small `sales` table to find the total quantity sold for each product ID, but only for sales where the product ID is between 2 and 7.

**`sales` table:**

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.070" chapter="13" section="13.4.2 Tracing the Data Flow" kind="table" -->

| product_id | quantity |
| :--------- | :------- |
| 1          | 10       |
| 3          | 5        |
| 5          | 20       |
| 3          | 15       |
| 8          | 100      |
| 5          | 30       |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.071" chapter="13" section="13.4.2 Tracing the Data Flow" kind="code" -->

The query plan can be visualized as a stack of operators. The client at the top only interacts with the root of the tree.

```ascii
      [executeQuery loop]
              |
              v
+---------------------------+
| HashAggregationOperator   |  (Groups by product_id, SUMs quantity)
+---------------------------+
              ^
              |
+---------------------------+
|      SelectOperator       |  (Filters for product_id > 2 AND < 7)
+---------------------------+
              ^
              |
+---------------------------+
|       ScanOperator        |  (Reads from the 'sales' table)
+---------------------------+
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.072" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.1 Phase 1: Materialization" kind="list" -->

#### 13.4.2.1 Phase 1: Materialization

This phase is triggered by a single call: `hashAggregationOperator.open()`. Although it's just one line of code from the client's perspective, it sets off a chain reaction that consumes the entire input dataset.

1.  **`executeQuery` calls `hashAggregationOperator.open()`.**
2.  The `HashAggregationOperator` must prepare to receive data. As part of its own `open()` logic, it first calls `open()` on its child, the `selectOperator`.
3.  The `SelectOperator` does the same, calling `open()` on its child, the `scanOperator`. The `ScanOperator` prepares to read the first page of the `sales` table from disk. The pipeline is now initialized.
4.  Now, the crucial step occurs inside `hashAggregationOperator.open()`. It enters an internal `while` loop that repeatedly calls `selectOperator.next()`. This is the "pull" that drives the materialization.
5.  Let's trace the first tuple. `hashAggregationOperator` calls `selectOperator.next()`.
    *   `selectOperator` calls `scanOperator.next()`, which reads the first tuple: `{1, 10}`.
    *   `selectOperator` applies its predicate (`product_id > 2 AND < 7`). The tuple `{1, 10}` fails this test. The `selectOperator` loops, calling `scanOperator.next()` again.
6.  The `scanOperator` reads the second tuple: `{3, 5}`.
    *   This tuple passes the `selectOperator`'s filter. The `selectOperator` returns `true`, and its output buffer now holds `{3, 5}`.
7.  Control returns to the `hashAggregationOperator`'s internal loop. It receives the tuple `{3, 5}`.
    *   It extracts the group key, `product_id = 3`.
    *   It looks up `3` in its internal hash table. It's not there, so it creates a new entry: `3 -> {sum: 5}`.
8.  The `hashAggregationOperator`'s loop continues, calling `selectOperator.next()` again. This process repeats for the entire table:
    *   `{5, 20}` is read and passed by `Select`. The hash table is updated: `5 -> {sum: 20}`.
    *   `{3, 15}` is read and passed by `Select`. The hash table entry for key `3` is found and updated: `3 -> {sum: 5 + 15 = 20}`.
    *   `{8, 100}` is read but rejected by `Select`.
    *   `{5, 30}` is read and passed by `Select`. The hash table entry for key `5` is updated: `5 -> {sum: 20 + 30 = 50}`.
9.  Finally, the `scanOperator` reaches the end of the table and its `next()` method returns `false`. This `false` propagates up to the `selectOperator`, which in turn returns `false` to the `hashAggregationOperator`.
10. The internal `while` loop inside `hashAggregationOperator.open()` terminates. The materialization phase is complete. The operator's internal state now contains the final, aggregated results.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.073" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.1 Phase 1: Materialization" kind="table" -->

**`HashAggregationOperator` Internal State (after `open()`):**

| Key (product_id) | Aggregate State (SUM) |
| :--------------- | :-------------------- |
| 3                | 20                    |
| 5                | 50                    |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.074" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.1 Phase 1: Materialization" kind="prose" -->

Only now, after all this work, does the `hashAggregationOperator.open()` method finally return control to the `executeQuery` function.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.075" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output" kind="code" -->

#### 13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output

With the aggregates fully computed and stored in memory, the `executeQuery` function's main loop can begin.

```cpp
while (hashAggregationOperator.next()) {
    // ... get and print output
}
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.076" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output" kind="list" -->

This phase is much simpler. The `HashAggregationOperator` has already done the hard work. It now acts like a simple iterator over its materialized results.

1.  **First call to `hashAggregationOperator.next()`:**
    *   The operator consults its internal hash table iterator. Let's say it points to the entry for key `3`.
    *   It constructs an output tuple from the key and the final aggregate value: `{3, 20}`.
    *   It advances its internal iterator to the next entry (key `5`).
    *   It returns `true`.
    *   The `executeQuery` loop then calls `getOutput()` to retrieve `{3, 20}` and prints it.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.077" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output" kind="list" -->

2.  **Second call to `hashAggregationOperator.next()`:**
    *   The operator's internal iterator is already pointing at the entry for key `5`.
    *   It constructs the output tuple `{5, 50}`.
    *   It advances its iterator. The iterator now reaches the end of the hash table's contents.
    *   It returns `true`.
    *   The loop retrieves and prints `{5, 50}`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.078" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output" kind="list" -->

3.  **Third call to `hashAggregationOperator.next()`:**
    *   The operator's internal iterator has already reached the end.
    *   It returns `false`.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.079" chapter="13" section="13.4.2.2 Phase 2: Output" kind="quote" -->

The `while` loop in `executeQuery` terminates. The query is complete. The final step is the call to `hashAggregationOperator.close()`, which cascades down the tree, allowing each operator to release any resources it holds.

This two-phase process—materialize then iterate—is the defining characteristic of a query plan with a blocking operator. It's a powerful pattern but comes with an important trade-off: the blocking operator may require a significant amount of memory to store its intermediate state (the hash table, in this case). If the number of distinct groups is very large, this could become a performance bottleneck, a challenge that more advanced database systems address with techniques we will explore in later chapters.

By adding just one new, composable operator, we have dramatically expanded the capabilities of BuzzDB, transforming it from a simple filter into an analytical engine.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> 1.  **Average Calculation:** Suppose you were implementing the `AVG` aggregate function. Why would this still require a blocking operator? What two pieces of information would the operator need to store for each group in its hash table to compute the final average?
> 2.  **Plan Execution:** In the v041 `executeQuery` code, what would happen if the `while` loop mistakenly called `selectOperator.next()` instead of `hashAggregationOperator.next()`? What would the output look like for our example `sales` table?
> 3.  **Memory Usage:** Consider a query that calculates `COUNT(*)` for a table with 1 billion rows and 100 million unique groups. What is the primary memory pressure created by the `HashAggregationOperator` in this scenario?

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.080" chapter="13" section="13.5 Broader Context and Alternative Strategies" kind="prose" -->

## 13.5 Broader Context and Alternative Strategies

In the previous section, we dissected BuzzDB’s `HashAggregationOperator`. It is an elegant and effective implementation of a core database feature. The logic is straightforward: as it pulls tuples from its child operator, it uses an in-memory hash table to collect them into groups. For each tuple, it extracts the `GROUP BY` key, hashes it, finds the corresponding entry in the table, and updates the running aggregate values. Once the entire input has been consumed, the operator iterates through the hash table and transforms the completed groups into output tuples.

This design is a perfect example of a *blocking operator*. The call to `open()` does all the work, reading every single input tuple before the first call to `next()` can return a result. You can see this clearly in the implementation: the `while (input->next())` loop on line 994 must complete and populate the `hash_table` before the operator can even begin to prepare its `output_tuples`.

This approach works wonderfully as long as one critical assumption holds: the hash table, which contains one entry for every distinct group, must fit entirely in main memory. For a query like `SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY country`, this is a safe bet. There are fewer than 200 countries in the world; the hash table will be trivially small. But what about a query like `SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM web_logs GROUP BY user_id` on a table with billions of rows and millions of unique users? The `hash_table` could easily grow to consume gigabytes of RAM, potentially exhausting available memory and causing the entire query to fail.

Source excerpts:

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.084" chapter="13" section="13.5 Broader Context and Alternative Strategies" kind="prose" -->

This pressure—the need to process datasets that are larger than main memory—is one of the defining challenges in database system design. It forces us to look beyond simple in-memory data structures and consider algorithms that can gracefully "spill" to disk. For aggregation, the most important alternative to hashing is an approach based on sorting.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.085" chapter="13" section="13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation" kind="code" -->

### 13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation

Instead of using a hash table to logically bring tuples with the same key together, a sorting-based approach physically rearranges the data. If we sort the entire dataset by the `GROUP BY` key(s), all tuples belonging to the same group will become adjacent to one another in the sorted output. This simple fact allows us to compute aggregates with a single, efficient scan over the sorted data.

The algorithm works like a state machine. It reads one tuple at a time from the sorted input, keeping track of the "current" group's key and its running aggregate values. When it encounters a tuple whose key is different from the current group's key, it knows that the previous group is complete. At that moment, it can emit the final aggregate result for the completed group and then initialize a new group using the data from the tuple it just read.

Let's trace this process with a concrete example. Imagine we have an `Employees` table and we want to run the following query:

```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department;
```

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.086" chapter="13" section="13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation" kind="table" -->

Suppose our `Employees` table contains the following unsorted data:

| EmpID | Name | Department |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 101 | Alice | Engineering |
| 102 | Bob | Sales |
| 103 | Charlie | Engineering |
| 104 | Diana | HR |
| 105 | Eve | Sales |
| 106 | Frank | Engineering |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.087" chapter="13" section="13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation" kind="table" -->

**Step 1: Sort the Data**

The first step is to sort the entire table based on the `GROUP BY` key, which is `department`. The result is a new, temporary arrangement of the data where all employees in the same department are contiguous.

| EmpID | Name | Department |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 101 | Alice | Engineering |
| 103 | Charlie | Engineering |
| 106 | Frank | Engineering |
| 104 | Diana | HR |
| 102 | Bob | Sales |
| 105 | Eve | Sales |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.088" chapter="13" section="13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation" kind="list" -->

**Step 2: Scan and Aggregate**

Now, the aggregation operator can scan this sorted run. It only needs to maintain two pieces of state: the key of the group it's currently processing (`current_department`) and the running aggregate value (`current_count`).

1.  **Initialize:** `current_department` is `NULL`, `current_count` is `0`.
2.  **Read Row 1:** `(101, Alice, Engineering)`. The department 'Engineering' is different from `current_department`. This marks the start of a new group.
    *   Set `current_department = 'Engineering'`.
    *   Set `current_count = 1`.
3.  **Read Row 2:** `(103, Charlie, Engineering)`. The department 'Engineering' matches `current_department`. We are still in the same group.
    *   Increment `current_count` to `2`.
4.  **Read Row 3:** `(106, Frank, Engineering)`. The department 'Engineering' still matches.
    *   Increment `current_count` to `3`.
5.  **Read Row 4:** `(104, Diana, HR)`. The department 'HR' is different from `current_department` ('Engineering'). This signals the end of the 'Engineering' group.
    *   **Emit Output Row: `('Engineering', 3)`**.
    *   Start a new group for 'HR'. Set `current_department = 'HR'` and `current_count = 1`.
6.  **Read Row 5:** `(102, Bob, Sales)`. The department 'Sales' is different from `current_department` ('HR'). The 'HR' group is finished.
    *   **Emit Output Row: `('HR', 1)`**.
    *   Start a new group for 'Sales'. Set `current_department = 'Sales'` and `current_count = 1`.
7.  **Read Row 6:** `(105, Eve, Sales)`. The department 'Sales' matches `current_department`.
    *   Increment `current_count` to `2`.
8.  **End of Input:** There are no more rows to read. The last group we were processing ('Sales') is now complete.
    *   **Emit Output Row: `('Sales', 2)`**.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.089" chapter="13" section="13.5.1 Alternative: Sorting-Based Aggregation" kind="prose" -->

This scan-based approach requires very little memory for the aggregation step itself—just enough to hold the state for a single group. The main cost is the initial sort. Crucially, database systems are not limited to in-memory sorting. They employ a technique called *external merge sort* to sort datasets that are far too large to fit in RAM. This algorithm works by making multiple passes over the data, creating smaller, sorted chunks (called "runs") on disk and then progressively merging them into a single sorted output. While a full discussion of external sorting is a topic for another chapter, its existence is what makes sorting-based aggregation a robust and scalable strategy, unlike the simple in-memory hash aggregation in BuzzDB, which fails when memory is exhausted.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.090" chapter="13" section="13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs" kind="list" -->

### 13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs

We now have two fundamentally different algorithms for aggregation. BuzzDB uses hashing, while many industrial-strength systems can use either hashing or sorting, letting the query optimizer choose the best strategy based on the query, the data, and the system's state. The choice is a classic engineering trade-off, balancing memory usage, I/O patterns, and other performance characteristics.

**Memory Usage**

The most significant difference lies in how the two algorithms use memory.

*   **Hashing:** As we've seen in BuzzDB's `HashAggregationOperator`, memory consumption is directly proportional to the number of distinct groups. The `std::unordered_map<..., FieldVectorHasher> hash_table` on line 992 stores one key-value pair for each unique `GROUP BY` key. This is highly efficient for low-cardinality keys (e.g., `GROUP BY status`, where status is one of a few fixed values) but becomes a liability for high-cardinality keys (e.g., `GROUP BY session_id`).
*   **Sorting:** The memory required for the final aggregation *scan* is constant and minimal. The main memory consumer is the sort operation itself. A fully in-memory sort would require enough RAM to hold the entire dataset. However, an external sort can operate with a fixed-size memory buffer, using it to create and merge runs on disk. Its memory footprint is therefore determined by the buffer size allocated by the system, not by the cardinality of the data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.091" chapter="13" section="13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs" kind="list" -->

**I/O and CPU Patterns**

*   **Hashing:** A simple in-memory hash aggregation performs a single pass over the input data. Its access pattern within the hash table is random, which is fast for in-memory operations. However, if the hash table grows so large that the operating system begins to page it to virtual memory on disk, this random access pattern becomes catastrophically slow, a phenomenon known as thrashing. The CPU cost is dominated by computing hashes for each key and managing the hash table data structure.
*   **Sorting:** An external sort performs multiple passes over the data, but its I/O is almost entirely sequential—reading unsorted data, writing sorted runs, and reading runs to merge them. Sequential I/O is orders of magnitude faster than random I/O, especially on traditional spinning disks. The final aggregation is also a single sequential scan. The CPU cost is dominated by the comparisons required to sort the data.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.092" chapter="13" section="13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs" kind="list" -->

**Output Order**

A subtle but important side effect is the order of the results.

*   **Hashing:** The output of a hash-based aggregation is inherently unordered. The final loop in BuzzDB's `open()` method (lines 1018-1030) iterates over the `hash_table`'s elements. The C++ standard provides no guarantee on the iteration order of `std::unordered_map`. If a user submits a query like `SELECT department, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY department ORDER BY department`, the database must perform the aggregation and then add a completely separate `SortOperator` to the query plan to order the results.
*   **Sorting:** A sorting-based aggregation produces results that are naturally sorted by the `GROUP BY` key. This is a powerful synergy. For the same query, the database can use a single sort operation to satisfy both the `GROUP BY` and the `ORDER BY` clauses. The aggregation scan is performed on the sorted data, and the results are already in the desired order, eliminating the need for a second, costly sort.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.093" chapter="13" section="13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs" kind="table" -->

The following table summarizes these trade-offs:

| Feature | Hashing-Based Aggregation (e.g., BuzzDB) | Sorting-Based Aggregation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Memory Usage** | Proportional to the number of distinct groups. Excellent for low-cardinality keys. | Requires memory for sorting (can be a fixed-size buffer for external sort). Independent of group cardinality. |
| **I/O Pattern** | One pass over the data. Random memory access. Can be slow if hash table pages to disk. | Multiple sequential passes for external sort. Final aggregation is one sequential scan. |
| **Output Order** | Unordered. Requires a separate sort step for `ORDER BY`. | Naturally ordered by the `GROUP BY` key(s). |
| **Handling Data > Memory** | Simple in-memory versions (like BuzzDB's) fail. Requires complex "spilling" logic (e.g., partitioned hashing). | Handled gracefully by external sorting algorithms. |
| **CPU Cost** | Dominated by hash computations and hash table lookups/insertions. | Dominated by tuple comparisons during the sort phase. |

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.094" chapter="13" section="13.5.2 Hashing vs. Sorting: The Trade-offs" kind="prose" -->

For a simple educational database like BuzzDB, implementing hash aggregation first is a sensible choice. It's conceptually clean and performs very well on smaller datasets with low-cardinality groups. But for a system to be robust, it must be prepared for the worst-case scenario. Sorting-based aggregation provides that robustness, ensuring that queries can complete successfully even when the data is much larger than memory.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.095" chapter="13" section="13.5.3 Beyond Aggregation: Duplicate Elimination" kind="list" -->

### 13.5.3 Beyond Aggregation: Duplicate Elimination

The algorithmic patterns of hashing and sorting are not limited to `GROUP BY` queries. They are fundamental tools for any set-oriented operation. The most common of these is duplicate elimination, as requested by the `SELECT DISTINCT` clause in SQL.

Consider the query `SELECT DISTINCT department, manager FROM Employees`. The goal is to produce a list of unique `(department, manager)` pairs. This problem is structurally identical to aggregation. We can think of it as grouping the data by *all* the selected columns and then, for each group, returning just one representative row. In other words, `SELECT DISTINCT c1, c2` is semantically equivalent to `SELECT c1, c2 ... GROUP BY c1, c2` with no aggregate functions.

Because the problems are the same, the solutions are the same:

1.  **Hashing-Based Duplicate Elimination:** The operator maintains an in-memory hash set. For each input tuple, it attempts to insert it into the set. If the insertion succeeds, the tuple is a new, unique value, and it is passed along as output. If the tuple is already in the set, the insertion fails, and the input tuple is discarded as a duplicate.
2.  **Sorting-Based Duplicate Elimination:** The operator first sorts the entire input stream based on all the relevant columns. Then, it performs a linear scan. It keeps track of the last unique tuple it emitted. If the current input tuple is identical to the last one, it's a duplicate and is discarded. If it's different, it's a new unique value, so it is emitted, and the operator updates its state to remember it as the "last seen" tuple.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.096" chapter="13" section="13.5.3 Beyond Aggregation: Duplicate Elimination" kind="quote" -->

This connection explains a classic piece of SQL performance advice regarding the `UNION` and `UNION ALL` operators. `UNION ALL` takes the results of two queries and simply concatenates them. It is a fast, streaming operation that does not need to see all the data before producing output. `UNION`, however, is defined by the SQL standard to have *set semantics*: it must concatenate the results *and then eliminate all duplicate rows*.

This duplicate elimination step is expensive. To implement it, the database must fully materialize the results of both sides of the `UNION`, then apply one of the blocking algorithms we've discussed. It will either sort the entire combined result set or build a hash table of it to find the unique rows. Both options require significant memory and CPU time, and they prevent any results from being returned to the user until the entire process is complete.

> #### Check Your Understanding
>
> A colleague is writing a query to combine sales data from 2022 and 2023. They know for a fact that there are no overlapping records between the two years because the primary key includes the transaction date. They write the following query:
>
> ```sql
> (SELECT * FROM sales_2022)
> UNION
> (SELECT * FROM sales_2023);
> ```
>
> You suggest changing `UNION` to `UNION ALL`. Explain, in terms of query execution operators and their costs, why your suggestion will likely make the query run much faster.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch13.097" chapter="13" section="13.5.3 Beyond Aggregation: Duplicate Elimination" kind="prose" -->

By choosing to implement a hash-based operator, BuzzDB provides a powerful tool for set-oriented queries. But as we've seen, this is just one side of the story. Understanding the trade-offs between hashing and sorting is essential for appreciating how real-world database systems deliver robust performance across a wide variety of queries and data scales. These same algorithmic choices will reappear when we consider other complex operators, such as the joins used to combine data from multiple tables.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch14.001" chapter="14" section="Chapter 14. From Logical Operators to Physical Execution" kind="prose" -->

# Chapter 14. From Logical Operators to Physical Execution

A database system must translate a user's declarative query into an efficient, step-by-step execution plan. This chapter explores how to build a query plan from modular operators and contrasts this flexible, interpretive approach with a faster, hand-coded 'compiled' query.

<!-- tokensmith:chunk id="ch14.002" chapter="14" section="14.1 The Query Translation Problem" kind="prose" -->

## 14.1 The Query Translation Problem

A database management system exists to answer questions. A user poses a question, usually in a high-level, declarative language like SQL, and the system provides a correct and timely answer. The user's focus is on the *what*: "What are the names of all students majoring in Computer Science?" They are not concerned with the *how*: the intricate sequence of steps the database must perform to find those names. This separation is one of the most powerful abstractions in data management. It frees users from needing to know about file layouts, memory management, or search algorithms.

This convenience, however, creates a fundamental challenge for the database implementer. The system cannot simply "understand" the user's intent. It must translate the declarative "what" into a procedural "how." This procedural recipe, known as a **query plan** or **execution plan**, is a sequence of concrete operations that, when executed, will produce the correct answer. For any non-trivial query, there isn't just one possible plan; there are many. A modern database might consider thousands or even millions of potential plans for a single complex SQL query.

The choice of plan is critical because the performance difference between a good plan and a bad one can be staggering. A query that could complete in milliseconds with an efficient plan might take hours or even days with a naive one. The central task of the database's **query processor** is to navigate this vast space of possible plans and find one that is not just correct, but efficient. This translation from a simple question to a sophisticated, high-performance answer is the core of query processing.

Source excerpts:
